akv-p1.s: Guthrun, Gjuki's daughter, avenged her brothers, as is well known. First she killed Atli's sons, and after that she killed Atli and burned the hall with his whole company. This poem was made about it:

l: Long ago Atli | sent to Gunnar
a keen-witted rider, | Knefröth men called him;
he came to Gjuki's home | and to Gunnar's dwelling,
with benches round the hearth, | and to the beer so sweet.
Then the followers, hiding | their falseness, all drank
their wine in the war-hall, | wary of the Huns' wrath;
and Knefröth spoke loudly, | his words were crafty,
the hero from the south, | sitting on the high bench:
"Now Atli has sent me | to ride on his errand,
on my bit-champing horse | through secret Myrkvidr,
to invite you, Gunnar, | to come to his benches,
with helmets round the hearth, | and to visit Atli's home.
"There you shall choose shields | and shafts of ash-wood,
gold-adorned helmets | and slaves from Hunland,
silver-gilt saddle-cloths, | shirts of bright scarlet,
lances and spears too, | and bit-champing horses.
"You shall be given the field | of wide Gnitaheith,
with loud-ringing lances | and stems overlaid with gold,
very great treasures | and the home of Danp,
and the mighty forest | that is called Myrkvidr."
Gunnar turned his head | and said to Hogni:
"What is your advice, young hero, | when we hear such things?
I know of no gold | lying on Gnitaheith
so fine that we do not have | its equal ourselves.
"We have seven halls, | each one full of swords,
(and the hilt of each | is all of gold;)
my horse is the swiftest, | my sword the sharpest,
my bows adorn the benches, | my mail-coats are golden,
my helmet is the brightest | that came from Kjar's hall,
(my own is better | than all the Huns' treasure.)"
Hogni said:
"What does she mean to say, | sending us a ring
woven with a wolf's hair? | I think it is a warning;
in the red ring I found | a hair of the heath-dweller;
our road will be wolf-like | if we ride on this journey."
His comrades were not eager, | nor the men of his kin,
neither the wise nor the wary, | nor the bold warriors.
But Gunnar spoke out | as befitted a king,
noble in the beer-hall, | and bitter was his scorn:
"Step forward now, Fjornir! | and here onto the floor
you shall bring the warriors | the beakers all of gold.
"Then the wolves shall rule | the wealth of the Niflungs,
wolves old and grey, | if Gunnar is lost,
and black-coated bears | shall bite with tearing teeth
and gladden the dogs, | if Gunnar does not return."
A gallant company | set out with the ruler,
yet they wept as they left | their home with the hero;
and Hogni's little heir | called out loudly:
"Go safely now, wise ones, | wherever you wish!"
Then the bold heroes let | their bit-champing horses
gallop over the mountains | and through secret Myrkvidr;
all Hunland shook | where the hard-souled ones rode;
on the whip-fearers they went | through fields that were green.
Then they saw Atli's halls | and his high watch-towers;
on the lofty walls | stood the warriors of Buthli;
the hall of the southerners | was surrounded with seats,
with bound bucklers | and shields very bright.
Among weapons and lances | Atli drank his wine
in the war-hall; | outside were his watchmen,
waiting for Gunnar, | if he should come out;
with their ringing spears | they would fight the ruler.
Their sister saw this | as soon as her brothers
had entered the hall; | she had drunk little ale:
"You are betrayed, Gunnar! | What defence have you, hero,
against the plots of the Huns? | Flee the hall quickly!
"Brother, it would have been far better | to come in a mail-coat,
with your household helmeted, | to see Atli's home,
and to sit in the saddle | all day beneath the sun,
(so that the sword-norns might weep | for the death-pale warriors,
and the Hunnish shield-maids | might not shun the sword,)
and to send Atli himself | to the den of snakes;
(now the den of snakes | is destined for you.)"
Gunnar said:
"It is too late, sister, | to summon the Niflungs;
it is a long way to reach | the throng of our comrades,
the gallant heroes, | from the hills of the Rhine."
Then they seized Gunnar | and set him in chains,
the king of the Burgundians, | and bound him fast.
Hogni killed seven | with his keen sword,
and an eighth he flung | into the hot fire;
that is how a hero | should fight his enemies,
as Hogni fought | on Gunnar's behalf.
They asked the leader | if he wished to buy
his life with gold, | the king of the Goths.
Gunnar said:
"First you shall lay | the heart of Hogni in my hands,
all bloody, cut | from the breast of the bold one
with a keen-biting sword, | from the son of the king."
They cut out the heart | from the breast of Hjalli,
they carried it on a platter | and brought it to Gunnar.
Then Gunnar spoke out, | the lord of the people:
"Here I have the heart | of Hjalli the coward,
unlike the heart | of Hogni the brave,
for it still trembles | as it stands on the platter;
it trembled twice as much | in the breast of the man."
Then Hogni laughed | when they cut out the heart
of the living helm-hammerer; | he had no tears.
They carried it on a platter | and brought it to Gunnar.
Then Gunnar spoke out, | the spear of the Niflungs:
"Here I have the heart | of Hogni the brave,
unlike the heart | of Hjalli the coward;
it trembles little | as it lies on the platter,
and it trembled still less | when it lay in his breast.
"As far, Atli, | from all men's eyes
shall you be as you | .....from the gold.
"To no one but me | is the secret known
of the Niflungs' hoard, | now Hogni is dead;
once there were two of us, | while we both were alive;
now there is none but me, | for I alone am living.
"The swift Rhine shall keep | the strife-gold of heroes,
that once was the gods', | the wealth of the Niflungs;
in the depths of the waters | the death-rings shall glitter,
and not shine on the hands | of the Hunnish men."
Atli said:
"Bring the wagon, | for now he is bound."
On long-maned Glaum | rode Atli the great,
about him were warriors | .......
But Guthrun, akin | to the gods of slaughter,
did not give way to her tears | in the hall of tumult.
Guthrun said:
"It shall go with you, Atli, | as you kept with Gunnar
the oaths often sworn | and made firm long ago,
by the sun in the south, | by Sigtyr's mountain,
by the horse of the rest-bed | and the ring of Ull."
Then the champer of bits | drew the great chieftain,
the gold-guarder, down | to the place of death.
By the host of warriors | the living hero
was cast into the den | where serpents
were crawling about within, | but soon Gunnar
struck in anger | the harp-strings with his hand;
the strings resounded; | so shall a hero,
a ring-breaker, guard | his gold from his enemies.
Then Atli rode | on his earth-treading horse,
making for home | from the place of slaughter;
there was a clatter of hooves | of the horses in the courtyard,
and the clashing of weapons | as they came from the field.
Then Guthrun came out | to meet Atli
with a golden beaker | as a gift for the king:
"Now, chieftain, you may eat | within your dwelling,
gladly with Guthrun, | young beasts freshly slaughtered."
Atli's wine-heavy | ale-cups rang
when there in the hall | the Hunnish youths clamoured,
and the bearded warriors, | the brave ones, came in.
Then in came the shining one, | ......
...... | and she brought them drink;
unwilling and bitter | she brought food to the warrior,
until in scorn she spoke | to the white-faced Atli:
"Giver of swords, | you have eaten in honey
your own sons' hearts, | all heavy with blood;
you shall stomach, hero, | the flesh of the slain,
to eat at your feast | and to send to your followers.
"Never again shall you call | to your knees
Erp or Eitil, | when merry with ale;
never again shall you see | in their seats
the sharers of gold | shaping their lances,
(clipping the manes | or minding their horses.)"
There was clamour on the benches | and the cry of men,
the clashing of weapons | and the weeping of the Huns,
all but Guthrun alone; | she never wept
for her bear-fierce brothers | or the boys so dear,
so young and so unhappy, | whom she had with Atli.
She scattered gold, | the swan-white one,
and rings of red gold | she gave to the followers;
she let fate grow | and the shining wealth go,
nor did she spare the treasure | of the temple itself.
Atli was unwise then, | he had drunk himself wild;
he had no weapon | and was not wary of Guthrun;
their play was often better | when both in gladness
embraced each other | among all the princes.
With her sword she gave | the bed blood to drink,
with her death-dealing hand, | and she loosed the hounds;
she woke the slaves | and threw a firebrand
in at the door of the hall; | so she had her vengeance.
To the flames she gave all | who were still inside
and had come from Myrkheim | from the murder of Gunnar;
the old timbers fell, | the temple was in flames,
the dwelling of the Buthlungs, | and the shield-maids burned;
they were killed in the house, | they sank in the hot flames.
Now the tale is all told, | and never in later times
will a woman in a mail-coat | so avenge her brothers;
to three kings of the people | the fair one
brought the doom of death | before she died herself.
Alvis said:
"Now the bride shall | adorn my benches,
and hurry home at once;
eager for marriage | I shall seem to all,
and at home they shall not rob me of rest."
Thor said:
"What are you, then? | Why so pale round the nose?
Have you lain lately with the dead?
You look like a giant, | it seems to me;
you were not born for the bride."
Alvis said:
"I am Alvis, | and under the earth
I have my home beneath the rocks;
with the wagon-guider | I seek a word;
let the gods not break their bond."
Thor said:
"Break it I shall, | for over the bride
her father has the first right;
I was not at home | when you had the promise,
and I alone of the gods give her."
Alvis said:
"What hero claims | to hold such a right
over the bride who shines so bright?
Not many will know you, | you wandering man!
Who was bought with rings to bear you?"
Thor said:
"I am Vingthor, | who has wandered widely,
and I am Sithgrani's son;
against my will | you shall get the maiden
and win the promise of marriage."
Alvis said:
"Your goodwill now | I shall quickly get,
and win the promise of marriage;
I long to have, | and would not be without,
this snow-white maiden for my own."
Thor said:
"The maiden's love | I cannot keep you
from winning, wise guest,
if of every world | you can tell me all
that I now wish to know.
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the earth, | that lies before all,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Earth' to men, 'Field' | to the gods it is,
'The Ways' it is called by the Wanes;
'Ever Green' by the giants, | 'The Grower' by elves,
'The Moist' by the holy ones on high."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the heaven, | beheld by the high one,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Heaven' men call it, | 'The Height' the gods,
the Wanes 'The Weaver of Winds';
giants 'The Up-World', | elves 'The Fair-Roof',
the dwarfs 'The Dripping Hall'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the moon, | that men look upon,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Moon' among men, 'Flame' | among the gods,
'The Wheel' in the house of hell;
'The Goer' the giants, | 'The Gleamer' the dwarfs,
the elves 'The Teller of Time'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the sun, | that all men see,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"Men call it 'Sun', | gods 'Orb of the Sun',
'The Deceiver of Dvalin' the dwarfs;
the giants 'The Ever-Bright', | elves 'Fair Wheel',
'All-Glowing' the sons of the gods."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the clouds, | that keep the rains,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Clouds' men name them, | 'Rain-Hope' gods call them,
the Wanes call them 'Kites of the Wind';
'Water-Hope' giants, | 'Weather-Might' elves,
'The Helmet of Secrets' in hell."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the wind, | that travels most widely,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Wind' men call it, | the gods 'The Waverer',
'The Neigher' the holy ones on high;
'The Wailer' the giants, | 'Roaring Traveller' the elves,
in hell 'The Blustering Blast'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the calm, | that lies quiet,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Calm' men call it, | 'The Quiet' the gods,
the Wanes 'The Hush of the Winds';
'The Sultry' the giants, | elves 'Day's Stillness',
the dwarfs 'The Shelter of Day'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the sea, | on which men sail,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Sea' men call it, | gods 'The Smooth-Lying',
'The Wave' it is called by the Wanes;
'Eel-Home' the giants, | 'Drink-Stuff' the elves,
for the dwarfs its name is 'The Deep'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the fire, | that flames for men,
in each of all the worlds?"
Alvis said:
"'Fire' men call it, | and 'Flame' the gods,
by the Wanes it is called 'Wildfire';
'The Biter' by giants, | 'The Burner' by dwarfs,
'The Swift' in the house of hell."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the wood, | that grows for mankind,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"Men call it 'The Wood', | gods 'The Mane of the Field',
'Seaweed of Hills' in hell;
'Flame-Food' the giants, | 'Fair-Limbed' the elves,
'The Wand' it is called by the Wanes."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the night, | the daughter of Nor,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Night' men call it, | 'Darkness' gods name it,
'The Hood' the holy ones on high;
the giants 'The Lightless', | the elves 'Sleep's Joy',
the dwarfs 'The Weaver of Dreams'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the seed, | that is sown by men,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"Men call it 'Grain', | and 'Corn' the gods,
'Growth' in the world of the Wanes;
'The Eaten' by giants, | 'Drink-Stuff' by elves,
in hell 'The Slender Stem'."
Thor said:
"Answer me, Alvis! | You know all,
dwarf, of the doom of men:
what do they call the ale, | that is drunk by men,
in each and every world?"
Alvis said:
"'Ale' among men, | 'Beer' among the gods,
in the world of the Wanes 'The Foaming';
'Bright Draught' with giants, | 'Mead' with dwellers in hell,
'The Feast-Draught' with Suttung's sons."
Thor said:
"In a single breast | I have never seen
a greater wealth of old wisdom;
but with treacherous tricks | I must now betray you:
the day has caught you, dwarf!
(Now the sun shines here in the hall.)"
There are many who know | how men long ago
gathered in council; | little good did it bring them;
they plotted in secret, | it was bitter for them later,
and for Gjuki's sons, | whose trust they betrayed.
Fate grew for the princes, | they were given to death;
Atli's plan was ill, | though he was shrewd enough;
he felled his strong bulwark, | and made his own sorrow,
soon he sent a message | that his kinsmen should visit him.
The woman was wise, | she wished to use her wisdom,
she saw well the meaning | of all they said in secret;
it was hidden from her heart | how she might give help,
they were to sail the sea, | while she herself was not to go.
She fashioned runes, | but Vingi made them false,
the speeder of hatred, | before he sought to give them;
then soon the warriors set out | whom Atli had sent,
and came to Limafjord, | to the home of the kings.
They were friendly with ale, | and they lit fires,
they suspected no trickery | from the guests who had come;
they took the gifts | that the noble one gave them,
they hung them on the pillars, | and felt no fear.
Then Kostbera came forward, | the wife of Hogni,
very kindly she was, | and she welcomed them both;
and Glaumvor was glad too, | the wife of Gunnar,
she knew well how to care | for the needs of the guests.
Then they asked Hogni | if he was more eager,
the deceit was quite clear, | if they had been on their guard;
then Gunnar promised, | if Hogni would go,
and Hogni answered | as the other advised.
Then the famed ones brought mead, | and the feast was fine,
many were the horns, | till the men had drunk deep;
then the couples made ready | their beds for resting.
Kostbera was wise, | and skilled in rune-craft,
she meant to read the letters | by the light of the fire;
but very quickly her tongue | stuck to her palate,
so strange did they seem | that she could not see their meaning.
Very soon then Hogni | went to seek his bed,
the clear-souled one dreamed, | and did not keep her dream to herself,
the wise one spoke to the warrior | when she woke:
"You mean to leave here, Hogni, | but heed my advice,
the runes are known to few, | and put off your journey;
I have now read the runes | that your sister wrote,
and this time the bright one | did not ask you to come.
"I wonder greatly, | and I cannot well see,
why the wise woman | has written so wildly;
but it seems to me | that the meaning beneath
is that both will be killed | if you go soon.
But she missed one rune, | or else others have spoiled it."
Hogni said:
"All women are fearful; | I do not feel so,
I do not look for ill | till I soon must avenge it;
the king will now give us | the glow-red gold;
I shall never be afraid, | though I know of dangers."
Kostbera said:
"You go into danger, | if you travel there,
you will find this time | no friendly welcome;
for I have just dreamed, Hogni, | and I will hide nothing,
your journey will be evil, | if my fear is right.
"I saw your bed-cover | burning in the flames,
and the fire burst high | through the walls of my home."
Hogni said:
"That linen garment lying there | is of little worth,
it will soon be burned, | and so you saw the bed-cover."
Kostbera said:
"I saw a bear come in, | he broke the pillars,
and he brandished his claws | so that our courage failed;
he seized many in his mouth, | and we were powerless,
and the uproar was loud, | it was not slight."
Hogni said:
"Now a storm is brewing, | and it grows wild quickly,
a dream of a polar bear | means a gale from the east."
Kostbera said:
"I saw an eagle flying | from the end through the house,
our fate must be bad, | for he sprinkled us with blood;
from the evil I fear | that it was Atli's spirit."
Hogni said:
"They will slaughter soon, | and so we see blood,
it often means oxen | when one dreams of eagles;
Atli's heart is true, | whatever you dream."
Then they were silent, | and said nothing further.
The high-born ones woke, | and their talk was alike,
then Glaumvor told | how she dreamed in terror,
.....Gunnar | two roads they were to go.
Glaumvor said:
"I saw a gallows ready, | you went to your hanging,
serpents ate your flesh, | and yet I found you living;
the doom of the gods came down; | now say what it meant."
"I saw a bloody sword | drawn from your clothes,
such a dream is hard | to tell a husband,
a spear, I thought, stood | thrust through your body,
and at head and feet | the wolves were howling."
Gunnar said:
"The hounds are running, | their barking is heard loud,
often the clamour of hounds | follows the flying of spears."
Glaumvor said:
"I saw a river run | the length of the hall,
it roared very swiftly, | it swept over the benches;
it broke over the feet | of you two brothers,
the water would not yield; | there was some meaning in it."
"I dreamed that by night | dead women came here,
their clothing was sad, | and they were looking for you;
they told you to come quickly | to their benches,
and the Norns, I think, | could do nothing to help you."
Gunnar said:
"You speak too late, | for so it is settled;
I will not turn from the journey, | the going is fixed,
though it is likely | that our lives will be short."
Then the morning shone bright, | the men were all ready,
they said, and yet each | would hold the other back;
five were the warriors, | and their followers in all
only twice as many, | their minds knew no wisdom.
Snævar and Solar, | they were sons of Hogni,
Orkning he was called | who came with the others,
cheerful was the shield-tree, | the brother of Kostbera;
the finely adorned ones followed, | till the fjord parted them,
they pleaded very hard, | but the others would not listen.
Then Glaumvor spoke up, | the wife of Gunnar,
to Vingi she said | what seemed wise to her:
"I do not know if you | repay our welcome well,
your coming was very ill | if evil follows."
Then Vingi swore, | and his speech was very glib,
"May giants take me now | if I have told you lies,
and the gallows if I had | any hostile thought."
Then Bera spoke up, | and her thought was kind,
"May you sail happily now, | and have victory,
may nothing bar your way | from faring as I bid you."
Then Hogni answered, | he held his kin dear,
"Take courage, wise ones, | whatever may come;
though many may speak, | yet evil is often mighty,
and words do little | to lead one home."
They looked tenderly | till each turned on his way,
then with changing fate | their journeys were parted.
They rowed very stoutly, | and the keel split apart,
their backs strained at the oars, | and their strength was fierce;
the oar-loops burst, | the thole-pins broke,
and they did not make the ship fast | before they left her.
It was not long after, | I must tell the end,
that they saw the home | that Buthli once had;
the gates rang loud | when Hogni struck them;
then Vingi spoke a word | that would have been better unsaid:
"Go far from the house, | for its entrance is false,
soon I shall burn you, | you are swiftly struck down;
I asked you here fairly, | but falseness lay beneath,
now wait far off | while I make your gallows."
Then Hogni answered, | his heart yielded little,
and he feared nothing | that his fate held in store:
"Do not try to frighten us, | you will seldom succeed;
if you say more, | then your fate grows worse."
Then they struck Vingi, | and they sent him to hell,
they hacked him with their axes | while the death-rattle came.
Atli summoned his men, | they hurried in mail-coats,
all ready they came, | and the courtyard lay between.
Then they came to words, | and they were very angry:
"Long ago we planned | how soon we might kill you."
Hogni said:
"It matters little | if you have planned it long;
for you wait unarmed, | and we have felled one,
we struck him down to hell, | he was once of your host."
Then their anger was wild | when all heard his words;
their fingers were swift | to seize their bowstrings,
they shot very sharply, | they were guarded by their shields.
Into the house came word | how the heroes outside
fought in front of the hall; | they heard a slave tell it;
Guthrun was grim then, | when she heard the grief,
with fine necklaces, | and she flung them all from her,
(she hurled the silver | so that the rings burst apart.)
Then she went out, | she flung open the doors,
quite fearless she went, | and she welcomed the guests;
to the Niflungs she went, | it was her last greeting,
in her speech truth was clear, | and she wished to say much.
"For your safety I tried | to make you stay at home;
no one escapes his fate, | and so you had to come here."
She spoke very wisely, | if they might yet win peace,
but they would listen to nothing, | and they all said "No."
Then the high-born one saw | that their battle was hard,
in fierceness of heart | she flung off her cloak;
she grasped her naked sword | to guard her kinsmen's lives,
her hands were not gentle | in the hewing of battle.
Then the daughter of Gjuki | struck down two warriors,
she killed Atli's brother, | and then they carried him out;
(so fiercely she fought | that she cut off his feet;)
another she struck | so that he never stood again,
she sent him to hell, | her hands never trembled.
Far and wide went the fame | of the battle they fought,
it was the greatest of the deeds | of the sons of Gjuki;
men say that the Niflungs, | while they themselves were living,
fought mightily with their swords, | they tore mail-coats apart,
and they hewed helmets, | as their hearts were fearless.
All the morning they fought | until midday shone,
(all the dusk as well | and the dawning of day,)
when the battle was ended, | the field flowed with blood;
before they fell, eighteen | of their enemies were killed,
by the two sons of Bera | and her brother as well.
Then the warrior spoke, | and his anger was wild:
"This is evil to see, | and it is all your doing;
once we were thirty, | we thanes keen for battle,
now eleven are left, | and our loss is great.
"There were five of us brothers | when we lost Buthli;
now Hel has half of them, | and two lie here struck down.
I had a great kinship, | I cannot hide the truth;
from a wife who brings slaughter | I could win little joy.
We have seldom lain together | since you were given to me;
now all my kin are gone, | I am robbed of my gold;
and worst of all, you sent | my sister to hell."
Guthrun said:
"Hear me now, Atli! | The first evil was yours;
you took my mother, | and murdered her for gold;
my sister's daughter | you starved in a prison.
It seems a joke to me | that you tell of your sorrow,
and I think it good | that grief comes to you."
Atli said:
"Go now, you warriors, | and make greater the grief
of the woman so fair, | for I long to see it;
fight so fiercely | that Guthrun shall weep;
I would gladly see | her happiness lost.
"Now seize Hogni, | and hack him with knives;
cut out his heart, | be quick to do this;
and grim-hearted Gunnar | you shall bind on the gallows;
do it swiftly, | then throw him to the serpents."
Hogni said:
"Do now as you will, | for I await it gladly;
you will find me brave, | I have faced worse before;
we held you at bay | while we fought unwounded;
now we are spent with wounds, | so you can work your will."
Then Beiti spoke, | he was Atli's steward:
"Let us seize Hjalli now, | and spare Hogni!
Let us kill the sluggard, | he is fit for death;
he has lived too long, | and men call him lazy."
The pot-watcher was afraid, | he fled here and there,
and mad with terror | he climbed into the corners:
"This fighting is bad for me, | if I pay for your fierceness,
and sad is the day | to die and leave my pigs
and all the fine food | that I used to have."
They seized Buthli's cook, | and came with the knife;
the frightened slave howled | before he felt the edge;
he was willing, he cried, | to dung the courtyard well,
to do the lowest work, | if they would spare him;
Hjalli would be very happy | if he might have his life.
Then Hogni was willing, | there are few who would do so,
to beg for the slave | that he should go from there safe;
"I would find it far better | to feel this knife-play;
why must we all listen | to this howling any longer?"
Then they seized the brave one; | the bold warriors had
no chance left | to delay his fate longer;
Hogni laughed loudly, | all the sons of day heard him;
so valiant was he | that he could suffer well.
Gunnar seized a harp, | he struck it with his toes;
he played so well | that the women all wept,
and the men lamented | when they heard it clearly;
noble was his song, | the rafters burst apart.
Then the heroes died | before the day had come;
they left their fame | to live high for ever.
Atli seemed very mighty | as he stood over them;
he blamed the wise woman, | and his words reproached her:
"It is morning, Guthrun; | now you miss your dear ones,
but the blame is partly yours | that it has turned out so."
Guthrun said:
"You are joyful, Atli, | for you tell of evil,
but sorrow is yours | if you could see everything;
a heavy inheritance | I can tell you of here:
you will never lose sorrow | unless I die."
Atli said:
"I am not free of guilt; | I shall find a way
that is better by far, | we have often shunned the fairest;
I will console you with slaves, | with gems fair to see,
and with snow-white silver, | as you yourself shall choose."
Guthrun said:
"This shall give you no hope, | I will not take your gifts;
I spurned compensation | when my sorrows were smaller;
once I seemed grim, | but now my grimness is greater;
nothing seemed too hard | while Hogni was alive.
"We spent our childhood | in a single house,
we played many a game, | we grew up in the grove;
then Grimhild gave us | gold and necklaces;
you shall never make amends | for my brother's murder,
nor ever win me | to think it was well.
"But the fierceness of men | rules the fate of women;
the tree-top bows low | if stripped of its leaves,
the tree bends over | if the roots are cut beneath it;
now you, Atli, may | rule over everything here."
Very heedless was the warrior | to trust her,
her guile was so clear | if he had been on his guard;
but Guthrun was crafty, | she spoke with cunning,
she made her look pleasant, | she played with two shields.
Then she brought the beer | for her brothers' funeral feast,
and Atli made a feast | for his dead followers;
they spoke no more, | the mead was made ready,
soon the men were gathered | with mighty uproar.
So bitterly she planned, | and threatened Buthli's race,
and would take terrible vengeance | on her husband;
she called the little ones, | she laid them on a block;
the proud ones were afraid, | but their tears did not fall;
they went to their mother's arms, | and asked what she wanted.
Guthrun said:
"No, ask me no more! | I shall murder you both,
for I have long wished | to steal your lives from you."
The boys said:
"Kill your boys as you will, | for no one can prevent it;
short is the angry one's peace | if you do it all."
Then the grim one killed both | of the young brothers;
hard was her deed | when she struck off their heads;
Atli wished to know | where they had gone now,
the boys from their play, | for he saw them nowhere.
Guthrun said:
"I shall seek my fate, | telling Atli everything;
the daughter of Grimhild | does not hide the deed from you;
you have no joy, Atli, | if you hear it all;
you woke great sorrow | when you killed my brothers.
"I have seldom slept | since the hour they were killed;
my threats were deadly, | now I bid you recall them;
you said it was morning, | I remember too well;
now evening has come, | and you ask this question.
"Now both your sons | you have lost...
....... | as you never should;
you had the skulls of your boys | as beer-cups,
and the drink I made you | was mixed with their blood.
"I cut out their hearts, | I cooked them on a spit,
I came to you with them, | and called them calf's flesh;
you ate them alone, | and left none.
You bit greedily, | and your teeth were busy.
"Now you know about your sons; | few suffer more sorrow;
I have told my guilt, | it shall never bring me fame."
Atli said:
"You were grim, Guthrun, | in so grievous a deed,
to mix my drink | with the blood of your boys;
you have killed your own kin, | it suited you very badly,
and you leave me little | between my sorrows."
Guthrun said:
"I would seek still more | to kill you yourself;
enough harm seldom comes | to such as you;
you did folly in the past, | such that no one shall find
in the whole world of men | a match for such madness.
Now you have added this | that we lately learned of;
you have grasped great evil, | and made your own funeral feast."
Atli said:
"They shall burn you with fire, | and first they shall stone you;
so then you will have earned | what you have always sought."
Guthrun said:
"Such woes you shall tell | for yourself in the morning;
from a finer death I | pass to another light."
They sat together, | and their thoughts were grim,
their words unfriendly, | and neither found joy;
hatred grew in Hniflung, | he had great plans;
his anger against Atli | was told to Guthrun.
The fate of Hogni | came always to her heart;
she told him it would be well | if he should win vengeance;
so Atli was killed, | it was not long to wait;
Hogni's son killed him, | and Guthrun herself.
Then the warrior spoke, | as he woke from sleep;
soon he knew that for his wounds | a bandage would do nothing:
"Now you shall tell the truth: | who has killed Buthli's son?
I am sorely wounded, | and can see no hope."
Guthrun said:
"The daughter of Grimhild | never hides her deed from you;
I own to the guilt | that is ending your life,
and the son of Hogni too; | that is why your wounds bleed."
Atli said:
"You have gone to murder, | foul though it must seem;
it is wrong to betray your friend | who trusted you well.
"Not gladly did I leave home | to seek your hand, Guthrun;
you were famed in your widowhood, | but men found you haughty;
my belief did not lie, | as we have now learned;
I brought you home here, | and a host of men with us.
"All was most noble | when we journeyed long ago;
we had great honour | from very worthy heroes;
we had plenty of cattle, | and we prospered greatly;
our wealth was mighty, | and many received it.
"To the famous one as bride-gift | I gave fair jewels,
I gave thirty slaves, | and seven handmaids;
there was honour in such gifts, | yet the silver was greater.
"But all this was to you | as if it were worth nothing,
while the land lay before you | that Buthli had left me;
you worked in secret | so that I did not win the treasure;
you often made | my mother sit weeping;
I found no wedded joy | in fullness of heart."
Guthrun said:
"You are lying now, Atli, | though I care little;
if I was seldom kind, | you were very cruel;
you brothers fought young, | quarrels brought you to battle,
and half the sons of your house | went to hell,
and all was destroyed | that should ever have done good.
"My two brothers and I | were bold in our thoughts;
we went out from the land, | we travelled with Sigurth;
we sailed very swiftly, | each steering his ship;
so we always sought our fate | till we came to the East.
"First we killed the king, | and seized the land;
the princes served us, | such was their fear;
from the forest we called | those we wished to have guiltless,
and we made many rich | who had lost everything.
"The Hun-king was killed, | happiness soon vanished;
in her grief the widow, | so young, sat weeping;
yet the sorrow seemed worse | of going to Atli's house;
my husband was a hero, | and his loss was hard.
"You never came from the Thing, | so we have heard,
having won your quarrels, | or struck down warriors;
you always gave way, | your will was never firm;
in silence you suffered, | ........"
Atli said:
"You are lying now, Guthrun, | but it will bring
little good to either, | for we have lost all;
but, Guthrun, be kind | of heart once more,
for the honour of us both, | when I am carried out."
Guthrun said:
"I will buy a ship, | and a bright-coloured coffin;
I will wax the shroud well | to wind around your body;
I will see to everything | as if we had always been dear."
Then Atli died, | and his heirs' grief doubled;
the high-born woman did | as she had promised him;
then Guthrun the wise | sought to go to her death,
but she waited for days, | and it was long before she died.
Very happy shall he be | who has such offspring,
or children so gallant, | as Gjuki fathered;
for ever shall live, | in lands far and wide,
their heroic valour, | wherever men hear of it.
Once the gods | were met together,
and the goddesses came | and held council,
and the far-famed ones | sought to find the truth,
why evil dreams | had come to Baldr.
Then Othin rose, | the old enchanter,
and laid the saddle | on Sleipnir's back;
from there he rode down | to deep Niflhel,
and met the hound | that came from hell.
Bloody he was | on his breast in front,
and at the father of magic | he howled from afar;
forward rode Othin, | the earth resounded,
till he reached | the high house of Hel.
Then Othin rode | to the eastern door;
there, he knew well, | was the wise-woman's grave;
he spoke magic | and mighty charms,
till spellbound she rose, | and in death she spoke:
"What man is this, | unknown to me,
who has made me travel | the troublesome road?
I was snowed on with snow, | and beaten with rain,
and drenched with dew; | long was I dead."
Othin said:
"Vegtam is my name, | I am Valtam's son;
speak of hell, | for of heaven I know:
for whom are the benches | bright with rings,
and the platforms gaily | decked with gold?"
The Wise-Woman said:
"Here for Baldr | the mead is brewed,
the shining drink, | and a shield lies over it;
but their hope is gone | from the mighty gods.
Unwillingly I spoke, | and now would be silent."
Othin said:
"Wise-woman, do not stop! | I seek from you
to know all | that I wish to ask:
who shall be | the death of Baldr,
and steal the life | from Othin's son?"
The Wise-Woman said:
"Hoth brings there | the far-famed branch;
he shall be | the death of Baldr,
and steal the life | from Othin's son.
Unwillingly I spoke, | and now would be silent."
Othin said:
"Wise-woman, do not stop! | I seek from you
to know all | that I wish to ask:
who shall win vengeance | for the evil deed,
or bring to the flames | the slayer of Baldr?"
The Wise-Woman said:
"Rind bears Vali | in Vestrsalir,
and one night old | Othin's son fights;
he shall not wash his hands, | nor comb his hair,
till he brings to the flames | the slayer of Baldr.
Unwillingly I spoke, | and now would be silent."
Othin said:
"Wise-woman, do not stop! | I seek from you
to know all | that I wish to ask:
what maidens are they | who then shall weep,
and toss to the sky | the yards of the sails?"
The Wise-Woman said:
"You are not Vegtam, | as I thought before;
you are Othin, | the old enchanter."
Othin said:
"You are no wise-woman, | and have no wisdom;
you are the mother | of three giants."
The Wise-Woman said:
"Ride home, Othin, | be ever proud;
for no man | shall seek me again
till Loki wanders | loose from his bonds,
and the destroyers come | to the last strife."
The fire raged, | the earth shook,
the flames leapt high | to heaven itself;
few were the bold | heroes who would dare
to ride or leap | the raging flames.
Sigurth then urged Grani | on with his sword,
the fire slackened | before the hero,
the flames sank low | for the one greedy for fame,
the armour flashed | that Regin had made.
Sigurth killed | the dragon, and that
men will recall | while the world lasts;
but your brother | had little boldness
to ride or leap | the raging flames.
Out went Sigurth, | and sought no talk,
the friend of heroes, | with his head bowed;
such was his grief | that his mail-coat,
all wrought of iron, | burst apart.
Hogni said:
"(What evil deed | has Sigurth) done,
that you wish to have | the hero's life?"
Gunnar said:
"Sigurth has sworn | oaths to me,
sworn oaths, | and broken them all;
he betrayed me there | where, I think,
he ought most truly | to have kept all his oaths."
Hogni said:
"Brynhild has whetted | your heart to hate,
to work evil | and win harm;
she grudges the honour | that Guthrun has,
and that you still | have the joy of her."
They cooked a wolf, | they cut up a snake,
they gave Gotthorm | the greedy one's flesh,
before the men, | with murder in mind,
laid their hands | on the bold hero.
Sigurth was killed | south of the Rhine;
from a branch a raven | called very loudly:
"Your blood shall redden | Atli's blade,
and your oaths shall bind | you both in chains."
Outside stood Guthrun, | Gjuki's daughter;
hear now the words | that she spoke first:
"Where is Sigurth now, | the noble king,
that my kinsmen come | riding ahead of him?"
Only this | did Hogni answer:
"We have killed | Sigurth with our swords;
the grey horse mourns | by his dead master."
Then Brynhild spoke, | the daughter of Buthli:
"Well may you enjoy | weapons and lands;
Sigurth alone | would have been lord of all,
if his life had lasted | a little longer.
"It would not be right | that he should so rule
over Gjuki's wealth | and the race of the Goths;
five are the sons, | fit to rule the people
and greedy for battle, | that he has fathered."
Then Brynhild laughed, | and the building echoed,
only once, | with all her heart;
"Long may you enjoy | lands and men,
now that you have killed | the noble hero."
Then Guthrun spoke, | the daughter of Gjuki:
"You say much | in evil speech;
cursed be Gunnar, | Sigurth's killer;
vengeance shall come | for his cruel heart."
Evening came early, | and ale was drunk,
and long and loud | they talked among themselves;
they all slept | when they went to their beds,
but Gunnar alone | was long awake.
His feet were restless, | he talked to himself,
and the slayer of hosts | began to heed
what the two in the tree | had told him then,
the raven and the eagle, | as they rode home.
Brynhild awoke, | the daughter of Buthli,
the warrior's daughter, | before the dawn of day:
"Love me or hate me, | the harm is done,
and my grief cries out, | or else I die."
All were silent | who heard her speak,
and they knew nothing | of the queen's heart,
who wept such tears | to tell of the thing
that once, laughing, | she had won from the men.
Brynhild said:
"Gunnar, I dreamed | a very grim dream:
in the hall were corpses; | my bed was cold;
and you, ruler, | rode joyless,
bound with fetters | in the throng of your foes.
Now your Niflung race | shall die,
all of it, utterly; | you have broken your oaths.
"You have forgotten, | Gunnar, the deed,
when you both mingled | blood in your footprints;
you have repaid | all with evil to him
who wished to make you | the foremost of kings.
"He proved well, | when he rode proudly
to win me then | to be your wife,
how truly the host-slayer | had always kept
the oaths he had made | with the young king.
"Then the wound-staff, | all wound with gold,
the hero let | lie between us;
its edge was forged | very keen with fire,
and the blade was damp | with drops of poison."

br-p1.s: This poem tells of the death of Sigurth, and here the story is that they killed him out of doors; but some say that they killed him in the house, in his bed while he was asleep. But Germans say that they killed him out of doors in the forest; and the old Guthrun lay likewise says that Sigurth and Gjuki's sons had ridden to the council-place, and that he was killed there. But on this they all agree: that they betrayed his trust in them, and attacked him when he was lying down and unprepared.

drn-p1.s: Gunnar and Hogni then took all the gold that had been Fafnir's. There was strife between the Gjukungs and Atli, for he held the Gjukungs guilty of Brynhild's death. It was agreed that they should give him Guthrun as his wife, and they gave her a drink of forgetfulness before she would consent to marry Atli. The sons of Atli were Erp and Eitil, and Svanhild was the daughter of Sigurth and Guthrun. King Atli invited Gunnar and Hogni to visit him, and sent Vingi or Knefröth as his messenger. Guthrun knew of the treachery, and sent with him a message in runes that they should not come, and as a token she sent Hogni the ring Andvaranaut and tied a wolf's hair in it. Gunnar had sought Oddrun, Atli's sister, as his wife, but did not get her; then he married Glaumvor, and Hogni's wife was Kostbera; their sons were Solar and Snævar and Gjuki. And when the Gjukungs came to Atli, Guthrun begged her sons to plead for the lives of both the Gjukungs, but they would not do it. Hogni's heart was cut out, and Gunnar was thrown into the serpents' den. He played the harp and put the serpents to sleep, but an adder stung him in the liver.

l: I am the offspring | of nine mothers,
I am the son | of nine sisters.
Svipdag said:
"What giant is this, | in front of the house,
refusing the traveller a welcome?"
Fjolsvith said:
"You will never find | a friendly greeting,
so get yourself home from here.
"I am Fjolsvith, | and I am known as wise,
but I am miserly with food;
you shall never come | inside the house;
go on your way like a wolf!"
Svipdag said:
"Few will turn away | from the joy of their eyes
when they seek the sight of their loves;
the gates of the golden hall | shine bright,
and here I shall enjoy a home."
Fjolsvith said:
"Tell me now, fellow, | who your father is,
and the family you come from."
Svipdag said:
"I am Vindkald, | and Varkald's son,
and his father was Fjolkald.
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
who is it that holds | and has for his own
the rule of this rich hall?"
Fjolsvith said:
"She is Mengloth; | her mother bore her
to the son of Svafrthorin;
it is she who holds | and has for her own
the rule of this rich hall."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what do they call the gate? | For among the gods
no man ever saw so grim a sight."
Fjolsvith said:
"They call it Thrymgjol; | it was made by the three,
the sons of Solblindi;
and fast as a fetter | it holds the traveller,
whoever lifts the latch."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what do they call the house? | For no man has seen
among the gods so grim a sight."
Fjolsvith said:
"It is Gastropnir; | I made it long ago
from the limbs of Leirbrimir;
I braced it so strongly | that it will stand firm
as long as the world lasts."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what do they call the tree | that spreads
its branches over every land?"
Fjolsvith said:
"Mimameith is its name, | and no man knows
what root runs beneath it;
and few can guess | what will fell the tree,
for neither fire nor iron will fell it."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what grows from the seed | of that great tree
that neither fire nor iron will fell?"
Fjolsvith said:
"Women sick | with child shall seek
its fruit to carry to the flames;
then out will come | what was hidden within,
and so it is mighty among men."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what cock is that | on the highest bough,
glittering all with gold?"
Fjolsvith said:
"Vithofnir is his name, | and now he shines
like lightning on Mimameith's branches;
and great is the trouble | with which he grieves
both Surt and Sinmora."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what do they call the hounds | that before the house
are so fierce and angry?"
Fjolsvith said:
"One they call Gif, | and the other Geri,
if now you want to know the truth;
they are great, | and their strength will grow
till the gods are doomed to death."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
can no man hope | to enter the house
while the hungry hounds are sleeping?"
Fjolsvith said:
"They never sleep together, | for so it was fixed
when the guard was given to them;
one sleeps by night, | the other by day,
so no man may ever enter."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
is there no food | that men can give them,
and leap inside while they eat?"
Fjolsvith said:
"There are two wing-joints | in Vithofnir's body,
if now you want to know the truth;
that alone is the food | that men can give them,
and leap inside while they eat."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what weapon can send | Vithofnir to seek
the house of Hel below?"
Fjolsvith said:
"Lævatein is there, | which Lopt with runes
once made by the doors of death;
in Lægjarn's chest | it lies with Sinmora,
and nine locks hold it fast."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
can a man come back | who goes there
and tries to take the sword?"
Fjolsvith said:
"He can come back | who goes there
and tries to take the sword,
if he carries with him | what few can win,
to give to the goddess of gold."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what treasure is there | that men can take
to gladden the pale giantess?"
Fjolsvith said:
"Carry in your pouch | the bright sickle
found among Vithofnir's feathers;
give it to Sinmora, | and then she will grant
that you may win the weapon."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what do they call the hall | surrounded here
with flickering magic flames?"
Fjolsvith said:
"It is called Lyr, | and long shall it
tremble on the tip of a spear-point;
of the noble house | mankind has heard,
but has never known more."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
which of the gods | has made so great
the hall I see within?"
Fjolsvith said:
"Uni and Iri, | Bari and Jari,
Var and Vegdrasil,
Dori and Ori, | Delling, and there
was Loki, the fear of the people."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what do they call the mountain | on which the maiden
lies, so lovely to see?"
Fjolsvith said:
"It is Lyfjaberg, | and long shall it be
a joy to the sick and the sore;
for she will grow well, | each woman who climbs it,
though she has long lain sick."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
what maidens are those | who at Mengloth's knees
sit so gladly together?"
Fjolsvith said:
"One is named Hlif, | another Hlifthrasa,
the third they call Thjothvara;
Bjort and Bleik, | Blith and Frith,
Eir and Aurbotha."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
do they bring help to all | who give offerings,
if there is need of it?"
Fjolsvith said:
"They soon help all | who give offerings
on the high holy altars;
and if they see danger | for the sons of men,
they guard each one from harm."
Svipdag said:
"Now answer me, Fjolsvith, | the question I ask,
for now I want to know the truth:
is there a man living | who in the arms
of fair Mengloth may seek to sleep?"
Fjolsvith said:
"There is no man | who in the arms
of fair Mengloth may seek to sleep,
except Svipdag alone, | for the sun-bright maiden
is destined to be his bride."
Svipdag said:
"Fling back the gates! | Make the gateway wide!
Here you may see Svipdag!
Go from here and find out | whether Mengloth
will soon give me gladness."
Fjolsvith said:
"Listen, Mengloth, | a man has come;
go and see the guest!
The hounds are fawning, | the house bursts open;
it is Svipdag, I think."
Mengloth said:
"On the high gallows | hungry ravens
shall soon pluck out your eyes,
if you lie in saying | that here at last
the hero has come to my hall.
"Where have you come from? | How did you come here?
What name do your kinsmen call you?
Your family and your name | I must know as a sign
that I am destined to be your bride."
Svipdag said:
"I am Svipdag, | and Solbjart's son;
from there I came by wind-cold ways;
no man can fight | against the words of Urth,
though her gifts are given unearned."
Mengloth said:
"You are welcome, | for I have waited long;
you shall have the kiss of welcome!
For two who love, | the longed-for meeting
is the greatest gladness of all.
"Long have I sat | here on Lyfjaberg,
waiting for you day by day;
and now I have | what I always hoped for,
for here you have come to my hall.
"We yearned alike; | I longed for you,
and you have longed for my love;
but now from this day | we know that together
we shall live our lives to the end."

fm-p1.s: Sigurth and Regin went up to the Gnitaheith, and there they found the track that Fafnir made when he crawled to the water. Then Sigurth dug a great trench across the path and took his place in it. When Fafnir crawled from his gold, he blew out poison, and it ran down from above onto Sigurth's head. But when Fafnir crawled over the trench, Sigurth thrust his sword into his body, right to the heart. Fafnir writhed and struck out with his head and tail. Sigurth leaped from the trench, and each looked at the other. Fafnir said:

l: "Youth, oh, youth! | Of whom then, youth, were you born?
Say whose son you are,
who reddened your bright blade | in Fafnir's blood,
and struck your sword to my heart."

fm-p2.s: Sigurth concealed his name because it was believed in the old days that the words of a dying man could have great power if he cursed his enemy by name. He said:

l: "The Noble Hart | is my name, and I go
through the world a motherless man;
I had no father, | as others have,
and I always live alone."
Fafnir said:
"If you had no father, | as others have,
by what wonder were you born?
(Though you hide your name | on the day of my death,
you know now that you are lying.)"
Sigurth said:
"My family, I think, | is unknown to you,
and so am I myself;
Sigurth is my name, | and I am Sigmund's son,
who struck you so with the sword."
Fafnir said:
"Who drove you on? | Why were you driven
to make me lose my life?
The bright-eyed youth | had a brave father,
for you are bold in boyhood."
Sigurth said:
"My heart drove me, | my hand carried it out,
and my shining sword so sharp;
few are bold | when old age comes
who are timid in boyhood."
Fafnir said:
"If you could grow up | among your friends,
one might see you fight fiercely;
but you are bound, | and taken in battle,
and prisoners are prone to fear."
Sigurth said:
"You blame me, Fafnir, | that I see from afar
the wealth that was my father's;
I am not bound, | though taken in battle;
you have found that I live free."
Fafnir said:
"In all I say | you see hatred,
yet I tell only the truth;
the ringing gold, | the glow-red wealth,
and the rings will be your death."
Sigurth said:
"Someone shall always | hold the hoard,
till the destined day comes;
for there is a time | when every man
shall journey from here to hell."
Fafnir said:
"The fate of the Norns | before the headland
you will find, and a fool's doom;
you will drown in the water | if you row against the wind;
every danger is near to death."
Sigurth said:
"Tell me then, Fafnir, | for you are famed as wise,
and you know much now:
who are the Norns | who help in need,
and bring the baby from the mother?"
Fafnir said:
"Of many births | the Norns must be,
and they were not of one race;
some are kin to gods, | others to elves,
and some are Dvalin's daughters."
Sigurth said:
"Tell me then, Fafnir, | for you are famed as wise,
and you know much now:
what do they call the island | where all the gods
and Surt shall mingle sword-sweat?"
Fafnir said:
"It is Oskopnir, | where all the gods
shall seek the play of swords;
Bilrost breaks | when they cross the bridge,
and the horses shall swim in the flood.
"I wore the fear-helm | to terrify mankind,
while I lay guarding my gold;
I seemed mightier | than any man,
for I never found a fiercer."
Sigurth said:
"The fear-helm surely | shields no man
when he faces a brave enemy;
often one finds, | on meeting the enemy,
that he is not the bravest of all."
Fafnir said:
"I breathed poison | when I lay shining
on the hoard my father had;
(there was none so mighty | as dared to meet me,
and I feared neither weapons nor wiles.)"
Sigurth said:
"Glittering serpent, | your hissing was loud,
and you showed a hard heart;
but the sons of men | have more hatred
for the one who owns the helm."
Fafnir said:
"I advise you, Sigurth, | heed my words,
and ride home from here;
the ringing gold, | the glow-red wealth,
and the rings will be your death."
Sigurth said:
"Your advice is given, | but I shall go
to the gold hidden in the heather;
and you, Fafnir, | are fighting with death,
lying where Hel shall have you."
Fafnir said:
"Regin betrayed me, | and will betray you;
he will bring us both to death;
Fafnir, I think, | must lose his life,
for you were the mightier man."

fm-p3.s: Regin had gone some distance away while Sigurth fought Fafnir, and came back while Sigurth was wiping the blood from his sword. Regin said:

l: "Hail to you, Sigurth! | You have the victory,
and have killed Fafnir in the fight;
of all the men | who walk the earth,
you are the most fearless, I think."
Sigurth said:
"No one knows, | when all are together,
(the sons of the glorious gods,)
who will seem the bravest born;
some are brave | who redden no sword
in the blood of an enemy's breast."
Regin said:
"You are glad, Sigurth, | of the battle won,
as you clean Gram on the grass;
my fierce brother | you have killed in the fight,
and I did something myself."
Sigurth said:
"You went far off | while Fafnir reddened
my keen blade with his blood;
I matched my strength | with the dragon's might,
while you hid in the heather."
Regin said:
"Longer you would | have left in the heather
that grey old giant hiding,
if the weapon had not served | that I once forged,
the keen-edged blade you carried."
Sigurth said:
"Courage is better | than a mighty blade
for one who must fight fiercely;
the brave man will | fight well and win,
though his blade may be blunt.
"Brave men are better | than cowards
when the clash of battle comes;
and the glad man better | than the gloomy
will face what lies before him.
"It was your advice | that I should ride
here over the high mountains;
the glittering serpent | would have wealth and life
if you had not mocked my strength."
"Sit now, Sigurth, | for I will sleep;
hold Fafnir's heart to the fire;
for all his heart | shall be eaten,
since I have drunk deep of blood."

fm-p5.s: Sigurth took Fafnir's heart and cooked it on a spit. When he thought it was fully cooked, and the blood foamed out of the heart, he tested it with his finger to see whether it was done. He burned his finger and put it in his mouth. But when Fafnir's heart's-blood touched his tongue, he understood the speech of birds. He heard nuthatches chattering in the thickets. A nuthatch said:

l: "There sits Sigurth, | sprinkled with blood,
and Fafnir's heart | he cooks at the fire;
the breaker of rings | would be wise, I think,
to eat the life-muscles, | bright as they are."
A second said:
"There Regin lies, | and he lays plans
to betray the youth | who trusts him well;
lying words | he will speak with cunning,
till the maker of mischief | avenges his brother."
A third said:
"Shorter by a head | let the grey old chatterer
go from here to hell;
then all of the wealth | he alone can command,
the gold that Fafnir guarded."
A fourth said:
"He would seem wise | if he would heed
the good advice | we sisters give;
he would take thought, | and gladden the ravens;
there is always a wolf | where I see his ears."
A fifth said:
"The tree of battle | must be less wise
than I would think | a leader of men,
if he lets | one brother go,
when he is | the other's killer."
A sixth said:
"He seems most foolish | if he spares
his enemy, the bane of the people;
there Regin lies, | who has wronged him so,
yet he knows nothing of falsehood."
A seventh said:
"Let the head be hewn | from the frost-cold giant,
and let him be robbed of rings;
then all the wealth | that was Fafnir's
will belong to you alone."
Sigurth said:
"Regin shall not have | so rich a fate
as to tell the tale of my death;
for soon both | the brothers shall die,
and go from here to hell."

fm-p6.s: Sigurth cut off Regin's head, and then he ate Fafnir's heart and drank the blood of both Regin and Fafnir. Then Sigurth heard what the nuthatch said:

l: "Bind the golden rings | together, Sigurth;
it is not kingly | to fear anything;
I know a maiden, | none is so fair,
rich in gold, | if you could win her.
"Green are the paths | that lead to Gjuki,
and his fate shows | the wanderer the way;
the valiant king | has a daughter,
whom you, Sigurth, | may buy as a bride."
Another said:
"A hall stands high | on Hindarfjoll,
all with flame | it is ringed outside;
wise warriors | made it once
out of the flaming | light of the flood.
"On the mountain sleeps | a battle-maid,
and about her plays | the bane of the wood;
Ygg with the thorn | has struck her so,
for she felled the fighter | he wished to save.
"There you may see | the helmeted maiden,
who rode from the fight | on Vingskornir;
the victory-bringer | shall not break her sleep,
son of heroes, | so the Norns have decreed."
Alfödr works,
the Alfar discern,
the Vanir know,
the Nornir point the way,
the Ividia gives birth,
men endure,
the Thursar wait,
the Valkyriur long.
The Æsir suspected
the forebodings to be evil;
treacherous Vættar had
confounded the runes.
Urd was charged
to guard Odhroerir,
to protect it with her power
against the growing multitude.
Hug
then goes out,
explores the heavens;
the powers fear
disaster from delay.
It was Thrain's belief
that the dream was ominous;
Dain's thought was that
the dream was dark.
Among the dwarfs
virtue decays;
worlds sink down
to Ginnung's abyss.
Often Asvid will
strike them down,
often gather
the fallen again.
No longer shall
earth or sun stand.
The stream of air,
laden with corruption,
shall not cease.
Hidden in Mim's
clear well
is men's certain knowledge.
Do you understand yet, or what?
In the dales lives
the foreseeing Dis,
sunk down
from Yggdrasil's ash,
of the race of the Alfar,
Idun by name,
the youngest of Ivaldi's
elder children.
She bore her descent
badly,
confined under the trunk
of the hoary tree.
She would not be happy
with Nörvi's daughter,
being used to a pleasanter
dwelling at home.
The triumphant gods saw
Nanna
grieving
in earth's deep sanctuaries;
they gave her a wolf's skin,
and she clothed herself in it,
changed her feelings,
practised deceit,
altered her appearance.
Vidrir chose
Bifröst's guardian
to ask the keeper
of the Giöll-sun
all that she knew
of every world;
Bragi and Lopt
were to bear witness.
They sang magic songs,
they rode on wolves,
the god
and gods.
At the heavenly house
Odin listened
in Hlidskjalf;
he let them set out
on their long way.
The wise god asked
the cupbearer
of the gods' offspring
and their companions
whether she knew the origin,
the duration or the end
of heaven, of Hel,
or of earth.
She did not speak,
she could bring out
no words
for the anxious gods,
nor utter a sound;
tears flowed from the orbs of her head;
held back with pain,
they flow again.
As from the east,
from Elivagar,
the thorn is driven by
the ice-cold Thurs,
with which Dain
strikes all people
over fair Midgard;
when every faculty is dulled,
the hands drop,
the bright, sword-girt As
sways with drowsiness;
the giantess's
soothing charm
drives away the current
of the troubles in the minds
of all people,
so to the gods
Jorun seemed to be affected,
swollen with sorrows,
when they got no answer;
they pressed the harder
the more they were refused;
still less than they had hoped
did their words achieve.
When the leader
of the inquiring travellers,
the guardian of Herian's
loud-sounding horn,
took the son of Nal
as his companion,
Grimnir's poet
kept watch at the place.
Vidur's servants
reached Vingolf,
both carried
by Forniot's kin.
They went in
and at once
greeted the Æsir
at Ygg's merry gathering.
They hailed Hangatyr,
the most blissful of the Æsir;
they wished him to enjoy
strong drink in the high seat,
and the gods to sit
happy at the feast,
always sharing pleasure
with Yggiung.
Seated on benches,
at Bölverk's bidding,
the company of gods
ate their fill of Sæhrimnir.
Skögul at the tables,
from Hnikar's vessel,
measured out the mead
in Mimir's
horns.
About many things,
when the meal was over,
the high gods asked Heimdall,
the goddesses asked Loki,
whether the maiden had uttered
prophecies or wise words,
from noon
until twilight came.
They made it plain
that it had gone badly,
their errand fruitless,
with little glory in it.
It seemed likely
that no plan could be found
for getting an answer
from the maiden.
Omi answered:
"Night is the time
for new counsel;
until tomorrow let each one
think it over who is able
to give advice
helpful to the Æsir."
Along the ways
of mother Rind ran
the longed-for meal
of Fenrisulf.
Hropt and Frigg
left the feast
and bade the gods farewell,
as, before Hrimfaxi,
the son of Delling
urged on his horse,
adorned with
precious jewels.
Over
Mannheim
shines
the horse's mane;
the steed drew Dvalin's deluder
in his chariot.
At the northern edge
of the wide earth,
under the outermost root
of the noble tree,
Gygiar and Thursar
went to their beds,
spectres, dwarfs,
and Murk Alfs.
The powers rose,
the Alfs' illuminator
chased the night
northwards towards Niflheim.
Up Argjöll ran
Ulfrun's son,
the mighty hornblower
of heaven's heights.

gdr1-p1.s: Guthrun sat by the dead Sigurth. She did not weep as other women do, but her heart was close to bursting with grief. The men and women came to her to console her, but that was not easy to do. People say that Guthrun had eaten some of Fafnir's heart, and that she understood the speech of birds. This is a poem about Guthrun.

l: Then Guthrun | thought to die,
when she sat sorrowing | by Sigurth;
she shed no tears, | nor wrung her hands,
nor ever wailed, | as other women do.
The wise warriors | came to her there,
longing to lighten | her heavy grief;
in her grief | Guthrun could not weep,
so sad her heart, | it seemed it would break.
Then the wives | of the warriors came,
adorned with gold, | and sought out Guthrun;
each one then | spoke of her own grief,
the bitterest pain | she had ever borne.
Then Gjaflaug spoke, | Gjuki's sister:
"I am the most joyless | of all on earth;
five husbands | were taken from me,
(two daughters then, | and three sisters,)
eight brothers, | yet I have lived."
In her grief | Guthrun could not weep,
such grief she had | for her dead husband,
and so grim her heart | by the hero's body.
Then Herborg spoke, | the queen of the Huns:
"I have a greater | grief to tell;
my seven sons | in the southern land,
and my husband, fell | in battle, all eight.
(Father and mother | and four brothers
the wind once struck | among the waves,
and the seas crashed through | the sides of the ship.)
"All the bodies | with my own hands then
I made ready for the grave, | and I buried the dead;
one half-year brought me | all this to bear,
and no one came | to comfort me.
"Then I was bound | and taken in war,
one more sorrow | in the same half-year;
they made me dress | and tie the shoes
of the monarch's wife | every morning.
"In jealous rage | she spoke her anger,
and often beat me | with heavy blows;
I never knew | a better lord,
and never found | a worse woman."
In her grief | Guthrun could not weep,
such grief she had | for her dead husband,
and so grim her heart | by the hero's body.
Then Gollrond spoke, | Gjuki's daughter:
"Your wisdom does not find, | my foster-mother,
the way to comfort | so young a wife."
She told them to uncover | the warrior's corpse.
She lifted the shroud | from Sigurth, laying
his well-loved head | on the knees of his wife:
"Look on your loved one, | and lay your lips
to his as if | the hero still lived."
Only once | did Guthrun look;
she saw his hair | all clotted with blood,
the blinded eyes | that once shone bright,
the hero's breast | that the blade had pierced.
Then Guthrun bent, | bowed on her pillow,
her hair came loose, | her cheek was hot,
and the tears like raindrops | ran down.
Then Guthrun, daughter | of Gjuki, wept,
and through her tresses | the tears flowed;
and from the court | came the cry of geese,
the fair birds | of the hero's bride.
Then Gollrond spoke, | the daughter of Gjuki:
"I never knew | a greater love
than yours among | all people on earth;
you were happy nowhere, | at home or abroad,
my sister, | with Sigurth away."
Guthrun said:
"My Sigurth stood | above Gjuki's sons
as the spear-leek grows | above the grass,
or the bright jewel | set on the band,
the precious stone | that princes wear.
"To the leader of men | I seemed loftier
and higher than all | of Herjan's maids;
now I am as little | as the leaf
hanging on the willow; | my hero is dead.
"In his seat, in his bed, | I no longer see
my heart's true friend; | the fault is theirs,
the sons of Gjuki, | for all my grief,
that their sister | weeps so bitterly.
"Your land shall lose | its people
just as you have kept | the oaths you once swore;
Gunnar, the gold | shall give you no joy,
(the rings shall soon | be your killers,)
you who once swore | oaths with Sigurth.
"There was greater gladness | in the court then,
the day my Sigurth | saddled Grani,
and went out to win | Brynhild's hand,
that evil woman, | in an evil hour."
Then Brynhild spoke, | the daughter of Buthli:
"May the witch now lack | husband and children
who, Guthrun, loosed | your tears at last,
and with magic today | has made you speak."
Then Gollrond, daughter | of Gjuki, spoke:
"Do not speak such words, | you hated woman;
you have always been | the ruin of the noble,
(you are carried | on an evil wave,
you have brought sorrow | to seven kings,)
and left many a woman | without love."
Then Brynhild, daughter | of Buthli, spoke:
"Atli is guilty | of all the sorrow,
(son of Buthli | and brother of mine,)
when we saw in the hall | of the Hunnish race
the flame of the snake's bed | flash round the hero;
(I have paid dearly | for that journey since,
and I always seek | to forget the sight.)"
She stood by the pillars | and gathered her strength;
from the eyes of Brynhild, | Buthli's daughter,
fire burned, | and she breathed out poison,
when she saw the wounds | on Sigurth then.

gdr1-p2.s: Guthrun went away from there to a forest in the wilderness, and travelled all the way to Denmark, and stayed there seven half-years with Thora, daughter of Hokon. Brynhild would not live after Sigurth. She had eight of her slaves killed, and five serving-women. Then she killed herself with a sword, as is told in the Short Lay of Sigurth.

gdr2-p1.s: King Thjothrek was with Atli, and had lost most of his men. Thjothrek and Guthrun lamented their griefs together. She spoke to him, saying:

l: A maid of maids | my mother bore me,
bright in my bower, | I loved my brothers,
till Gjuki dowered | me with gold,
dowered me with gold, | and gave me to Sigurth.
Sigurth rose | above Gjuki's sons
as the leek grows green | above the grass,
or the stag stands | above all the beasts,
or as glow-red gold | above grey silver.
Till my brothers | would no longer let me
have the best of heroes | as my husband;
they could not sleep, | or settle quarrels,
till at last | they had killed Sigurth.
From the Thing ran Grani | with thundering feet,
but Sigurth himself | never came from there;
the saddle-bearer | was covered with sweat,
used to bearing | the warrior's weight.
Weeping I went | to speak with Grani,
with tear-wet cheeks | I asked for the tale;
the head of Grani | was bowed to the grass,
the horse knew well | his master was killed.
Long I waited | and pondered well
before I ever asked | the king for news.
Gunnar bowed his head, | but Hogni told
the bitter news | of Sigurth killed:
"Hewn to death | at our hands he lies,
Gotthorm's slayer, | given to the wolves.
"On the southern road | you shall see Sigurth,
where you can hear | the ravens cry;
the eagles cry, | craving food,
and about your husband | wolves are howling."
"Why, Hogni, | do you let me hear
such a horror, | left as I am without joy?
Ravens shall yet | tear your heart
in a land | you have never known."
Hogni's words | were few,
his heart bitter | from heavy sorrow:
"Your grief, Guthrun, | shall be greater
if the ravens | tear my heart so."
I soon turned away | from the one who spoke,
to find in the woods | what the wolves had left;
I shed no tears, | nor wrung my hands,
nor went wailing, | as other women do,
(when I sat | by the slain Sigurth).
Never had the night | seemed so black
as when I sat | in sorrow by Sigurth;
the wolves...........
It seemed to me | it would be best of all
if I could only | lose my life,
or be burned | like birch-wood.
From the mountain | I travelled five days,
till I saw | Hoalf's high hall;
seven half-years | I stayed with Thora,
Hokon's daughter, | in Denmark then.
She embroidered with gold, | to bring me joy,
southern halls | and Danish swans;
on the tapestry we wove | warriors' deeds,
and the hero's thanes | in our handiwork;
(flashing shields | and armed fighters,
sword-throng, helm-throng, | the host of the king).
Sigmund's ship | was sailing by the land,
golden the figure-head, | bright the prows;
on board we wove | the warriors sailing,
Sigar and Siggeir, | south to Fjon.
Then Grimhild asked, | the Gothic queen,
whether I would | willingly......
She threw her needlework | aside, and called
her sons to ask, | with stern resolve,
who would make amends | to their sister for her son,
or repay the wife | for her husband killed.
Gunnar was ready | to give gold,
amends for my hurt, | and Hogni too;
then she wished to know | who would now go
to saddle the horse, | to harness the wagon,
(to ride the horse, | to fly the hawk,
and to shoot arrows | from bows of yew).
(Valdar, king | of the Danes, had come,
with Jarizleif, Eymoth, | and Jarizskar).
Like princes | they all came in,
the long-beard men, | with red cloaks,
short their mail-coats, | mighty their helmets,
swords at their belts, | and brown their hair.
Each was eager | to give me gifts,
to give gifts, | and to speak kindly;
in this way they tried | to bring me comfort
for my great sorrows, | but I did not trust them.
Grimhild gave me | a draught to drink,
bitter and cold; | I forgot my cares;
for mingled in it | was magic earth,
ice-cold sea, | and the blood of swine.
In the cup were runes | of every kind,
written and reddened; | I could not read them;
a heather-fish | from the Haddings' land,
an uncut ear of corn, | and the entrails of beasts.
Much evil was brewed | into the beer,
blossoms of trees, | and burnt acorns,
dew of the hearth, | and holy entrails,
the liver of swine, | to still all grief.
Then I forgot, | when they gave me the draught,
there in the hall, | my husband's killing;
all three kings | knelt on their knees,
before she herself | began to speak:
"Guthrun, I give you | gold,
the wealth that once | was your father's,
rings to have, | and Hlothver's halls,
and all the hangings | that the monarch had.
"Hunnish women, | skilled in weaving,
who work gold finely | to give you joy,
and the wealth of Buthli | shall be yours,
gold-decked one, | as Atli's wife."
Guthrun said:
"I will not have | a husband now,
nor be the wife | of Brynhild's brother;
it is not fitting for me | to be happy
with Buthli's son, | and bear him heirs."
Grimhild said:
"Do not seek to avenge | your sorrows on men,
though the blame at first | was ours;
you shall be as happy | as if both still lived,
Sigurth and Sigmund, | if you bear sons."
Guthrun said:
"Grimhild, I cannot | find gladness,
nor hold out hopes | to heroes now,
since the raven | and the ravening wolf
once hungrily lapped | Sigurth's heart's-blood."
Grimhild said:
"Noblest of birth | is the ruler
I have now found for you, | and foremost of all;
you shall have him | as long as you live,
or be without a husband | if you will not choose him.
Guthrun said:
"Do not seek so eagerly | to send me
to be a bride | of that baneful race;
on Gunnar first | his anger shall fall,
and he will tear the heart | from Hogni's breast."
Weeping, Grimhild | heard the words
that foretold a bitter fate | for her sons,
(and would bring | great sorrow on them;)
"I give you lands, | with all who live there,
(Vinbjorg is yours, | and Valbjorg too,)
have them for ever, | but hear me, daughter."
So I had to do | as the kings begged,
and marry against my will | for my kinsmen's sake;
I never had joy | with my husband,
and my sons were not saved | by my brothers' fate.
I could not rest | till I had robbed of life
the bold warrior, | the maker of battles.
Soon each hero | was on horseback,
and the foreign women | riding in wagons;
for a week we went | through lands so cold,
and a second week | we beat the waves,
(and a third through lands | that had no water).
Now the watchmen | on the high walls
opened the gates, | and in we rode.
Atli woke me, | for I always seemed
full of bitterness | for my brothers' death.
Atli said:
"Now the Norns | have woken me from sleep
with visions of terror; | I will tell you them;
I dreamed that you, Guthrun, | Gjuki's daughter,
pierced my body | with a poisoned blade."
Guthrun said:
"A dream of steel | means fire will follow,
and one of a woman's wrath | means wilful pride;
I shall burn | a deadly sore from you,
and tend and heal you, | though you are hated."
Atli said:
"I dreamed of plants, | drooping in the garden,
that I would gladly | have had grow tall;
torn up by the roots, | and red with blood,
they brought them here, | and told me to eat.
"I dreamed my hawks | had flown from my hand,
eager for food, | to an evil house;
I dreamed I ate | their hearts with honey,
soaked in blood, | and my sorrow was heavy.
"I dreamed of hounds | I loosed from my hand,
loudly they howled | in hunger and pain;
it seemed their flesh | was eagles' food,
and now I must | eat their bodies."
Guthrun said:
"Men shall soon | speak of sacrifice,
and cut the heads | off beasts;
they shall die | before day has dawned,
a few nights from now, | and the people shall have them."
Atli said:
"I sank on my bed, | and did not seek sleep,
weary with grief; | I remember it well."

gdr3-p1.s: Herkja was the name of a serving-woman of Atli's; she had been his concubine. She told Atli that she had seen Thjothrek and Guthrun together. Atli was very angry at this. Then Guthrun said:

l: "What is your sorrow, Atli, | Buthli's son?
Is your heart heavy? | Why do you never laugh?
It would suit | the warrior far better
to speak with men, | and to look at me."
Atli said:
"It troubles me, Guthrun, | Gjuki's daughter,
what Herkja has told me | here in the hall,
that you lie | in bed with Thjothrek,
beneath the linen, | as lovers do."
Guthrun said:
"This I shall | now swear with oaths,
swear by the sacred | stone so white,
that there was nothing | with Thjothmar's son
that man or woman | may not know.
"Not even once | did my arms embrace
the brave hero, | the leader of hosts;
our meeting | was of another kind,
when we told | our sorrows in secret.
"With thirty warriors | Thjothrek came,
and of all his men | not one remains;
you have murdered my brothers | and mail-clad men,
you have murdered all | the men of my race.
"Gunnar does not come, | I do not greet Hogni,
I no longer see | my dear brothers;
Hogni would avenge | my sorrow with the sword,
now I myself | must win payment for my wrongs.
"Summon Saxi, | the southerners' king,
for he can hallow | the boiling cauldron."
Seven hundred | were there in the hall,
before the queen thrust | her hand into the cauldron.
She reached to the bottom | with her bright hand,
and brought out | the flashing stones:
"See, you warriors, | I am fully cleared
of sin by the cauldron's | sacred boiling."
Then Atli's heart | laughed with happiness,
when he saw | Guthrun's hand unhurt;
"Now Herkja shall come | to try the cauldron,
she who planned | grief for Guthrun."
No man ever saw | a sadder sight than this,
how Herkja's hands | were burned then;
they threw the maid | into a foul bog,
and so Guthrun's | grief was repaid.

ghv-p1.s: Guthrun went down to the sea after she had killed Atli. She walked out into the sea and wanted to drown herself, but she could not sink. The waves carried her across the fjord to the land of King Jonak; he married her, and their sons were Sorli, Erp and Hamther. Svanhild, Sigurth's daughter, was brought up there; she was married to the mighty Jormunrek. With him was Bikki, who advised that Randver, the king's son, should have her. Bikki told the king of this. The king had Randver hanged, and Svanhild trampled to death under horses' hooves. And when Guthrun learned this, she spoke to her sons.

l: I have heard of a quarrel, | the most sorrowful of all,
a speech spoken | from the fullness of grief,
when, fierce of heart, | Guthrun goaded
her sons to the fight | with grim words.
"Why do you sit idle, | why sleep your lives away,
why does it not grieve you | to speak in gladness?
For Jormunrek | has trampled your young sister
