beneath the hooves | of horses,
(white and black | on the battle-road,
grey, used to the road, | the steeds of the Goths.)
"You are not like | Gunnar of old,
nor have you hearts | such as Hogni's was;
you would soon have | vengeance for her
if you were brave | as my brothers of old,
or your hearts as hard | as the Hunnish kings'."
Then Hamther spoke, | the high of heart:
"Little you loved | the deed of Hogni,
when they woke Sigurth | from his sleep;
your white bed-covers | were red with the blood
of your husband, drenched | with gore from his heart.
"You had bloody revenge | for your brothers,
evil and bitter, | when you killed your sons;
otherwise we might all | together yet
avenge on Jormunrek | our sister's killing.
Give us now the gear | of the Hunnish kings!
You have goaded us so | to the battle of swords."
Laughing, Guthrun | went to her chamber,
the helmets of the kings | she took from the cupboards,
and broad mail-coats, | and brought them to her sons;
the heroes leapt | onto their horses' backs.
Then Hamther spoke, | the high of heart:
"Never again home | to see his mother
comes the spear-god, fallen | among the Gothic people;
one death-draught | you shall drink for us all,
for Svanhild then | and for your sons as well."
Weeping, Guthrun, | Gjuki's daughter,
went sadly to sit | before the gate,
and with tear-stained cheeks | to tell the tale
of her mighty griefs, | of so many kinds.
"Three home-fires I knew, | three hearths I knew,
I was brought home | by three husbands;
but Sigurth alone | of them all was dear,
he whom my brothers | brought to his death.
"A greater sorrow | I never saw or knew,
yet it seemed | I must suffer still more
when the great princes | gave me to Atli.
"I called the brave boys | to speak in secret;
I could not win | repayment for my woes
until I had cut off | the heads of the Hniflungs.
"I went to the sea, | my heart full of bitterness
towards the Norns, whose anger | I now wished to escape;
but the high waves | carried me undrowned,
until I came to land, | and so must live longer.
"Then to the bed | (it was better in the old days!)
of a king of the people | I came a third time;
I bore boys | to be his heirs,
heirs so young, | the sons of Jonak.
"But around Svanhild | handmaidens sat,
she was always the dearest | of all my children;
Svanhild seemed | in my hall
as a ray of the sun | is fair to see.
"I gave her gold | and bright garments,
before I let her go | to the Gothic people;
of my heavy woes | the hardest was
when Svanhild's fair hair | was trampled
in the mud by the hooves | of wild horses.
"The most painful was | when my Sigurth,
robbed of victory, | they killed in his bed;
and the grimmest of all | when to Gunnar's heart
crept the bright-coloured | crawling snakes.
"And the keenest of all | when they cut the heart
from the living breast | of the king so brave;
many woes I remember, | ........
"Bridle, Sigurth, | your black steed,
let your swift horse | run here;
here there sits | no son or daughter
who will yet give | gifts to Guthrun.
"Remember, Sigurth, | what we once said,
when the two of us | sat on the bed together,
that you would come | in your might to me
from hell, and I | from earth to you.
"Pile up, jarls, | the pyre of oak,
make it the highest | a hero ever had;
let the fire burn | my grief-filled breast,
my sorely pressed heart, | till my sorrows melt."
May all nobles | know less sorrow,
and the woes of women | grow less,
now that the tale | of this lament is told.
Svipdag said:
"Wake, Groa! | Wake, good mother!
At the doors of the dead I call you;
your son, remember, | you told to seek
your help at the hill of death."
Groa said:
"What evil troubles | my only son,
what dreadful fate have you met,
that you call your mother, | who lies in the earth,
and has left the world of the living?"
Svipdag said:
"The false woman | whom my father embraced
has set me an evil game;
for she told me to go out | where no one may go,
and to seek the maid Mengloth."
Groa said:
"Long is the way, | long must you wander,
but love lasts long as well;
you may find, perhaps, | what you wish to have,
if the fates will give their favour."
Svipdag said:
"Then chant good charms | for me, mother,
and seek to guard your son;
for I fear death | on the way I must go,
and I am young in years, I think."
Groa said:
"Then first I will chant for you | the well-tried charm
that Rani taught to Rind;
shake from your shoulder | whatever displeases you,
for you shall have yourself as helper.
"Then next I will chant for you, | if you must travel
and wander a purposeless way:
the bolts of Urth | shall on every side
be your guards on the road you go.
"Then third I will chant for you, | if threatening rivers
should bring danger of death:
yet Horn and Ruth | shall both turn to Hel,
and the waters shall fail before you.
"Then fourth I will chant for you, | if your enemies come
against you on the gallows-way:
their hearts shall be given | into your hands,
and the warriors shall wish for peace.
"Then fifth I will chant for you, | if fetters perhaps
should bind your bending limbs:
over your thighs I chant | a loosening-charm,
and the lock is burst from the limbs,
and the fetters fall from the feet.
"Then sixth I will chant for you, | if storms at sea
have power unknown to man:
yet wind and wave | shall never do harm,
and calm is the course of your boat.
"Then seventh I chant for you, | if frost should seek
to kill you on high crags:
the deadly cold | shall not grip your flesh,
and your body shall be whole.
"Then eighth I will chant for you, | if ever by night
you wander on murky ways:
yet never shall the curse | of a Christian woman
from the dead do you harm.
"Then ninth I will chant for you, | if you must contend
in words with a warlike giant:
your heart shall have | a good store of wit,
and your mouth of wise words.
"Now go on the way | where danger waits,
let no evils lessen your love!
I have stood at the door | of the earth-fixed stones,
while I chanted charms for you.
"Carry away, my son, | what your mother has said,
and let it live in your breast;
the best of fortune | shall always be yours,
as long as my words shall last."

grm-p1.s: King Hrauthung had two sons: one was called Agnar, and the other Geirröth. Agnar was ten winters old, and Geirröth eight. Once the two of them rowed out in a boat with their fishing tackle to catch small fish, and the wind drove them out to sea. In the darkness of the night they were wrecked on the shore; they went up and found a poor peasant, and stayed with him through the winter. The peasant's wife looked after Agnar, and the peasant looked after Geirröth and taught him wisdom. In the spring the peasant gave him a boat; and when the couple took them down to the shore, the peasant spoke privately with Geirröth. They had a fair wind and came to their father's landing-place. Geirröth was in the bow of the boat; he leapt ashore, but pushed the boat out and said, "Go now where evil may take you!" The boat drifted out to sea. Geirröth, however, went up to the house and was well received, but his father was dead. Then Geirröth was made king, and became a famous man.

Othin and Frigg sat in Hlithskjolf and looked out over all the worlds. Othin said: "Do you see Agnar, your foster-son, fathering children with a giantess in the cave? But Geirröth, my foster-son, is a king, and now rules over his land." Frigg said: "He is so miserly that he tortures his guests if he thinks too many of them have come to him." Othin replied that this was the greatest of lies, and they made a wager on the matter. Frigg sent her maidservant, Fulla, to Geirröth. She told the king to beware of a magician who had come to his land, in case he should bewitch him, and gave this sign to know him by: that no dog was so fierce that it would leap at him. Now it was a very great slander that King Geirröth was not hospitable; but all the same he had his men seize the man whom the dogs would not attack. He wore a dark-blue cloak and called himself Grimnir, but said nothing more about himself, though he was questioned. The king had him tortured to make him speak, and set him between two fires, and he sat there for eight nights. King Geirröth had a son ten winters old, called Agnar after his father's brother. Agnar went to Grimnir, gave him a full horn to drink from, and said that the king did wrong to have him tormented without cause. Grimnir drank from the horn; the fire had come so close that the cloak was burning on Grimnir's back. He said:

l: You are hot, fire! | Far too fierce;
be gone now, you flames!
The cloak is burnt, | though I hold it up high,
and the fire scorches the fur.
Between the fires now | eight nights I have sat,
and no man brought me food,
except Agnar alone, | and he alone shall rule,
Geirröth's son, over the Goths.
Hail to you, Agnar! | For you are hailed
by the voice of Veratyr;
for a single drink | you shall never receive
a greater gift as reward.
The land is holy | that lies close by
the gods and the elves together;
and Thor shall always | live in Thruthheim,
till the gods go to destruction.
Ydalir they call | the place where Ull
has set up a hall for himself;
and Alfheim the gods | once gave to Freyr
as a tooth-gift in ancient times.
There is a third home, | thatched with silver
by the hands of the gracious gods:
Valaskjolf it is, | in days of old
set up by a god for himself.
Sökkvabekk is the fourth, | where cool waves flow,
and amid their murmur it stands;
there daily Othin | and Saga drink
in gladness from cups of gold.
The fifth is Glathsheim, | and there, gold-bright,
stands Valhall stretching wide;
and there Othin | chooses each day
the men who have fallen in battle.
It is easy to know | for one who comes
to Othin and sees the hall;
its rafters are spears, | it is roofed with shields,
on its benches breastplates are strewn.
It is easy to know | for one who comes
to Othin and sees the hall;
a wolf hangs there | by the western door,
and over it an eagle hovers.
The sixth is Thrymheim, | where Thjazi lived,
the giant of marvellous might;
now Skathi lives, | the god's fair bride,
in the home that her father had.
The seventh is Breithablik; | there Baldr has
set up a dwelling for himself,
in the land I know | that lies so fair,
and is free from evil fate.
Himinbjorg is the eighth, | and Heimdall there
holds sway over men, it is said;
in his well-built house | the watchman of heaven
gladly drinks the good mead.
The ninth is Folkvang, | where Freyja decides
who shall have seats in the hall;
half of the dead | she chooses each day,
and half Othin has.
The tenth is Glitnir; | its pillars are gold,
and its roof is set with silver;
there Forseti lives | most of his days,
and puts an end to all strife.
The eleventh is Noatun; | there Njorth has
set up a dwelling for himself;
the sinless ruler | of men sits there
in his high-timbered temple.
Filled with growing trees | and high-standing grass
is Vithi, Vithar's land;
but there the son | leapt down from his steed,
when he wished to avenge his father.
In Eldhrimnir | Andhrimnir cooks
Sæhrimnir's seething flesh,
the best of food, | but few men know
on what fare the warriors feast.
Freki and Geri | Herjafödr feeds,
the far-famed fighter of old:
but on wine alone | the weapon-decked god,
Othin, lives for ever.
Over Mithgarth Hugin | and Munin both
set out each day to fly;
for Hugin I fear | that he may not come home,
but I worry more for Munin.
Loud roars Thund, | and Thjothvitnir's fish
swims joyfully in the flood;
hard it seems | to the host of the slain
to wade the wild torrent.
There Valgrind stands, | the sacred gate,
and behind are the holy doors;
the gate is old, | but there are few
who can tell how tightly it is locked.
Five hundred doors | and forty there are,
I think, in Valhall's walls;
eight hundred Einherjar | go through one door
when they go to war with the wolf.
Five hundred rooms | and forty there are,
I think, built in Bilskirnir;
of all the homes | whose roofs I have seen,
my son's seemed to me the greatest.
Heithrun is the goat | who stands by Herjafödr's hall,
and bites the branches of Lærath;
she fills the pitcher | with fair, clear mead,
the foaming drink never fails.
Eikthyrnir is the stag | who stands by Herjafödr's hall
and bites the branches of Lærath;
from his horns a stream | drops into Hvergelmir,
and from there all the rivers run.
Sith and Vith, | Sækin and Ækin,
Svol and Fimbulthul, | Gunnthro and Fjorm,
Rin and Rinnandi,
Gipul and Gopul, | Gomul and Geirvimul,
that flow through the fields of the gods;
Thyn and Vin, | Thol and Hol,
Groth and Gunnthorin.
Vino is one, | Vegsvin another,
and Thjothnuma a third;
Nyt and Not, | Non and Hron,
Slith and Hrith, | Sylg and Ylg,
Vith and Von, | Vond and Strond,
Gjol and Leipt, | that go among men,
and from here they fall to Hel.
Kormt and Ormt | and the two Kerlaugs
Thor shall wade through each day,
(when he goes out | to give judgements
at the ash-tree Yggdrasil;)
for heaven's bridge | burns all in flame,
and the sacred waters seethe.
Glath and Gyllir, | Gler and Skeithbrimir,
Silfrintopp and Sinir,
Gisl and Falhofnir, | Golltopp and Lettfeti,
on these steeds the gods shall go
when to give judgements | they ride each day
to the ash-tree Yggdrasil.
Three roots there are | that run three ways
beneath the ash-tree Yggdrasil;
beneath the first lives Hel, | beneath the second the frost giants,
beneath the last are the lands of men.
Ratatosk is the squirrel | who shall run there
on the ash-tree Yggdrasil;
from above he carries | the eagle's words,
and tells them to Nithhogg below.
Four stags there are, | that nibble the highest twigs
with necks bent back;
Dain and Dvalin, | ......
Duneyr and Dyrathror.
More serpents there are | beneath the ash
than an unwise ape would think;
Goin and Moin, | Grafvitnir's sons,
Grabak and Grafvolluth,
Ofnir and Svafnir | shall always, I think,
gnaw at the twigs of the tree.
Yggdrasil's ash | suffers great evil,
far more than men know;
the stag bites its top, | its trunk is rotting,
and Nithhogg gnaws beneath.
Hrist and Mist | bring the horn at my will,
Skeggjold and Skogul;
Hild and Thruth, | Hlok and Herfjotur,
Gol and Geironul,
Randgrith and Rathgrith | and Reginleif
bring beer to the Einherjar.
Arvak and Alsvith | shall drag up,
weary, the weight of the sun;
but a cooling iron | the kindly gods
set long ago under their yokes.
In front of the sun | Svalin stands,
the shield for the shining god;
mountains and sea | would be set in flames
if it fell from before the sun.
Skoll is the wolf | that to the sheltering wood
follows the glittering god,
and the son of Hrothvitnir, | Hati, awaits
the burning bride of heaven.
Out of Ymir's flesh | the earth was made,
and the ocean out of his blood;
from his bones the hills, | from his hair the trees,
from his skull the high heavens.
Mithgarth the gods | made from his eyebrows,
and set for the sons of men;
and out of his brain | the grim clouds
they made to move on high.
His is the favour of Ull | and of all the gods
who first reaches into the flames;
for the house can be seen | by the sons of the gods
if the cauldron were cast aside.
In days of old | Ivaldi's sons
fashioned Skithblathnir fair,
the best of ships | for the bright god Freyr,
the noble son of Njorth.
The best of trees | Yggdrasil must be,
Skithblathnir the best of boats;
of all the gods | Othin is the greatest,
and Sleipnir the best of steeds;
Bilrost of bridges, | Bragi of poets,
Hobrok of hawks, | and Garm of hounds.
To the race of the gods | I have raised my face,
and I have woken the wished-for help;
for the message has gone | to all the gods
who sit in Ægir's seats,
who drink within Ægir's doors.
Grim is my name, | I am Gangleri,
Herjan and Hjalmberi,
Thekk and Thrithi, | Thuth and Uth,
Helblindi and Hor;
Sath and Svipal | and Sanngetal,
Herteit and Hnikar,
Bileyg, Baleyg, | Bolverk, Fjolnir,
Grim and Grimnir, | Glapsvith, Fjolsvith.
Sithhott, Sithskegg, | Sigfather, Hnikuth,
Alfödr, Valfather, | Atrith, Farmatyr:
a single name | I have never had
since first I travelled among men.
Grimnir they call me | in Geirröth's hall,
with Asmund I am Jalk;
Kjalar I was | when I travelled in a sledge,
at the council I am called Thror,
as Vithur I go to the fight;
Oski, Biflindi, | Jafnhor and Omi,
Gondlir and Harbarth among the gods.
I deceived the giant, | old Sokkmimir,
as Svithur and Svithrir long ago;
of Mithvitnir's son | I was the killer
when the famous one met his doom.
You are drunk, Geirröth, | you have drunk too much,
you have lost much, | for you have no more help
from me or the Einherjar.
You paid little heed | to all that I told,
and the words of your friends were false;
for now I see | the sword of my friend,
that waits all wet with blood.
Your sword-pierced body | Ygg shall soon have,
for your life is ended at last;
the maids are hostile; | now look upon Othin!
Now come to me if you can!
Now I am Othin, | Ygg I was once,
before that they called me Thund;
Vak and Skilfing, | Vofuth and Hroptatyr,
Gaut and Jalk among the gods;
Ofnir and Svafnir, | and all, I think,
are names for none but me.

grm-p2.s: King Geirröth sat with his sword on his knee, half drawn from its sheath. But when he heard that Othin had come there, he stood up and tried to take Othin from the fire. The sword slipped from his hand and fell hilt down. The king stumbled and fell forward, and the sword pierced him through and killed him. Then Othin vanished, but Agnar ruled there as king for a long time.

grp-p1.s: Sigmund, the son of Volsung, was a king in the land of the Franks. Sinfjotli was his eldest son, the second was Helgi and the third Hamund. Borghild, Sigmund's wife, had a brother who was named ... Her stepson Sinfjotli and ... both courted the same woman, and for that reason Sinfjotli killed him. When he came home, Borghild told him to leave, but Sigmund offered her compensation, and she had to accept it. At the funeral feast Borghild brought in the ale; she took poison, a great hornful, and brought it to Sinfjotli. But when he looked into the horn he saw that it was poison, and said to Sigmund: "The drink is cloudy, Father!" Sigmund took the horn and drank from it. It is said that Sigmund was so hardy that poison could not harm him, either outside or in, but all his sons could withstand poison only on the outside, on their skin. Borghild brought Sinfjotli another horn and told him to drink, and everything happened as before. A third time she brought him a horn, and with it spoke scornfully of him if he would not drink from it. He spoke to Sigmund as before. Sigmund said: "Let it trickle through your beard, Son!" Sinfjotli drank, and was dead at once. Sigmund carried him a long way in his arms, and came to a long, narrow fjord, where there was a small boat with a man in it. He offered to take Sigmund across the fjord. But when Sigmund had carried the body out into the boat, the craft was full. The man told Sigmund to go round the inner end of the fjord. Then the man pushed the boat off, and disappeared.

King Sigmund lived for a long time in Denmark, in Borghild's kingdom, after he had married her. Afterwards Sigmund went south into the land of the Franks, to the kingdom he had there. There he married Hjordis, the daughter of King Eylimi; their son was Sigurth. King Sigmund fell in a battle with the sons of Hunding, and Hjordis then married Alf, the son of King Hjalprek. There Sigurth grew up in his boyhood. Sigmund and all his sons were far above all other men in strength and stature and courage and every kind of ability. Sigurth, however, was the foremost of all, and in the old tales all men call him the noblest of mankind and the mightiest leader.

Gripir was the name of Eylimi's son, the brother of Hjordis; he ruled over lands and was the wisest of all men and the most far-seeing. Sigurth was once riding alone and came to Gripir's hall. Sigurth was easy to recognise; out in front of the hall he found a man whose name was Geitir. Then Sigurth questioned him and asked:

l: "Who is it that has | this dwelling here,
and what do men call | the people's king?"
Geitir said:
"Gripir is the name | of the good chieftain
who rules the people | and the firm-ruled land."
Sigurth said:
"Is the all-knowing king | now within?
Will the monarch come | to speak with me?

the woman so fair; | it is Grimhild's work."

you would tell me | of more joy
in my life to come | if you could."

The day after, | the frost giants came
to win some word of Hor
(and into the hall of Hor);
they asked about Bolverk: | was he back among the gods,
or had Suttung killed him there?
Othin, I think, | swore the oath on his ring;
who shall trust his pledge now?
He sought to betray | Suttung with drink,
and he left Gunnloth to grief.
It is time to chant | from the chanter's stool;
I was by Urdarbrunnr,
I saw and was silent, | I saw and thought,
and heard the speech of Hor.
(Of runes I heard words, | and counsels were not lacking,
at the hall of Hor,
in the hall of Hor;
such was the speech I heard.)
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
do not rise at night, | unless you are seeking news,
or wish to go to the outhouse.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
beware of sleeping | on a witch's breast,
and do not let her limbs ensnare you.
Such is her power | that you have no mind
for the council or the meeting of men;
you hate your food, | you have no joy,
and sadly you go to sleep.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
never seek to win | another man's wife,
or long for her secret love.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
if over mountains or gulfs | you wish to go,
see well to your food for the way.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
you must not let | an evil man
bring any harm to you;
for an evil man | will never give
a reward for a worthy thought.
I saw a man | who was sorely wounded
by an evil woman's word;
a lying tongue | dealt him his death-blow,
and there was no word of truth in it.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
if you have a friend | whom you fully trust,
then go to see him often;
for brambles grow | and waving grass
on the rarely trodden road.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
find a good man | to hold in friendship,
and pay heed to his healing charms.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
never be the first | to break with your friend
the bond that holds you both;
care eats the heart | if you cannot tell
another all your thoughts.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
you must never | exchange words
with a witless ape.
For you can never | get from an evil man
a good return;
but a good man will often | win you the greatest love
through words of praise.
Love is mingled | when a man can tell
another all his thoughts;
nothing is so bad | as to be false;
no friend speaks only fair words.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
do not exchange three words | in dispute with a worse man;
often the better man fares badly
when the worse man wields a sword.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
be a shoemaker, | or a maker of shafts,
only for yourself alone;
if the shoe is badly made, | or the shaft proves false,
then men think ill of you.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
if you know of evil, | proclaim it as evil,
and make no friendship with enemies.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
never take | joy in evil,
but let the good make you glad.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
do not look up | when the battle is on,
(the sons of men | become like madmen,)
in case men bewitch your wits.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
if you want to win | a woman's love,
and get gladness from her,
let your promise be fair | and well fulfilled;
no one loathes the good he gets.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
I bid you be wary, | but not fearful;
(be most wary with ale | or another man's wife,
and thirdly beware | that a thief does not outwit you.)
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
never treat | with scorn or mockery
a guest or a traveller.
Often he who sits in the house | hardly knows
what kind of man it is who comes;
no one is so good | that he has no faults,
nor so wicked that he is worth nothing.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
never scorn | the grey-haired singer;
the old often speak good;
(often from shrivelled skin | come skilful counsels,
though it hangs with the hides,
and flaps with the pelts,
and is blown with the bellies.)
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
do not curse your guest, | nor show him the gate;
deal well with a man in want.
Strong is the beam | that must be raised
to give an entrance to all;
give it a ring, | or grim will be
the wish it would work on you.
I counsel you, Loddfafnir, | and hear my counsel;
you will profit if you hear it,
you will gain greatly if you learn it:
when you drink ale, | seek the might of earth,
(for earth cures drink, | and fire cures ills,
the oak cures tightness, | the ear cures magic,
rye cures rupture, | the moon cures rage,
grass cures the scab, | and runes the sword-cut;)
the field absorbs the flood.
Now Hor's words | are spoken in the hall,
kind for the kindred of men,
cursed for the kindred of giants:
hail to the speaker, | and to him who learns!
May he profit who has them!
Hail to those who listen!
I know that I hung | on the windy tree,
hung there for nine whole nights;
I was wounded with the spear, | and I was offered
to Othin, myself to myself,
on the tree of which | no one can ever know
from what root it rises.
No one cheered me | with loaf or horn,
and I looked down below;
I took up the runes, | shrieking I took them,
and at once I fell back.
Nine mighty songs | I got from the son
of Bolthorn, Bestla's father;
and I got a drink | of the fine mead
poured out from Othrörir.
Then I began to thrive | and to gain wisdom,
I grew and did well;
each word led me on | to another word,
each deed to another deed.
Runes you shall find, | and fateful signs,
that the king of singers coloured,
and the mighty gods have made;
very strong the signs, | very mighty the signs
that the ruler of gods writes.
Othin for the gods, | Dain for the elves,
and Dvalin for the dwarfs,
Alsvith for giants | and all mankind,
and some I wrote myself.
Do you know how to write, | do you know how to interpret?
Do you know how to tint, | do you know how to make trial?
Do you know how to ask, | do you know how to offer?
Do you know how to send, | do you know how to sacrifice?
Better no prayer | than too big an offering;
measure your gift by what you get;
better none | than too big a sacrifice,
So Thund wrote of old | before the race of men began,
where he rose on high | when he came home.
I know the songs | that king's wives do not know,
nor men who are sons of men;
the first is called help, | and help it can bring you
in sorrow and pain and sickness.
A second I know, | which men will need
who long to practise healing;
A third I know, | if I have great need
of fetters to hold my enemy;
I blunt | my enemy's blade,
and neither his sword nor his staff will bite.
A fourth I know, | if men fasten
bonds on my bent legs;
so strong is the charm | that I can walk free,
the fetters spring from my feet,
the bonds break from my hands.
A fifth I know, | if I see from afar
an arrow flying against the host;
it does not fly so fast | that I cannot stop it,
if only my eyes catch sight of it.
A sixth I know, | if someone seeks
to send me harm with a sapling's roots;
the hero himself | who wreaks his hate
shall taste the ill before I do.
A seventh I know, | if I see in flames
the hall over my comrades' heads;
it does not burn so widely | that I will not quench it;
I know that song to sing.
An eighth I know, | which is for all
of the greatest good to learn;
when hatred grows | among heroes' sons,
I can soon set it right.
A ninth I know, | if the need comes
to shelter my ship on the flood;
I calm the wind | upon the waves,
and I put the sea to sleep.
A tenth I know, | whenever I see
house-riders flying on high;
I can work it | so that they go wildly,
showing their true shapes,
away to their own homes.
An eleventh I know, | if I must lead
my long-loved friends to the fight;
I sing in the shields, | and in strength they go
whole to the field of battle,
whole from the field of battle,
and whole they come home from there.
A twelfth I know, | if high on a tree
I see a hanged man swing;
I so write | and colour the runes
that he walks out
and talks to me.
A thirteenth I know, | if I sprinkle
a very young thane well with water;
he shall not fall, | though he goes among the host,
nor sink beneath the swords.
A fourteenth I know, | if I wish to name
the mighty gods to men;
I know all about | the gods and elves;
few are the fools who know this.
A fifteenth I know, | which before the doors
of Delling Thjothrörir the dwarf sang;
he sang might for the gods, | and glory for elves,
and wisdom for wise Hroptatyr.
A sixteenth I know, | if I seek to win
delight from a wise girl;
I turn the mind | of the white-armed girl,
and so change all her thoughts.
A seventeenth I know, | so that a young girl
will seldom leave me;
These songs, Loddfafnir, | you will long
seek in vain to sing;
yet it would be good | if you could get them,
well if you would learn them,
a help if you had them.
An eighteenth I know, | which I will never tell
to a girl or a man's wife;
the best is what none | but oneself knows,
so comes the end of the songs;
except only to her | in whose arms I lie,
or who else is my sister.
Freyja said:
"Maiden, awake! | Wake up, my friend,
my sister Hyndla, | in your hollow cave!
Darkness is coming already, | and we must ride
to Valhall to seek | the sacred hall.
"Let us seek to find | the favour of Herjafödr;
to his followers | he gladly gives gold;
to Hermoth he gave | helmet and mail-coat,
and to Sigmund he gave | a sword as a gift.
"Triumph to some, | and treasure to others,
to many wisdom | and skill with words,
fair winds to the sailor, | to the singer his art,
and a manly heart | to many a hero.
"I shall honour Thor, | and this I shall ask,
that you may always find | his true favour;
though he has little love | for the brides of the giants.
"Now lead out from the stall | one of your wolves,
and let him run | alongside my boar;
for my boar goes slowly | on the road of the gods,
and I would not weary | my worthy steed."
Hyndla said:
"Falsely you ask me, | Freyja, to go,
for I see it | in the glance of your eyes;
on the way of the slain | your lover goes with you,
Ottar the young, | the son of Instein."
Freyja said:
"Your dreams are wild, I think, | when you say
my lover is with me | on the way of the slain;
there shines the boar | with bristles of gold,
Hildisvini, | he who was made
by Dain and Nabbi, | the cunning dwarfs.
"Now let us leap down | from our saddles,
and talk of the lineage | of the two heroes;
the men who were born | of the gods above,
"They have made a wager | in the foreign metal,
Ottar the young | and Angantyr;
we must see to it | that the young hero has
his father's wealth, | the fruits of his line.
"He made me a shrine | of stones,
and now the rock | has turned to glass;
often it was red | with the blood of beasts;
Ottar always trusted | in the goddesses.
"Tell me now | the ancient names,
and the lines of all | who were born of old:
who are of the Skjoldungs, | who of the Skilfings,
who of the Othlings, | who of the Ylfings,
who are the free-born, | who are the high-born,
the noblest of men | who live in Mithgarth?"
Hyndla said:
"You, Ottar, are | the son of Instein,
and Instein the son | of Alf the Old,
Alf of Ulf, | Ulf of Sæfari,
and Sæfari's father | was Svan the Red.
"Your mother, bright | with fine bracelets,
was called, I think, | the priestess Hledis;
Frothi was her father, | and Friaut her mother;
her line must seem | to be of the mightiest men.
"Of old the noblest | of all was Ali,
before him Halfdan, | foremost of the Skjoldungs;
famous were the battles | the hero fought,
his deeds were carried | to the corners of heaven.
"Strengthened by Eymund, | the strongest of men,
he killed Sigtrygg | with the ice-cold sword;
his bride was Almveig, | the best of women,
and eighteen boys | Almveig bore him.
"From them come the Skjoldungs, | from them the Skilfings,
from them the Othlings, | from them the Ynglings,
from them come the free-born, | from them the high-born,
the noblest of men | who live in Mithgarth:
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"Hildigun then | was the name of her mother,
the daughter of Svava | and Sækonung;
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
It is much to know; | will you hear still more?
"The wife of Dag | was a mother of heroes,
Thora, who bore him | the bravest of fighters,
Frathmar and Gyrth | and the two Frekis,
Am and Jofurmar, | Alf the Old;
it is much to know; | will you hear still more?
"Her husband was Ketil, | the heir of Klypp,
he was your mother's | mother's father;
before the days | of Kari was Frothi,
and Hoalf then | was born of Hild.
"Next was Nanna, | daughter of Nokkvi,
her son became | your father's kinsman;
old is the line, | and longer still,
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"Isolf and Osolf, | the sons of Olmoth,
whose wife was Skurhild, | the daughter of Skekkil,
count them among | the mighty heroes,
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"Gunnar the Bulwark, | Grim the Hardy,
Thorir the Iron-shield, | Ulf the Gaper,
Brodd and Hörvir, | I knew them both;
they were in the household | of Hrolf the Old.
"Hervarth, Hjorvarth, | Hrani, Angantyr,
Bui and Brami, | Barri and Reifnir,
Tind and Tyrfing, | the two Haddings,
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"Eastward in Bolm | were born of old
the sons of Arngrim | and Eyfura;
with berserk tumult | and baleful deeds
like fire over land | and sea they went,
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"The sons of Jormunrek | all, long ago,
were given in death | as offerings to the gods;
he was kinsman of Sigurth, | hear well what I say,
the foe of hosts, | and Fafnir's slayer.
"From Volsung's seed | the hero was sprung,
and Hjordis was born | of Hrauthung's line,
and Eylimi | came from the Othlings,
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"Gunnar and Hogni, | the heirs of Gjuki,
and Guthrun as well, | who was their sister;
but Gotthorm was not | of Gjuki's line,
although he was | the brother of both:
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!
"Of Hvethna's sons | Haki was the best,
and Hjorvarth was | the father of Hvethna;
"Harald Battle-tooth | was born of Auth,
Hrörek the Ring-giver | was her husband;
Auth the Deep-minded | was Ivar's daughter,
but Rathbarth was | the father of Randver:
and all are your kinsmen, | Ottar, you fool!"
In olden days, | when eagles screamed,
and holy streams | fell from heaven's crags,
then was Helgi, | the hero-hearted,
Borghild's son, | born in Bralund.
It was night in the house, | and Norns came there,
who shaped the life | of the noble one;
they decreed he should be | the most famed of all fighters
and for ever | the best of princes.
Mightily they wove | the web of fate,
while all Bralund's towns | were trembling;
and there they wove | the golden threads,
and made them fast | in the moon's hall.
East and west | they hid the ends,
in the middle the hero | should have his land;
and Neri's kinswoman | cast northward
a chain, and bade it | hold firm for ever.
Once the Ylfings' son | had sorrow,
and grief the bride | who had borne the loved one.
Raven said to raven, | resting on a treetop,
seeking for food, | "There is something I know.
"In a mail-coat stands | the son of Sigmund,
half a day old; | now day is here;
his eyes flash sharp | as heroes' eyes do,
he is a friend of the wolves; | we are very glad."
The warrior throng | thought him a ruler,
good times, they said, | mankind would see;
the king himself | came from the press of battle
to give the prince | a noble leek.
He named him Helgi, | and gave him Hringstathir,
Solfjoll, Snæfjoll, | and Sigarsvoll,
Hringstoth, Hotun, | and Himinvangar,
and an adorned blood-snake | to Sinfjotli's brother.
Mighty he grew | among his friends,
the fair-born elm, | in fortune's glow;
to his comrades | he gladly gave gold,
the hero did not spare | the blood-flecked hoard.
A short time only | the chieftain waited for war,
when he was | fifteen winters old;
he killed Hunding, | the hardy man
who long had ruled | over lands and men.
From Sigmund's son | they next sought
hoard and rings, | the sons of Hunding;
they told the prince | to pay compensation
for plunder stolen | and a father slain.
The prince did not let | their pleas prevail,
nor did the kinsmen get | gold for their dead;
waiting, he said, | was a mighty storm
of grey lances | and Othin's wrath.
The warriors went | out to the battle,
they chose the field | at Logafjoll;
Frothi's peace | they broke among foes,
through the island hungrily | went Vithrir's hounds.
The king then sat, | when he had killed
Eyjolf and Alf, | beneath the eagle-stone;
Hjorvarth and Hovarth, | Hunding's sons,
the kin of the spear-wielder, | he had killed them all.
Then light glittered | from Logafjoll,
and from the light | the flashes leapt;
high under helmets | at Himinvangar;
their mail-coats all | were red with blood,
and from their spears | the sparks flew out.
Early then | in the wolf-wood
the mighty king | asked the southern maid
if she would come | home with the hero
that night; | the weapons clashed.
Down from her horse | sprang Hogni's daughter,
the shields were still, | and she spoke to the hero:
"We have other tasks, | I think,
than drinking beer | with the breaker of rings.
"My father has pledged | his fair daughter
as bride to Granmar's | grim son;
but I, Helgi, | once called Hothbrodd
as fine a king | as the son of a cat.
"Yet the hero will come a few nights from now,
unless you bid him come to the battleground,
or take the maid from the mighty warrior."
Helgi said:
"Do not fear him, | though he felled Isung;
first our keen courage | must be tried,
before you go unwilling | with the scoundrel;
weapons will clash, | unless I come to my death."
Then the mighty one | sent messengers
by land and by sea, | to seek a host,
with a store of the wealth | of the water's gleam,
and to summon men, | and the sons of men.
"Tell them at once | to go to the ships,
and to be ready | off Brandey!"
There the chief waited | until there had come
men by the hundred | from Hethinsey.
Soon off Stafnsnes | the ships stood,
fair they glided, | bright with gold;
then Helgi spoke | to Hjorleif, asking:
"Have you counted | the gallant host?"
The young king answered | the other then:
"It would take long to count | from Tronueyr
the long-stemmed ships | laden with warriors
that come from outside | into Orvasund.
"There are twelve hundred | trusty men,
but in Hotun lies | the host of the king,
greater by half; | I have hope of battle."
The chieftain soon | struck the ship's tents,
and woke the whole | throng of warriors;
(the heroes saw | the red of dawn;)
and on the masts | the gallant men
made fast the sails | in Varinsfjord.
There was beat of oars | and clash of iron,
shield struck shield | as the ships' crews rowed;
swiftly went | the warrior-laden
fleet of the ruler | out from the land.
Such was the sound, | when together the sisters
of Kolga struck | against the long keels,
as if cliffs were breaking | under beating surf,
Helgi ordered the sails | hoisted higher,
nor did the ships' crews | shun the waves,
though dreadfully | Ægir's daughters
sought to sink | the steeds of the sea.
But from above | brave Sigrun
aided the men | and all their voyage;
mightily came | from the claws of Ron
the leader's sea-beast | off Gnipalund.
At evening there | in Unavagar
floated the fleet, | finely adorned;
but those who watched | from Svarinshaugr
looked on the host | with bitter hearts.
Then Gothmund asked, | a man of good birth,
"Who is the monarch | who guides the host,
and leads the warriors | to the land?"
Sinfjotli answered, | and up on an oar
raised a shield all red | with a golden rim;
he was a sea-sentry, | skilled in speech,
and good at contending | in words with princes.
"Say tonight | when you feed the swine,
and send your bitches | to seek their swill,
that out of the East | the Ylfings have come,
greedy for battle, | to Gnipalund.
"There Hothbrodd | will find Helgi,
in the midst of the fleet, | and he scorns flight;
often he has | gorged the eagles,
while you were at the quern, | kissing slave-girls."
Gothmund said:
"Hero, heed | the ancient sayings,
and bring no lies | to the nobly born.
"You have eaten | the entrails of wolves,
and been the slayer | of your brothers;
often your cold mouth | sought wounds to suck,
and, loathed, you lurked | in rocky dens."
Sinfjotli said:
"You were a witch | in Varin's isle,
a false woman, | and you fashioned lies;
of the mail-clad heroes | you would have
no other, you said, | but Sinfjotli alone.
"You were a Valkyrie, | loathsome witch,
evil and base, | in Alfödr's home;
the warriors all | must always fight,
cunning woman, | for your sake.
Nine we had | in Sogunes
of wolf-cubs; | I was their father."
Gothmund said:
"You did not father | Fenrir's-wolves,
though you are older | than all I know;
for they gelded you | in Gnipalund,
the giant-women | at Thorsnes once.
"Under houses the stepson | of Siggeir lay,
fond of the wolf's cry | out in the woods;
then every evil | came to your hands,
when you reddened | your brothers' breasts,
you won fame | for the foulest deeds.
"In Bravoll you were | Grani's bride,
golden-bitted | and ready to gallop;
I rode you many | a mile, and down
you sank, you giantess, | under the saddle."
Sinfjotli said:
"You seemed to be | a brainless fellow,
when once you milked | goats for Gollnir,
and another time | when as Imth's daughter
you went in rags; | will you wrangle longer?"
Gothmund said:
"I would sooner | at Frekastein
feed the ravens | with your flesh
than send your bitches | to seek their swill,
or feed the swine; | may the fiends take you!"
Helgi said:
"It would suit you better, | Sinfjotli,
to give battle | and gladden eagles,
than to utter | vain and empty words,
though ring-breakers often | wrangle in speech.
"I do not think well | of the sons of Granmar,
but it is fitting for heroes | to speak the truth;
at Moinsheimar | the men proved
that they had hearts | for wielding swords."
Mightily then | they made
Sviputh and Sveggjuth | run to Solheimar;
(by dewy dales | and dark chasms,
Mist's horse shook | where the men went by;)
they found the king | at his courtyard gate,
and told him the fierce | foe had come.
Out stood Hothbrodd, | helmeted for battle,
and watched the riding | of his warriors;
"Why are the Hniflungs | white with fear?"
Gothmund said:
"Swift keels lie | close to the land,
(mast-ring harts | and mighty yards,
wealth of shields | and well-planed oars;)
the king's fine host, | the proud Ylfings;
fifteen bands | have come to land,
but out in Sogn | are seven thousand.
"Lying at anchor | off Gnipalund
are fire-beasts black, | all fitted with gold;
there wait most | of the enemy's men,
and Helgi will not long | delay the battle."
Hothbrodd said:
"Send the horses running | to the Reginthing,
Melnir and Mylnir | to Myrkvidr now,
(and Sporvitnir | to Sparinsheith;)
let no man seek | to sit from now on
who knows well how to wield | the flame of wounds.
"Summon Hogni, | the sons of Hring,
Atli and Yngvi | and Alf the Old;
they are always | glad of battle;
let us go | against the Volsungs."
Swift as a storm | they struck together,
the flashing blades | at Frekastein;
always was Helgi, | Hunding's slayer,
first in the throng | where warriors fought;
(fierce in battle, | slow to flee,
hard was the heart | of the hero.)
From heaven there came | the helmeted maidens,
the clang of weapons grew, | who watched over the king;
fair Sigrun spoke, | the wound-givers flew,
and the horse of the giantess | had raven's-food:
"Hail to you, hero! | Happy among men,
offspring of Yngvi, | you shall always live,
for you have slain | the fearless foe
who had brought to many | the dread of death.
"Warrior, well | have you won for yourself
bright red rings | and the noble bride;
both now, warrior, | shall be yours,
Hogni's daughter | and Hringstathir,
wealth and triumph; | the battle wanes."

hh2-p1.s: King Sigmund, the son of Volsung, was married to Borghild, from Bralund. They named their son Helgi, after Helgi Hjorvarthsson; Hagal was Helgi's foster-father. There was a powerful king called Hunding, and Hundland is named after him. He was a mighty warrior, and had many sons with him on his campaigns. There was enmity and strife between the two of them, King Hunding and King Sigmund, and each killed the other's kinsmen. King Sigmund and his family were called Volsungs and Ylfings.
Helgi went in disguise as a spy to the home of King Hunding. Hæming, a son of King Hunding, was at home. When Helgi left, he met a young herdsman, and said:

l: "Tell Hæming | that Helgi knows
whom the heroes | hid in armour;
they had a grey wolf | within their hall,
whom King Hunding | took for Hamal."

hh2-p2.s: Hamal was the name of Hagal's son. King Hunding sent men to Hagal to look for Helgi, and Helgi could not save himself in any other way, so he put on the clothes of a slave woman and set to work at the mill. They searched for Helgi but did not find him.

l: Then Blind spoke out, | the evil-minded:
"The eyes of Hagal's | slave woman are bright;
the one who stands at the quern | is not of common stock;
the millstones break, | the boards are shattered.
"The hero has | a hard fate indeed,
that now he must | grind barley;
his hand is better fitted | to feel
the hilt of the sword | than the millstone's handle."
"It is little wonder | if boards are splintered;
the mill is turned | by a king's daughter;
once she used to ride | through the clouds,
and fought battles | like fighting men,
(till Helgi held her | fast as a captive;
she is the sister | of Sigar and Hogni,
and so the eyes are bright | of the Ylfings' maid.)"

hh2-p3.s: Helgi escaped and went to a warship. He killed King Hunding, and from then on was called Helgi Hundingsbane.

He lay with his army in Brunavagar, and there they held a slaughter on the shore, and ate the meat raw. There was a king called Hogni. His daughter was Sigrun; she was a Valkyrie and rode through the air and over the water; she was Svava reborn. Sigrun rode to Helgi's ship and said:

l: "Who commands the ship | by the shore so steep?
Where is the home | you warriors have?
Why do you wait | in Brunavagar,
or what is the way | that you wish to try?"
Helgi said:
"The ship is Hamal's | by the shore so steep,
we have our home | in Hlesey;
we wait for a fair wind | in Brunavagar,
eastward is the way | that we wish to try."
Sigrun said:
"Where, warrior, | have you wakened battle,
or gorged the birds | of the sisters of Guth?
Why is your mail-coat | spattered with blood,
why do you feast helmeted | on uncooked food?"
Helgi said:
"Latest of all, | the Ylfings' son
on the western sea, | if you wish to know,
captured bears | in Bragalund,
and fed the eagles | with the edge of the sword.
Now it is shown | why our shirts are bloody,
and why little of our food | is cooked with fire."
Helgi said:
"How did you know | that we have now,
wise maiden, | well avenged our kin?
There are many | sons of the mighty
who share alike | in our noble race."
Sigrun said:
"I was not far | from the lord of the people
yesterday morning, | when the king was slain;
though the son of Sigmund | is crafty, I think,
when he speaks of the fight | in slaughter-runes.
"Once on the longship | I saw you well,
when you stood | in the blood-stained bow,
(and icy waves | were raging round you;)
now the hero | would hide from me,
but Helgi is known | to Hogni's daughter."

hh2-p4.s: There was a mighty king called Granmar, who lived at Svarinshaugr. He had many sons; one was called Hothbrodd, another Gothmund, a third Starkath. Hothbrodd was at a meeting of kings, and he won the promise of having Sigrun, Hogni's daughter, as his wife. But when she heard this, she rode with the Valkyries through the air and over the sea to look for Helgi. Helgi was then at Logafjoll, and had fought with Hunding's sons; there he killed Alf and Eyolf, Hjorvarth and Hervarth. He was utterly weary from battle, and sat under the eagle-stone. There Sigrun found him, and ran to throw her arms around his neck, and kissed him, and told him her news, as is told in the old Volsung lay:

l: Sigrun sought | the joyful chieftain,
at once she took | Helgi's hand;
she greeted the helmeted hero | and kissed him,
the warrior's heart | turned to the woman.
From her heart | Hogni's daughter spoke,
Helgi was dear | to her, she said;
"Long with all | my heart I loved
Sigmund's son | before I ever saw him.
"At the meeting | I was promised to Hothbrodd,
but I would rather | have another hero;
yet, king, I fear | the wrath of my kin,
since I broke my father's | dearest wish."
Helgi said:
"Never fear | Hogni's anger,
nor your kinsmen's | cruel wrath;
maiden, you | shall live with me,
your kindred, fair one, | I shall not fear."

hh2-s19.s: Gothmund the son of Granmar said this:

l: "What great hero | is guiding the ships?
He flies a golden flag | at the stem;
I find no peace | at the head of your advance,
and round the fighters | the battle-light is red."
Sinfjotli said:
"Here Hothbrodd | may find Helgi,
the hater of flight, | in the midst of the fleet;
he holds the home | of all your race,
and he rules over | the realm of the fishes."
Gothmund said:
"First shall swords | at Frekastein
prove our worth | in place of words;
it is time, Hothbrodd, | to take vengeance,
if once we were | worsted in battle."
Sinfjotli said:
"Better, Gothmund, | to tend the goats,
and climb the rocks | of the mountain cliffs;
a hazel switch | to hold in your hand
would suit you better | than the hilt of a sword."
Helgi said:
"It would suit you better, | Sinfjotli,
to give battle | and gladden the eagles,
than to utter | vain and empty speech,
though warriors often | fight with words.
"I do not find | the sons of Granmar good,
but it is fitting for heroes | to speak the truth;
at Moinsheimar | the men proved
that they had hearts | for the wielding of swords,
(and the warriors | are always brave.)"
"Never shall Sigrun | from Sevafjoll,
King Hothbrodd, | be held in your arms;
Granmar's sons | have grown quite cold,
and the grey giant-steeds | gorge on corpses."

hh2-s26.s: Then she sought out Helgi, and was full of joy. He said:

l: "Maiden, not all | your fortune is fair,
I blame the Norns | that this should be;
this morning there fell | at Frekastein
Bragi and Hogni | by my hand.
"At Hlebjorg fell | the sons of Hrollaug,
King Starkath | at Styrkleifar;
I never saw | nobler fighters,
the body fought | when the head had fallen.
"Low on the ground | the slain are lying,
most of them | are men of your race;
you have won nothing, | for it was your fate
to bring brave men | to the battlefield."
Then Sigrun wept. | Helgi said:
"Do not grieve, Sigrun, | the battle is won,
the fighter cannot escape his fate."
Sigrun said:
"I would call to life | those who lie slaughtered,
if I might be safe on your breast."

hh2-p7.s: Helgi married Sigrun, and they had sons. Helgi did not reach old age. Dag, the son of Hogni, offered sacrifice to Othin to be avenged for his father's death; Othin gave Dag his spear. Dag found Helgi, his brother-in-law, at a place called Fjoturlund. He thrust the spear through Helgi's body. Then Helgi fell, and Dag rode to Sevafjoll and told Sigrun the news:

l: "I am sad, sister, | to tell you sorrow,
unwillingly I brought | grief to my kin;
this morning there fell | at Fjoturlund
the noblest prince | the world has known,
(and he set his heel | on the heroes' necks.)"
Sigrun said:
"Now may every | oath bite you
that you have sworn | with Helgi,
by the bright | water of Leipt,
and the ice-cold | stone of Uth.
"The ship shall not sail | in which you sail,
though a favouring wind | should follow behind;
the horse shall not run | on which you ride,
though you are eager | to flee your foe.
"The sword shall not bite | which you bear,
till it sings | about your own head.
"Vengeance would be mine | for Helgi's murder,
if you were a wolf | out in the woods,
possessing nothing | and knowing no joy,
having no food | but corpses to feed on."
Dag said:
"You are mad, sister, | and wild of mind,
to cast such a curse | on your brother;
Othin is ruler | of every ill,
who divides kin | with runes of spite.
"Your brother will give you | rings so red,
all Vandilsve | and Vigdalir;
take half my land | to pay for the harm,
ring-decked maiden, | and as recompense for your sons."
Sigrun said:
"I shall not sit happy | at Sevafjoll,
early or late, | loving my life,
if the light cannot show, | in the leader's band,
Vigblær bearing him | back to his home,
(the golden-bitted; | I shall never greet him.)
"Such was the fear | that Helgi's foes
always felt, | and all their kin,
as makes the goats, | mad with terror,
run from the wolf | among the rocks.
"Helgi rose | above all heroes
like the lofty ash | above lowly thorns,
or the noble stag, | sprinkled with dew,
bearing his head | above all beasts,
(and his horns gleam bright | to heaven itself.)"

hh2-p9.s: A hill was made in Helgi's memory. And when he came to Valhall, Othin invited him to rule over everything with him.

l: "Hunding, you shall | wash the feet
of every hero, | and kindle the fire,
tie up the dogs, | and tend the horses,
and feed the pigs | before you go to sleep."

hh2-p10.s: One of Sigrun's maids went one evening to Helgi's hill, and saw Helgi riding to the hill with many men. The maid said:

l: "Is this a dream | that I think I see,
or the doom of the gods, | that dead men ride,
and spurring this way | you urge your horses,
or is a homecoming now | granted to the heroes?"
Helgi said:
"This is no dream | that you think you see,
nor the end of the world, | though you behold us,
and spurring this way | we urge our horses,
nor is a homecoming now | granted to the heroes."

hh2-s42.s: The maid went home and said to Sigrun:

l: "Go out, Sigrun, | from Sevafjoll,
if you wish to find | the lord of the people;
(the hill is open, | Helgi has come;)
the sword-tracks bleed; | the king has asked
that you should now | heal his wounds."

hh2-s43.s: Sigrun went into the hill to Helgi, and said:

l: "Now I am as glad | of our meeting
as Othin's hawks, | so eager for prey,
when they scent slaughter | and flesh still warm,
or, wet with dew, | see the red of day.
"First I will kiss | the lifeless king,
before you cast off | the bloody mail-coat;
your hair, Helgi, | is heavy with frost,
and you are damp | with the dew of death;
(Hogni's kinsman | has ice-cold hands,
what, prince, can I do | to bring you ease?)"
Helgi said:
"You alone, Sigrun | of Sevafjoll,
are the cause that Helgi | is heavy with dew;
gold-decked maiden, | your tears are grievous,
(sun-bright maid of the south, | before you sleep;)
each falls like blood | on the hero's breast,
(burned-out, cold, | and crushed with care.)
"We shall drink well | a noble draught,
though love and lands | are lost to me;
no man shall sing | a song of sorrow,
though there are bleeding wounds | on my breast;
now in the hill | we hold our brides,
the heroes' loves, | beside their dead husbands."
Helgi said:
"Now I say | that in Sevafjoll
anything may happen, | early or late,
since you sleep clasped | in a corpse's arms,
so fair in the hill, | the daughter of Hogni!
(You come here living, | a daughter of kings.)
"Now I must ride | the reddened ways,
and set my bay horse | to tread the sky;
westward I go | to wind-helm's bridges,
before Salgofnir wakes | the warrior throng."

hh2-p11.s: Then Helgi and his followers rode on their way, and the women went home to the house. Another evening Sigrun told the maid to keep watch at the hill. And at sunset, when Sigrun came to the hill, she said:

l: "He would be here now, | if he could come,
Sigmund's son, | from Othin's seat;
hope of the hero's return | grows dim
when eagles sit | on the ash-tree boughs,
and men are seeking | the meeting of dreams."
The Maid said:
"You would seem mad | to seek alone,
daughter of heroes, | the house of the dead;
for all the ghosts of the dead | are mightier
now at night | than when day is bright."

hh2-p12.s: Sigrun died young of sorrow and grief. In the old days it was believed that people were born again, but that is now called old wives' folly. Of Helgi and Sigrun it is said that they were born again; he became Helgi Haddingjaskati, and she Kara the daughter of Halfdan, as is told in the Lay of Kara, and she was a Valkyrie.

hhv-p1.s: Hjorvarth was the name of a king who had four wives: one was called Alfhild, and their son was named Hethin; the second was called Særeith, and their son was named Humlung; the third was called Sinrjoth, and their son was named Hymling. King Hjorvarth had made a great vow to marry whichever woman he knew to be the most beautiful. He learned that King Svafnir had a daughter more beautiful than all others, whose name was Sigrlin. Ithmund was the name of one of his jarls; he had a son called Atli, who went to ask for Sigrlin's hand on the king's behalf. He stayed all winter with King Svafnir. There was a jarl called Franmar, Sigrlin's foster-father; his daughter was named Alof. The jarl told him that the girl's hand was refused, and Atli went home. One day Atli, the jarl's son, was standing in a certain wood; a bird sat in the branches above him, and it had heard his men call Hjorvarth's wives the most beautiful of women. The bird twittered, and Atli listened to what it said. It said:

l: "Have you seen Sigrlin, | Svafnir's daughter,
the fairest maiden | found in her homeland?
Though Hjorvarth's wives | are thought by men
good to look at | in Glasir's wood."
Atli said:
"Now with Atli, | Ithmund's son,
will you say more, | you bird so wise?"
The bird said:
"I may, if the prince | makes an offering,
and I have what I want | from the house of the king."
Atli said:
"Do not choose Hjorvarth, | nor his sons,
nor the fair wives | of the famous chief;
do not ask for the brides | that are the prince's;
let us deal fairly, | as friends do."
The bird said:
"A temple I will ask for, | and many altars,
gold-horned cattle | the prince shall give me,
if Sigrlin yet | shall sleep in his arms,
or of her free will | shall follow the hero."
"We had trouble, | but no news,
our horses failed | in the high mountains,
we had to wade | the waters of Sæmorn;
Svafnir's daughter, | adorned with rings,
she whom we sought, | was still denied us."

hhv-p3.s: The king ordered them to go a second time, and he went with them himself. But when they came up onto the mountain, they saw Svavaland burning and great clouds of dust from many horses. The king rode down from the mountain into the land, and camped for the night close by a stream. Atli kept watch and crossed the stream; there he found a house. A great bird sat on the roof to guard it, but he was asleep. Atli hurled his spear at the bird and killed it, and in the house he found Sigrlin the king's daughter and Alof the jarl's daughter, and he took them both away with him. Jarl Franmar had changed himself into the shape of an eagle, and guarded them from the enemy army by magic. Hrothmar was the name of a king, a suitor of Sigrlin; he killed the king of Svavaland and had plundered and burned his land. King Hjorvarth took Sigrlin, and Atli took Alof.

Hjorvarth and Sigrlin had a son, mighty and of noble stature; he was a silent man, and no name stuck to him. He sat on a hill, and saw nine Valkyries riding; one of them was the most beautiful of all. She said:

l: "You will be late, Helgi, | to have a hoard of rings,
you fierce battle-tree, | or shining fields,
the eagle screams soon, | if you never speak,
though your heart, hero, | may cry out fiercely."
Helgi said:
"What gift shall I have | with the name Helgi,
glorious maiden, | since the giving is yours?
All your words | I shall think on well,
but I do not want them | if I do not win you."
The Valkyrie said:
"I know of swords lying | in Sigarsholm,
fifty there are, | less only four;
there is one | that is the best of all,
the shield-destroyer, | shining with gold.
"In the hilt is fame, | in the haft is courage,
in the point is fear | for its owner's foes;
on the blade there lies | a blood-flecked snake,
and a serpent's tail | is twisted round the flat."

hhv-p4.s: Eylimi was the name of a king, whose daughter was Svava; she was a Valkyrie, and rode over air and sea. She gave Helgi this name, and often shielded him in battle afterwards. Helgi said:

l: "Hjorvarth, king, | your counsels are unsound,
famed though you are | for leading the people,
letting fire devour | the homes of heroes
who had never done you | any wrong.
"Yet Hrothmar still | holds the hoard,
the wealth that once | our kinsmen owned;
care very seldom | troubles the king,
he thinks himself | the heir of dead men."

hhv-p5.s: Hjorvarth answered that he would give Helgi a band of men if he wished to avenge his mother's father. Then Helgi got the sword that Svava had told him of. So he went, and Atli with him, and they killed Hrothmar, and did many great deeds.

He killed the giant Hati, whom he found sitting on a certain mountain. Helgi and Atli lay with their ships in Hatafjord. Atli kept watch during the first part of the night. Hrimgerth, Hati's daughter, said:

l: "Who are the heroes | in Hatafjord?
The ships are covered with shields;
you look brave, | and you fear little,
I want to know the name of the king."
Atli said:
"Helgi is his name, | and you can never
bring harm to the hero;
the prince's fleet | is fitted with iron,
and witches can do us no harm."
Hrimgerth said:
"Who are you now, | you mighty man?
By what name are you known to men?
He trusts you well, | the prince who wants
you to stand at the stem of his ship."
Atli said:
"I am Atli, | and you will find me ill to deal with,
I have great hatred for witches;
I have often been | in the dripping bows,
and brought death to dusk-riders.
"Corpse-hungry giantess, | what are you called?
Say, witch, who your father was!
May you sink | nine miles deeper down,
and a tree grow tall on your breast."
Hrimgerth said:
"I am Hrimgerth, | my father was Hati,
the mightiest of giants;
many a woman | he took from her home,
before Helgi cut him down."
Atli said:
"Witch, you were | in front of the ship,
and lay before the fjord;
you would have given | the ruler's men to Ron,
if a spear had not stuck in your flesh."
Hrimgerth said:
"You are dull, Atli, | you are dreaming, I think,
the lids lie over your eyes;
by the leader's ships | my mother lay,
I killed Hlothvarth's sons on the sea.
"You would neigh, Atli, | but you are gelded,
see, Hrimgerth hoists her tail;
your heart, I think, | is in your hind end,
though your voice is a stallion's cry."
Atli said:
"A stallion I seem | if you seek to try me,
and I leap to land from the sea;
I shall smash you to pieces, | if I so wish,
and Hrimgerth's tail sinks heavy."
Hrimgerth said:
"Go ashore then, Atli, | if you are sure of your strength,
let us go to Varin's cove;
your rounded ribs | shall be made straight
if you come within my claws."
Atli said:
"I will not go | till the warriors wake
to guard their chief again;
I should not wonder, | foul witch, if you
came up from beneath our keel."
Hrimgerth said:
"Wake now, Helgi, | and repay Hrimgerth
for cutting Hati down to his death;
if for a single night | she can sleep beside the prince,
then all her wrongs are repaid."
Helgi said:
"Lothin shall have you, | you are loathsome to men,
he has his home in Tholley;
the wise giant | is the worst of the wild-dwellers,
he is a fitting mate for you."
Hrimgerth said:
"You love her more, | who scanned the harbour
last night among the men;
(the gold-decked maiden | bore magic, I think,
when she came to land from the sea,
and she held your fleet fast;)
she alone is to blame | that I cannot bring
death to the monarch's men."
Helgi said:
"Hrimgerth, listen, | if I repay your hurts,
now tell the king the truth;
was there one who guarded | the warrior's ships,
or did many go together?"
Hrimgerth said:
"Three times nine there were, | but one rode first,
a helmeted maiden, white of hue;
their horses quivered, | from their manes there came
dew into the deep dales,
(hail on the high woods,
from which men have their harvest,
but what I saw was an ill sight.)"
Atli said:
"Look eastward, Hrimgerth, | for Helgi has struck you
down with the runes of death;
safe in harbour floats | the prince's fleet,
and safe are the monarch's men."
Helgi said:
"It is day, Hrimgerth, | for Atli has held you
until now you must lose your life;
as a harbour mark | men shall mock you,
where you shall stand in stone for ever."

hhv-p6.s: King Helgi was a mighty warrior. He came to King Eylimi and asked for the hand of his daughter, Svava. Then Helgi and Svava exchanged vows, and they loved each other greatly. Svava was at home with her father, while Helgi was away at war; Svava was still a Valkyrie as before.

Hethin was at home with his father, King Hjorvarth, in Norway. Hethin was coming home alone from the forest one Yule-eve, and met a troll-woman; she rode on a wolf, and had snakes in place of a bridle. She asked Hethin for his company. "No," he said. She said, "You shall pay for this at the king's toast." That evening the great vows were taken; the sacred boar was brought in, the men laid their hands on it, and took their vows at the king's toast. Hethin vowed that he would have Svava, Eylimi's daughter, the beloved of his brother Helgi; then such great grief seized him that he went away on wild paths southward over the land, and found Helgi, his brother. Helgi said:

l: "Welcome, Hethin! | What have you to tell
of the latest news | that comes from Norway?
Why did you leave | your land, prince,
and travel alone | to find us here?"
Hethin said:
"A deed more evil | I have done
than you, my brother, | can ever mend;
for I have chosen | the child of the king,
your bride, for mine | at the monarch's toast."
Helgi said:
"Do not grieve, Hethin, | for the words shall hold true
that we both | have sworn over the beer;
a warrior wants me | to go to the island,
(I shall come there | three nights from now;)
and my coming back | must be doubtful,
(so all may be well, | if fate so wills.)"
Hethin said:
"You said once, Helgi, | that Hethin was
a very good friend, | and you gave him gifts;
it would be more fitting | to redden your sword
than to give friendship | like this to your foe."

hhv-p7.s: Helgi spoke in this way because he foresaw his death, for his following-spirits had met Hethin when he saw the woman riding on the wolf. Alf was the name of a king, the son of Hrothmar, who had marked out a battlefield with Helgi at Sigarsvoll after a delay of three nights. Then Helgi said:

l: "On a wolf there rode, | when it was dusk,
a woman who wished | to have him follow;
she knew well | that now would fall
Sigrlin's son | at Sigarsvoll."
Helgi sent | Sigar riding
to seek out Eylimi's | only daughter:
"Tell her to be | ready quickly,
if she would find | her lover alive."
Sigar said:
"Helgi has now | sent me here
to speak with you, | Svava, yourself;
the hero said | he wished to see you
before life should leave | the nobly born."
Svava said:
"What has happened to Helgi, | Hjorvarth's son?
Harm has now | come hard upon me;
if the sea struck him, | or a sword bit him,
I shall bring ill | to all his foes."
Sigar said:
"In the morning he fell | at Frekastein,
the king who was noblest | beneath the sun;
Alf has all | the joy of victory,
though he never | has need of it."
Helgi said:
"Hail to you, Svava! | Master your sorrow,
this is our last | meeting in life;
the hero's wounds | are bleeding hard,
and the sword has come | close to my heart.
"I ask you, Svava, | do not weep, bride,
if you will listen | to these words of mine,
make the bed ready | for Hethin,
and give your love | to the young hero."
Svava said:
"I made a vow | in my dearly loved home,
when Helgi sought | to win me with rings,
that never willingly, | if the warrior died,
would I fold in my arms | a man without fame."
Hethin said:
"Kiss me, Svava, | I shall not come back
to see Rogheim | or Rothulsfjoll
till I have vengeance | for the son of Hjorvarth,
the king who was noblest | beneath the sun."

hlr-p1.s: After the death of Brynhild two funeral pyres were made, one for Sigurth, and that burned first, and on the other Brynhild was burned, and she was on a wagon covered with a rich cloth. It is said that Brynhild went in the wagon along the road to Hel, and passed by a house where a certain giantess lived. The giantess said:

l: "You shall go | no further forward
across my dwelling | ribbed with rocks;
it would be more fitting | to stay at your weaving
than to follow here | another's husband.
"What do you want | from Valland here,
fickle of heart, | in this house of mine?
Gold-goddess, now, | if you want to know,
you have washed heroes' blood | from your hands."
Brynhild said:
"Do not scold me, woman | from the rocky walls,
though once I used | to go to battle;
I shall seem | better than you
when men truly | know the two of us."
The giantess said:
"Brynhild, you were, | Buthli's daughter,
born into the world | for the worst of evils;
you have given to death | Gjuki's children,
and brought their lofty | house down low."
Brynhild said:
"From the wagon here | I tell you the truth,
witless one, | if you want to know
how the heirs of Gjuki | made me
joyless for ever, | a breaker of oaths.
"Hild the helmeted | in Hlymdalir
they called me of old, | all who knew me.
"The bold monarch | carried the swan-robes
of the eight sisters | beneath an oak;
I was twelve winters old, | if you want to know,
when I gave my oaths | to the young king.
"Next I let | the leader of the Goths,
Hjalmgunnar the old, | go down to hell,
and brought victory | to Autha's brother;
for this Othin's | anger was mighty.
"He ringed me with shields | in Skatalund,
red and white, | their rims overlapping;
he ordered that my sleep | should be broken
by him who had | nowhere found fear.
"Round my hall, | that looked to the south,
he let the branches' foe | burn leaping high;
across it he told | the hero to come
who brought me the gold | that Fafnir guarded.
"On Grani rode | the giver of gold,
where my foster-father | ruled his people;
he seemed to be | the best of all,
the prince of the Danes, | when the people met.
"Happy we slept, | we had one bed,
as if he had been | born my brother;
for eight nights | neither of us there
laid a loving hand | on the other.
"Yet Guthrun reproached me, | Gjuki's daughter,
that I had slept | in Sigurth's arms;
then I heard | what I wish had been hidden,
that they had betrayed me | in taking a mate.
"Ever with grief | and all too long
are men and women | born into the world;
but yet we shall live | our lives together,
Sigurth and I. | Sink down, Giantess!"
Great were the evils | that once grew,
with the sad dawning | of the sorrow of elves;
in the early morning | there awake for men
the evils that grief | will bring to each.
It was not now, | nor yet yesterday,
long is the time | that has passed since then,
so that there is little | that is half as old,
since Guthrun, daughter | of Gjuki, goaded
her sons so young | to vengeance for Svanhild.
"The sister you had | was called Svanhild,
and Jormunrek had her | trampled by horses,
white and black | on the road of battle,
grey, used to the road, | the steeds of the Goths.
"You are little like | the kings of the people,
for now you alone | of my race are living.
"I am lonely | as the forest aspen,
bare of kindred | as the fir of its boughs,
my joys are all lost | as the leaves of the tree
when the destroyer of twigs | turns from the warm day."
Then Hamther spoke out, | the high of heart:
"You gave small praise, Guthrun, | to Hogni's deed
when they woke your Sigurth | out of his sleep;
you sat on the bed | while his killers laughed.
"Your white bed-covers | were red with blood
from his wounds, and wet | with your husband's gore;
so Sigurth was killed, | you sat by his corpse,
and had no thought of gladness: | it was Gunnar's doing.
"You meant to strike at Atli | by the slaying of Erp
and the killing of Eitil; | your own grief was worse;
so each should wield | the wound-biting sword
that it kills another | but does not strike himself."
Then Sorli spoke out, | for he was always wise:
"I will never make | a quarrel with my mother;
neither of you, I think, | is at all short of words;
what do you ask, Guthrun, | that will give you no tears?
"You weep for your brothers, | and your boys so sweet,
your kinsmen by birth | killed on the battlefield;
now, Guthrun, you shall weep | for the two of us as well,
we sit doomed on our steeds, | and far from here we shall die."
Then the fame-glad one, | she was on the steps,
the slender-fingered, | spoke with her son:
"You will be in danger | if you do not heed counsel;
by two heroes alone | two hundred Goths
shall be bound or killed | in the high-walled stronghold."
From the courtyard they went, | and they breathed fury;
the youths went swiftly | over the wet mountain,
on their Hunnish steeds, | to have vengeance for the death.
On the way they found | the man so wise;
"What help can we have | from the brown weakling?"
Their half-brother | answered them then:
"I can aid my kinsmen | as well
as one foot | has help from the other."
"How can a foot | aid its fellow,
or a flesh-grown hand | help another?"
Then Erp spoke out, | his words were few,
as he sat haughty | on his horse's back:
"It is bad to show | the timid the way."
They called | the bold one a bastard.
From their sheaths they drew | their shining swords,
their blades, to give | joy to the giantess;
by a third they lessened | the might that was theirs,
the young fighter | they felled to the earth.
They shook their cloaks, | they sheathed their swords,
the high-born men | wrapped their mantles close.
They went on their road | and found an ill way,
and they saw their sister's son | on a tree,
on the wind-cold wolf-tree | west of the hall,
and cranes'-bait crawled; | no one would care to linger.
In the hall was a din, | the men drank deep,
and no one could hear | the horses' hoofs,
till the hardy warrior | sounded his horn.
Men came and told | the tale to Jormunrek,
how they saw helmeted | warriors outside:
"Take wise counsel, | for brave men have come;
you murdered the sister | of mighty men."
Then Jormunrek laughed, | he laid his hand on his beard,
he called for his arms, | for with wine he was warlike;
he shook his brown locks, | he looked at his white shield,
and raised high in his hand | the cup of gold.
"I would be happy, I think, | if I could see
Hamther and Sorli | here in my hall;
I would bind the men | with bowstrings,
and hang Gjuki's heirs | on the gallows."
In the hall was clamour, | the cups were shattered,
men stood in blood | from the breasts of the Goths.
Then Hamther spoke out, | the haughty of heart:
"You sought, Jormunrek, | to see us,
sons of one mother | seeking your dwelling;
you see your hands, | you look on your feet,
Jormunrek, flung | into the fire so hot."
Then the king roared, | of the race of the gods,
bold in his armour, | as a bear roars:
"Stone the men | that steel will not bite,
neither sword nor spear, | the sons of Jonak."
Sorli said:
"You did ill, brother, | when you opened the bag,
often from that bag | came evil counsel;
you have heart, Hamther, | if only you had knowledge!
A man without wisdom | is lacking in much."
Hamther said:
"His head would now be off | if Erp were living,
the brother so keen | whom we killed on our road,
the noble warrior; | it was the Norns that drove me
to kill the hero | who should be holy in fight.
"It does not befit us, | in the fashion of wolves,
to fight among ourselves,
like the hounds of the Norns, | that were reared
in greed amid wastes so grim.
"We have fought greatly, | we stand over the Goths
laid low by our blades, | like eagles on branches;
great is our fame, though we die | today or tomorrow;
no one outlives the night | when the Norns have spoken."
Then Sorli sank | beside the gable,
and Hamther fell | at the back of the house.

hrbl-p1.s: Thor was on his way back from a journey in the East, and came to a strait; on the other side of the strait was a ferryman with a boat. Thor called out:

l: "Who is that fellow over there, | on the far shore of the strait?"
The ferryman said:
"What kind of peasant is that, | calling across the bay?"
Thor said:
"Ferry me over the strait; | I will feed you for it in the morning;
I have a basket on my back, | and food in it, none better;
I ate at leisure, | before I left the house,
herrings and porridge, | so I had plenty."
The ferryman said:
"You are proud of your morning feats, | but you do not wholly know the future;
your homecoming is sorrowful: | your mother, I think, is dead."
Thor said:
"Now you have said | what must seem to everyone
the greatest grief, | that my mother is dead."
The ferryman said:
"Three good dwellings, | I think, you do not have;
you stand barefoot, | and wear a beggar's clothes;
you do not even have breeches."
Thor said:
"Steer the boat over here; | I will show you the landing place;
but whose is the craft | that you keep on the shore?"
The ferryman said:
"Hildolf is the one | who told me to keep it,
a wise hero; | his home is at Rathsey's strait.
He told me to ferry no robbers, | nor horse thieves,
but worthy men, | and those I know well.
Now say your name, | if you want to cross the strait."
Thor said:
"I will indeed tell my name, | though I am in danger,
and all my race; | I am Othin's son,
Meili's brother, | and Magni's father,
the strong one of the gods; | you can now have speech with Thor.
And now I would like to know | what your name is."
The ferryman said:
"I am Harbarth, | and I seldom hide my name."
Thor said:
"Why should you hide your name, | if you have no quarrel?"
Harbarth said:
"And even if I had a quarrel, | from such as you
I would guard my life | none the less,
unless I am doomed to die."
Thor said:
"It would be great trouble, I think, | to come to you,
to wade across the waters, | and wet my middle;
weakling, I shall pay you well | for your mocking words,
if I come across the strait."
Harbarth said:
"Here I shall stand | and wait for you here;
since Hrungnir died you have found | no fiercer man."
Thor said:
