"You are eager to tell | how I fought with Hrungnir,
the haughty giant, | whose head was made of stone;
and yet I felled him, | and laid him out before me.
What were you doing meanwhile, Harbarth?"
Harbarth said:
"Five full winters | I was with Fjolvar,
and lived on the island | that is called Algrön;
there we could fight, | and cut down the slain,
we could try for much, | and master girls."
Thor said:
"How did you succeed with your women?"
Harbarth said:
"Lively women we had, | if they were wise for us;
wise were the women we had, | if they were kind to us;
for they would try to wind | ropes of sand,
and to dig the bottom | out of the deepest valley.
I was wiser than all | in counsel,
and there I slept | by the seven sisters,
and I had great joy | from each of them.
What were you doing meanwhile, Thor?"
Thor said:
"I felled Thjazi, | the fierce giant,
and I hurled the eyes | of Alvaldi's son
to the hot heavens above;
these are the mightiest | marks of my deeds,
that all men since can see.
What were you doing meanwhile, Harbarth?"
Harbarth said:
"I worked much love-craft | with those who ride by night,
when I stole them by stealth from their husbands;
Hlebarth, I think, | was a hard giant:
he gave me his wand as a gift,
and I stole his wits away."
Thor said:
"You repaid good gifts with an evil mind."
Harbarth said:
"The oak must have | what it shaves from another;
in such things it is each for himself.
What were you doing meanwhile, Thor?"
Thor said:
"I went eastward, | and of the giants I felled
their evil-working women | who went to the mountain;
the giants' throng would be large | if all were alive;
there would be no men | in Mithgarth any more.
What were you doing meanwhile, Harbarth?"
Harbarth said:
"I was in Valland, | and I stirred up wars,
I angered princes, | and never brought peace;
Othin has the nobles | who fall in the fight,
and Thor has the race of slaves."
Thor said:
"You would give the gods | unequal gifts of men,
if you should have too much might."
Harbarth said:
"Thor has might enough, | but never a heart;
in cowardly fear | you were glad to crawl into a glove,
and there forgot you were Thor;
you were afraid there, | such was your fear,
to fart or sneeze | in case Fjalar should hear."
Thor said:
"You womanish Harbarth, | I would strike you straight to hell,
if my arm could reach across the strait."
Harbarth said:
"Why reach across the strait, | since there is no strife between us?
What did you do then, Thor?"
Thor said:
"I was in the east, | and I guarded the river well,
where the sons of Svarang | sought me out;
they hurled stones; | they had small joy of winning;
they came before me there | to ask for peace.
What were you doing meanwhile, Harbarth?"
Harbarth said:
"I was in the east, | and spoke with a certain one,
I played with the linen-white girl, | and met her in secret;
I gladdened the gold-decked one, | and she granted me joy."
Thor said:
"Your woman-finding was fair indeed."
Harbarth said:
"I needed your help then, Thor, | to hold the white girl fast."
Thor said:
"Gladly, had I been there, | I would have given you my help."
Harbarth said:
"I might have trusted you then, | if you were not one to betray your pledge."
Thor said:
"I am no heel-biter, truly, | like an old leather shoe in spring."
Harbarth said:
"What were you doing meanwhile, Thor?"
Thor said:
"In Hlesey I killed | the brides of the Berserkers;
they were most evil, | and they betrayed everyone."
Harbarth said:
"You won shame, | killing women, Thor."
Thor said:
"They were like she-wolves, | and little like women;
they shook my ship, | which I had trimmed well;
they threatened with iron clubs, | and drove Thjalfi off.
What were you doing meanwhile, Harbarth?"
Harbarth said:
"I was in the host | that came this way,
to raise the banners, | and to redden the spear."
Thor said:
"Will you now say | that you sought to bring us hatred?"
Harbarth said:
"A ring for your hand | shall make all right for you,
as the judge decides | who makes peace between us two."
Thor said:
"Where did you find | so foul and scornful a speech?
A fouler speech | I have never heard before."
Harbarth said:
"I learned it from men, | the men so old,
who live in the hills of home."
Thor said:
"You give a very good name | to heaps of stones
when you call them hills of home."
Harbarth said:
"That is how I speak of such things."
Thor said:
"Your sharpness of tongue | will bring you ill,
if I choose to wade the water;
louder, I think, | than a wolf you will cry,
if you get a blow of my hammer."
Harbarth said:
"Sif has a lover at home, | and you should meet him;
it would be more fitting | to use your strength on him."
Thor said:
"Your tongue still makes you say | what seems worst to me,
you witless man! You are lying, I think."
Harbarth said:
"I speak the truth, | but you are slow on your way;
you would have gone far | if you had now travelled in the boat."
Thor said:
"You womanish Harbarth! | you have held me here too long."
Harbarth said:
"I never thought | that Asathor would be hindered
from his journey like this by a ferryman."
Thor said:
"One piece of advice I give you now: | row your boat over here;
no more mockery; | take Magni's father across."
Harbarth said:
"Go away from the strait; | the passage is not yours."
Thor said:
"Then show me the way, | since you will not take me over the water."
Harbarth said:
"To refuse it is little, | to travel it is long;
a while to the stock, | and a while to the stone;
then the road to your left, | till you reach Verland;
and there Fjorgyn | shall find her son Thor,
and she will show him the road of her children | to Othin's realm."
Thor said:
"Can I get that far in a day?"
Harbarth said:
"With toil and trouble, perhaps,
while the sun still shines, | or so I think."
Thor said:
"Our talk shall now be short, | for you speak only in mockery;
I shall pay you for the passage you refused me | if ever we meet."
Harbarth said:
"Be off to where every evil thing shall have you!"
Of old the gods | feasted together,
and they looked for drink | before they had had their fill;
they shook twigs | and tried the blood:
rich fare in Ægir's hall | they found.
The mountain-dweller | sat merry as a boy,
but soon he seemed | like a blinded man;
the son of Ygg | looked him in the eyes:
"You shall prepare a feast | for the gods at once."
The word-wielder made | hard work for the giant,
and so he sought | revenge on the gods;
he told Sif's husband | to bring the cauldron:
"In it I shall brew | plenty of ale for you all."
The far-famed ones | could not find it,
and the holy gods | could get it nowhere;
until Tyr | spoke up truthfully,
and gave Hlorrithi | helpful advice.
"To the east | of Elivagar there lives
Hymir the wise, | at the end of heaven;
my fierce father | owns a cauldron,
a mighty vessel | a mile deep."
Thor said:
"Can we win, do you think, | this whirler of water?"
Tyr said:
"Yes, friend, we can, | if we are cunning."
Onward that day | they travelled at speed,
from Asgarth they came | to Egil's home;
the goats adorned with horns | he kept in his care;
then they hurried to the hall | where Hymir lived.
The youth found his grandmother, | whom he greatly loathed,
and a full nine hundred | heads she had;
but the other, fair | with gold, came forward,
and the bright-browed one | brought beer to her son.
"Kinsman of giants, | under the cauldron
I will put you both, | you bold heroes;
for many a time | my dearly loved husband
is angry with guests | and grim of mind."
Late to his home | came the misshapen Hymir,
the harsh giant, | back from his hunting;
the icicles rattled | as he came in,
for the fellow's chin-forest | was frozen.
"Hail to you, Hymir! | May your thoughts be good;
here your son | has now come to your hall;
(we have waited for him, | his journey was long;)
and with him travels | the enemy of Hroth,
the friend of mankind, | and Veur they call him.
"See where they sit | under the gable!
Behind the beam | they are hiding themselves."
The beam broke | at the giant's glance,
and the mighty pillar | fell in pieces.
Eight fell from the ledge, | and one alone,
the hard-hammered cauldron, | of them all stayed whole;
then they came forward, | and he sought his enemies,
the old giant, | and held them with his eyes.
His heart foretold | much sorrow when he saw
the giantess' enemy | step out onto the floor;
then three of the steers | they brought in;
the giant ordered | their flesh to be boiled.
Each was cut | shorter by a head,
and the beasts they carried | straight to the fire;
the husband of Sif, | before he went to sleep,
ate two of Hymir's | oxen by himself.
To Hrungnir's | grey-haired comrade
Hlorrithi's meal | seemed mighty indeed;
"Next time, in the evening, | we three must eat
the food we have | as the spoils of hunting."
Veur said he was eager | to row out to sea,
if the bold giant | would give him bait.
Hymir said:
"Go to the herd, | if you have a mind to,
you slayer of giants, | to look for your bait;
for there, I think, | you may soon find
bait from the oxen | easy to get."
Swiftly the hero | went to the wood,
until he found before him | an ox all black;
from the beast the slayer | of giants broke
the high fortress | of his double horns.
Hymir said:
"Your deeds, I think, | are far worse,
you steerer of ships, | than when you sit still."
The lord of the goats | told the ape-begotten
to steer further out | the steed of the rollers;
but the giant said | that his wish, in truth,
to row any longer | was little enough.
Two whales on his hook | the mighty Hymir
soon pulled up | at a single cast;
in the stern sat | the kinsman of Othin,
and Veur with cunning | prepared his cast.
The guardian of men, | the serpent's destroyer,
fixed on his hook | the head of the ox;
there gaped at the bait | the enemy of the gods,
the girdler of all | the earth, down below.
The poisonous serpent | was swiftly pulled
up to the boat | by Thor, the bold one;
with his hammer the loathsome | hill of the hair
of Fenrir's brother | he struck from above.
The monsters roared, | and the rocks resounded,
and all the ancient | earth was shaken;
then the fish sank | at once into the sea.
Joyless was the giant | as they rowed back;
Hymir sat speechless | at the oars,
with the rudder he sought | a second wind.
Hymir said:
"Will you take on | half our work with me,
and now make fast | our goat of the flood;
or will you carry | the whales home to the house,
across the gorge | of the wooded glen?"
Hlorrithi stood | and gripped the stem,
and lifted the sea-horse, | awash with water;
oars and bailer | and all he carried
with the surf-swine home | to the giant's house.
The giant wished again | to match his might,
for he was stubborn, | against the strength of Thor;
he would call no one truly strong, | however stoutly he rowed,
except one | who could break the cup.
Then Hlorrithi, | when he held the cup,
struck the pillars | of stone with the glass;
as he sat he shattered | the posts in pieces,
yet they brought the glass | to Hymir whole.
But the giant's | fair loved one found
a true piece of advice, | and told her thought:
"Strike the skull of Hymir, | heavy with food,
for it is harder | than any glass ever was."
The goats' mighty ruler | then rose on his knee,
and with all the strength | of a god he struck;
the fellow's helmet-stem | was whole,
but the rounded wine-cup | was shattered.
Hymir said:
"Fair is the treasure | that has gone from me,
now that the cup | lies shattered on my knees;"
so said the giant: | "No more can I say
in days to come, | 'You are brewed, my ale.'
"It will be enough | if you can carry
out of our house | this cauldron here."
Then Tyr twice | tried to move it,
but twice the cauldron | stood fast before him.
The father of Mothi | seized the rim firmly,
and stood before it | on the floor below;
up onto his head | Sif's husband lifted it,
and about his heels | the handles clattered.
They had not gone far | before he looked back,
the son of Othin, | to see once more;
from their caves in the east | he saw coming
with Hymir the throng | of the many-headed.
He stood and threw | the cauldron from his back,
and Mjollnir, the lover | of murder, he wielded;
so he killed all | the whales of the waste.
They had not gone far | before there lay
one of Hlorrithi's goats | half-dead on the ground;
the pole-horse there | was lame in his leg;
this was the doing | of the evil Loki.
But you have all heard, | for of those who have
the tales of the gods, | who can tell them better?
what prize he won | from the wilderness-dweller,
who gave him both | his children into the bargain.
The mighty one came | to the council of the gods,
and he had the cauldron | that had been Hymir's;
so the gods could gladly | drink their ale
in Ægir's hall | at autumn-time.

ls-p1.s: Ægir, who was also called Gymir, had prepared ale for the gods, after he had got the mighty cauldron, as has just been told. Othin and Frigg, his wife, came to this feast. Thor did not come, as he was on a journey in the East. Sif, Thor's wife, was there, and Bragi with Ithun, his wife. Tyr, who had only one hand, was there; the wolf Fenrir had bitten off his other hand when they had bound him. Njorth and Skathi his wife were there, Freyr and Freyja, and Vithar, the son of Othin. Loki was there, and Freyr's servants Byggvir and Beyla. Many of the gods and elves were there.

Ægir had two servants, Fimafeng and Eldir. They had glittering gold in place of firelight; the ale came in of itself; and the peace was great. The guests greatly praised the ability of Ægir's servants. Loki could not bear that, and he killed Fimafeng. Then the gods shook their shields and howled at Loki and drove him away to the forest, and after that they set to drinking again. Loki turned back, and outside he met Eldir. Loki spoke to him:

l: "Speak now, Eldir, | for not one step
further shall you go;
what ale-talk do they have | in here,
the sons of the glorious gods?"
Eldir said:
"They talk of their weapons | and their might in war,
the sons of the glorious gods;
among the gods and elves | who are gathered here
you will find no friend in words."
Loki said:
"In I shall go, | into Ægir's hall,
for I would gladly see the feast;
harm and hatred | I bring to the gods,
and I mix their mead with poison."
Eldir said:
"If you go in | to Ægir's hall,
and would gladly see the feast,
and would sprinkle the gods | with slander and spite,
take care that they do not wipe it on you."
Loki said:
"Remember, Eldir, | if you and I
are to quarrel with spiteful speech,
I grow richer | in ready words
if you say too much to me."

ls-p2.s: Then Loki went into the hall, but when those who were there saw who had come in, they all fell silent.

l: Loki said:
"Thirsty I come | into this hall of yours,
I, Lopt, from a long journey,
to ask the gods | that one of them give me
fine mead to drink.
"Why do you sit silent, | swollen with pride,
you gods, and give no answer?
Prepare me a place | and a seat at your feast,
or tell me to be gone."
Bragi said:
"A place and a seat | the gods will prepare
no more among them for you;
for the gods know well | which men they wish
to find at their mighty feasts."
Loki said:
"Remember, Othin, | that in the old days
we two mixed our blood together;
you promised then | to pour no ale
unless it was brought for us both."
Othin said:
"Stand up then, Vithar, | and let the wolf's father
find a seat at our feast,
so that Loki does not | speak evil aloud
here within Ægir's hall."

ls-p3.s: Then Vithar got up and poured drink for Loki; but before he drank he spoke to the gods:

l: "Hail to you, gods! | Hail, you goddesses!
Hail to the holy throng!
All but the god | who sits over there,
Bragi there on the bench."
Bragi said:
"A horse and a sword | I will give from my hoard,
and Bragi gives a ring as well,
so that you stir up no hatred | among the gods;
so do not rouse the great ones to anger."
Loki said:
"In horses and rings | you will never be rich,
Bragi, but will lack them both;
of the gods and elves | who are met together here
you are the least brave in battle,
(and you shrink most from the shot.)"
Bragi said:
"If I were outside now | as I am inside,
here in Ægir's hall,
I would carry your head | away in my hands,
and pay you the price of your lies."
Loki said:
"You are bold in your seat, | but not in your deeds,
Bragi, adorner of benches!
Go out and fight | if you feel angry;
no hero takes such forethought."
Ithun said:
"Come, Bragi, I beg you, | weigh his kinship,
since he was chosen as wish-son;
and do not speak to Loki | such words of spite
here within Ægir's hall."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Ithun! | You are, I say,
of all women the most lustful in love,
since you wound your washed-bright | arms
about your brother's killer."
Ithun said:
"I do not speak to Loki | with spiteful words
here within Ægir's hall;
and I calm Bragi, | who is hot with beer,
for I do not wish them to fight in anger."
Gefjun said:
"Why do you two gods, | with bitter tongues,
raise hatred among us here?
Loki is famed | for his foul mockery,
and he hates the dwellers in heaven."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Gefjun! | For now I shall say
who led you into an evil life;
the boy so fair | gave a bright necklace,
and your leg was laid about him."
Othin said:
"You are mad, Loki, | and of little wit,
to rouse the anger of Gefjun;
for the fate that is set | for all she sees
as well as I do, I think."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Othin! | You do not justly settle
the fate of the fight among men;
often you gave to him | who did not deserve the gift,
to the lesser man, the battle's prize."
Othin said:
"Though I gave to him | who did not deserve the gift,
to the lesser man, the battle's prize,
eight winters | you were under the earth,
milking the cows as a maid,
(yes, and you bore babies;
your soul must seem unmanly.)"
Loki said:
"They say that with spells | in Samsey once
you worked charms like witches;
and in a witch's guise | you went among men;
your soul must seem unmanly."
Frigg said:
"Of the deeds you two | did long ago
you should not speak among men;
whatever you have done | in days gone by,
old tales should never be told."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Frigg! | You are Fjorgyn's wife,
but always lustful in love;
for Vili and Ve, | you wife of Vithrir,
have both lain in your embrace."
Frigg said:
"If a son like Baldr | were beside me now,
here within Ægir's hall,
you would not get away | from the sons of the gods
until your fierceness in fight had been tested."
Loki said:
"You wish then, Frigg, | that I tell more
of the evil that I now know;
mine is the blame | that you no longer see
Baldr ride home to the hall."
Freyja said:
"You are mad, Loki, | to make known
the wrong and shame you have done;
Frigg knows well | the fate of all,
though she does not say it herself."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Freyja! | For I know you fully,
you are not sinless yourself;
of the gods and elves | who are gathered here,
each one has lain as your lover."
Freyja said:
"Your tongue is false, | and soon you will find
that it sings you an evil song;
the gods are angry, | and all the goddesses,
and in grief you will go home."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Freyja! | You foulest witch,
and steeped very deep in sin;
in your brother's arms | the bright gods caught you
when Freyja broke wind."
Njorth said:
"It does little harm | if a woman has
a husband or a lover or both;
but it is a wonder | that this womanish god
comes here, though he has borne babies."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Njorth; | you were sent eastward,
given to the gods as a hostage;
and the daughters of Hymir | had their privy
when they made use of your mouth."
Njorth said:
"Great was my gain, | though I was long away,
given to the gods as a hostage;
I had the son | whom no man hates,
and who is found foremost of gods."
Loki said:
"Take heed now, Njorth, | and do not boast too much,
I will hide it no longer;
with your sister you had | so fair a son,
so you had no worse a hope."
Tyr said:
"Of the brave heroes | Freyr is the best
here in the home of the gods;
he harms neither girls | nor the wives of men,
and frees the bound from their fetters."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Tyr! | For between two men
you could never make friendship;
I would gladly tell | how Fenrir once
tore your right hand from you."
Tyr said:
"I lack my hand, | but you lack Hrothvitnir,
and the loss brings longing to both;
it goes badly for the wolf, | who must forever await
in fetters the fall of the gods."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Tyr! | For your wife once happened
to have a son by me;
not a penny, I think, | were you paid for the wrong,
nor given an inch of redress, poor wretch."
Freyr said:
"By the mouth of the river | the wolf remains
until the gods go to destruction;
you too will soon, | if your tongue is not stilled,
be fettered, you forger of evil."
Loki said:
"The daughter of Gymir | you bought with gold,
and sold your sword as well;
but when Muspell's sons | ride through Myrkvidr,
you will wait weaponless, poor wretch."
Byggvir said:
"If I had a birth as famous | as Ingunar-Freyr's,
and sat in so lofty a seat,
I would crush to marrow | this croaker of evil,
and beat his whole body to bits."
Loki said:
"What little creature | goes crawling there,
snuffling and snapping about?
At Freyr's ears | you will always be found,
or muttering hard at the mill."
Byggvir said:
"Byggvir is my name, | and I am nimble,
as gods and men grant;
and here I am proud | that the children of Hropt
all drink ale together."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Byggvir! | You could never set
men their shares of the food;
hidden in straw on the floor, | they did not find you
when heroes were eager to fight."
Heimdall said:
"You are drunk, Loki, | and your deeds are mad;
why, Loki, do you not leave off?
For drink beyond measure | will lead all men
to take no thought of their tongues."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Heimdall! | In days long past
an evil fate was fixed for you;
with back held stiff | you must always stand,
to watch as guardian of heaven."
Skathi said:
"You are light of heart, Loki, | but you may no longer
flourish your tail in freedom;
on the rocks the gods bind you | with bowels torn
out of your frost-cold son."
Loki said:
"Though on rocks the gods bind me | with bowels torn
out of my frost-cold son,
I was first and last | at the deadly fight
where we caught Thjazi."
Skathi said:
"If you were first and last | at the deadly fight
where Thjazi was caught,
from my dwellings and fields | there shall always come
cold counsel for you."
Loki said:
"You spoke more lightly | with Laufey's son
when you invited me to your bed;
such things must be known | if we two now
are to seek to tell our sins."
"Hail to you, Loki, | and take here
the crystal cup of old mead;
me at least, | alone among the gods,
you know to be blameless."
"Alone you would be, | if you truly did
shun all men so shyly;
but I know one | very well, I think,
who had you from Hlorrithi's arms,
(Loki the crafty in lies.)"
Beyla said:
"The mountains shake, | and surely I think
Hlorrithi is coming now from his home;
he will silence the man | who is slandering here
both gods and men together."
Loki said:
"Be silent, Beyla! | You are Byggvir's wife,
and you are steeped deep in sin;
a greater shame | never came to the gods,
you are befouled with your filth."

ls-s57.s: Then Thor came forward and said:

l: "Stop, unmanly one, | or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close your mouth;
your shoulder-cliff | I shall strike from your neck,
and so your life shall be lost."
Loki said:
"Look, in has come | the son of Earth:
why do you threaten so loudly, Thor?
Less fiercely you will go | to fight with the wolf
when he swallows Sigfather up."
Thor said:
"Stop, unmanly one, | or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close your mouth;
I shall hurl you up | and out into the East,
where men shall see you no more."
Loki said:
"That you have travelled | out on the East-road
you should tell men no more;
in the thumb of a glove | you hid, you great one,
and there forgot you were Thor."
Thor said:
"Stop, unmanly one, | or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close your mouth;
my right hand shall strike you | with Hrungnir's slayer,
until all your bones are broken."
Loki said:
"I think to live | a long time yet,
though you threaten me so with your hammer;
the straps of Skrymir's bag | seemed tough
when you could not get at your food,
(and felt faint from hunger.)"
Thor said:
"Stop, unmanly one, | or the mighty hammer,
Mjollnir, shall close your mouth;
the slayer of Hrungnir | shall send you to hell,
and down to the gate of death."
Loki said:
"I have said to the gods | and the sons of the gods
the things that whetted my thoughts;
but before you alone | I now go out,
for you fight well, I think.
"You have brewed ale, | but now, Ægir,
you shall make such feasts no more;
over all that you have | here within
the flickering flames shall play,
(and your back shall be burnt with fire.)"

ls-p4.s: And after that Loki hid himself in Franang's waterfall in the shape of a salmon, and there the gods caught him. He was bound with the bowels of his son Vali, but his son Narfi was changed into a wolf. Skathi took a poisonous snake and fastened it up over Loki's face, and the poison dripped onto it. Sigyn, Loki's wife, sat there and held a shell under the poison, but when the shell was full she carried the poison away, and meanwhile the poison dripped on Loki. Then he struggled so hard that the whole earth shook with it; and that is now called an earthquake.

od-p1.s: There was a king called Heithrek, whose daughter was called Borgny. Her lover was a man called Vilmund. She could not give birth to a child until Oddrun, Atli's sister, had come to her; Oddrun had been the beloved of Gunnar, son of Gjuki. The following poem is about this story.

l: I have heard it told | in tales of old
how a maiden came | to Morningland;
no one at all | on the earth above
could give help | to Heithrek's daughter.
Oddrun, the sister of Atli, | learned of this,
that the maiden's sickness | was severe;
she brought the bit-bearer | out from his stall,
and laid the saddle | on the black steed.
She let the horse go | over the level ground,
till she reached the hall | that rose so high,
(and in she went | from the end of the hall;)
from the weary steed | she took the saddle;
hear now the words | that she spoke first:
"What news on earth, | .......
or what has happened | in Hunland now?"
A serving-maid said:
"Here Borgny lies | in bitter pain,
your friend, Oddrun, | and she seeks your help."
Oddrun said:
"Who brought this woe | upon the woman,
and why is Borgny | so suddenly sick?"
The serving-maid said:
"It is Vilmund, | the heroes' friend,
who wrapped the woman | in warm bedclothes,
(for five winters, | yet her father did not know)."
Then they spoke | no more, I think;
she went to sit | at the woman's knees;
with magic Oddrun | and mightily Oddrun
chanted for Borgny | potent charms.
At last were born | a boy and a girl,
son and daughter | of Hogni's slayer;
then the woman, so weak, | began to speak,
and said nothing | before she said this:
"So may the holy | ones help you,
Frigg and Freyja | and the favouring gods,
as you have saved me | from sorrow now."
Oddrun said:
"I did not come here | to help you like this
because you ever | earned my aid;
I fulfilled the oath | that I swore long ago,
that I should always | bring aid to all,
(when they shared the wealth | the warriors had)."
Borgny said:
"You are wild, Oddrun, | and witless now,
to speak to me | with such hatred;
I followed you | wherever you went,
as if we had been born | of two brothers."
Oddrun said:
"I remember the evil | you spoke one evening,
when I gave | a drink to Gunnar;
you said that never | had such a deed
been done by a maiden, | except by me alone."
Then the sorrowing woman | sat down
to tell the grief | of her great troubles.
"I grew up happy | in the hero's hall,
as the warriors wished, | and they loved me well;
I was glad | of my father's gifts,
for five winters, | while my father lived.
"These were the words | that the weary king,
before he died, | spoke last of all:
he told them to dower me | with red gold,
and to marry me in the South | to Grimhild's son.
"But Brynhild he told | to wear the helmet,
a bright wish-maid | he said she should be;
for a nobler maiden | would never be born
on earth, he said, | if death should spare her.
"Brynhild sat | weaving in her bower,
lands and people | alike she had;
the earth and the heaven | on high resounded
when Fafnir's slayer | saw the city.
"Then battle was fought | with the foreign swords,
and the city was broken | that Brynhild had;
not long afterwards, | but all too soon,
she knew full well | their evil tricks.
"Terrible for this | was her vengeance,
as we all learned | to our sorrow;
in every land | all men shall hear
how she killed herself | at Sigurth's side.
"Then I gave | my love to Gunnar,
to the breaker of rings, | as Brynhild might have;
to Atli they offered | rings so red,
and wished to give | mighty gifts to my brother.
"Fifteen dwellings | he would gladly give
for me, and the burden | that Grani carried;
but Atli said | he would never accept
marriage gold | from Gjuki's son.
"Yet we could not | overcome our love,
and I laid my head | on the hero's shoulder;
there were many | of my kinsmen
who said that they had seen | us together.
"Atli said | that I would never
plan evil | or do a wrong deed;
but no one may think this | of another,
or say it for certain, | when love is shared.
"Soon Atli | sent his men
to spy on me | in the murky wood;
they came there, | where they should not have come,
where we lay close | beneath one cover.
"We offered the warriors | red rings,
so that they would never | say anything to Atli;
but they hurried | swiftly home from there,
and eagerly | told Atli everything.
"But from Guthrun | they kept well hidden
what she ought to have known | first of all.
"Great was the clatter | of gilded hooves
when Gjuki's sons | rode through the gateway;
they cut the heart | out of Hogni then,
and the other they threw | into the serpents' cave.
"The wise hero | then struck his harp,
for help from me, | he still hoped in his heart,
the high-born king, | might come to him.
"I had gone alone | to Geirmund then,
to mix the drink | and make it ready;
suddenly I heard | clearly from Hlesey
how the strings of the harp | sounded in sorrow.
"I told the serving-maids | to make ready,
for I longed to save | the hero's life;
we sailed the boats | across the sound,
till we saw the whole | of Atli's home.
"Then the evil woman | came crawling,
Atli's mother, | may she rot for ever!
And she bit hard | into Gunnar's heart,
so I could not help | the brave hero.
"I have often wondered | how after this,
Serpents'-bed goddess! | I could still live,
for I loved | the brave warrior well,
the giver of swords, | as my very self.
"You saw and listened | while I told
the mighty grief | that was mine and theirs;
each man lives | as his longing wills.
Oddrun's lament | is ended now."

rm-p1.s: Sigurth went to Hjalprek's stud and chose himself a horse, which was afterwards called Grani. At that time Regin, the son of Hreithmar, had come to Hjalprek's home. He was more ingenious than any other man, and a dwarf in stature; he was wise, fierce and skilled in magic. Regin took charge of Sigurth's upbringing and teaching, and loved him dearly. He told Sigurth about his forefathers, and also about this: that Othin, Hönir and Loki had once come to Andvari's waterfall, and in the fall there were many fish. Andvari was a dwarf who had long lived in the waterfall in the shape of a pike, and there he got his food. "Otr was the name of a brother of ours," said Regin, "who often went into the fall in the shape of an otter. He had caught a salmon and sat on the high bank eating it with his eyes shut. Loki threw a stone at him and killed him. The gods thought they had had great good luck, and stripped the skin off the otter. That same evening they sought a night's lodging at Hreithmar's house and showed their booty. Then we seized them and told them, as ransom for their lives, to fill the otter skin with gold and to cover it completely on the outside as well with red gold. Then they sent Loki to get the gold. He went to Ron and got her net, then went to Andvari's fall and cast the net in front of the pike, and the pike leaped into the net." Then Loki said:

l: "What is the fish | that runs in the flood,
and cannot save itself from harm?
If you would redeem | your head from hell,
find me the water's flame."
Andvari said:
"I am Andvari, | and Oin was my father,
I have travelled through many a fall;
an evil Norn | in days of old
doomed me to live in the waters."
Loki said:
"Say, Andvari, | if you still seek
to live in the land of men,
what payment is set | for the sons of men
who make war with lying words?"
Andvari said:
"A mighty payment | those men must make
who wade in Vathgelmir's waters;
the lying words | lead on a long road
that one man utters to another."

rm-p2.s: Loki saw all the gold that Andvari had. But when Andvari had brought out all the gold, he held back one ring, and Loki took this from him. The dwarf went into his hole in the rock and said:

l: "Now the gold | that Gust once had
shall bring death | to two brothers,
and be evil | for eight heroes;
no man shall have | joy of my wealth."

rm-p3.s: The gods gave Hreithmar the gold, and filled up the otter skin, and stood it on its feet. Then the gods had to heap up gold and hide it. When that was done, Hreithmar came forward and saw a single whisker, and told them to cover it. Then Othin brought out the ring Andvaranaut and covered the hair. Then Loki said:

l: "The gold is given, | and great is the price
you have to save my head;
but your sons | shall find no fortune there,
it is the death of you both."
Hreithmar said:
"You gave gifts, | but you did not give kindly,
you did not give with whole hearts;
you would all have lost | your lives before this,
if I had seen this fate sooner."
Loki said:
"Worse is this | that I think I see,
for kinsmen shall clash over a maiden;
heroes unborn | shall by this,
I think, be doomed to hatred."
Hreithmar said:
"The gold so red | I shall rule, I think,
as long as I live;
I feel no fear | of your threats,
so be off to your homes."

rm-p4.s: Fafnir and Regin asked Hreithmar for a share of the wealth that had been paid for the killing of their brother, Otr. He refused, and Fafnir thrust his sword through the body of his father, Hreithmar, while he was sleeping. Hreithmar called to his daughters:

l: "Lyngheith and Lofnheith, | my life is gone,
and great now is my need!"
Lyngheith said:
"Though a sister loses | her father, seldom
does she bring revenge on her brother."
Hreithmar said:
"Bear a daughter, | woman with a wolf's heart,
if you have no son | with the brave hero;
if someone marries the maiden, | for the need is great,
their son may seek | vengeance for your hurt."

rm-p5.s: Then Hreithmar died, and Fafnir took all the gold. Regin then asked for his inheritance from his father, but Fafnir refused. Then Regin asked his sister Lyngheith for advice on how he should win his inheritance. She said:

l: "In a friendly way | you shall ask your brother
for the wealth, and for better will;
it is not fitting | to seek with the sword
to take Fafnir's treasure."

rm-p6.s: Regin told Sigurth all these things that had happened.
One day, when he came to Regin's house, he was gladly welcomed. Regin said:

l: "Here the son | of Sigmund has come,
the eager hero, | here to our hall;
his courage is greater | than an old man's,
and I hope for battle | from the hardy wolf.
"Here I shall foster | the fearless prince,
now Yngvi's heir | has come to us;
the noblest hero | beneath the sun,
the threads of his fate | enfold all lands."
"Loud will the sons | of Hunding laugh,
who laid Eylimi | low in death,
if the hero sooner | seeks to find
the red rings | than vengeance for his father."

rm-p8.s: King Hjalprek gave Sigurth a fleet to avenge his father. They ran into a great storm, and were off a certain headland. A man stood on the mountain and said:

l: "Who rides there | on Rævil's steeds,
over towering waves | and wild waters?
The sail-horses | are all dripping with sweat,
and the sea-steeds | cannot withstand the gale."
Regin answered:
"On the sea-trees here | are Sigurth and I,
the storm wind drives us | on to our death;
the waves crash down | on the forward deck,
and the roller-steeds sink; | who asks our names?"
The Man said:
"I was Hnikar | when Volsung once
gladdened the ravens | and gave battle;
call me now | the Man from the Mountain,
Feng or Fjolnir; | I will travel with you."
"Say, Hnikar, | for you see the fate
that is given to gods and men;
what sign is fairest | for one who fights,
and best for the swinging of swords?"
Hnikar said:
"Many are the signs, | if men only knew,
that are good for the swinging of swords;
it is well, I think, | if the warrior meets
a black raven on his road.
"It is another | if you have come out,
and are ready to set off,
to see on the path | in front of your house
two fighters greedy for fame.
"Third, it is well | if you hear
a wolf howling under the ash;
and fortune comes | if you see your foe
before the hero sees you.
"A man shall not fight | when he must face
the moon's bright sister | setting late;
he shall win | who can see well,
and forms his men | like a wedge for the fray.
"Foul is the sign | if your foot stumbles
as you go out to fight;
harmful goddesses | at both your sides
wish that you should be wounded.
"Combed and washed | the wise man shall go,
and take a meal in the morning;
for it is unknown | where he may be by evening;
it is bad to lose your luck."

rm-p10.s: Sigurth fought a great battle with Lyngvi, the son of Hunding, and his brothers; there Lyngvi fell, and his two brothers with him. After the battle Regin said:

l: "Now the bloody eagle | with a biting sword
is carved on the back | of Sigmund's killer;
few were fiercer | in battle than his son,
who reddened the earth | and gladdened the ravens."

rm-p11.s: Sigurth went home to Hjalprek's house; then Regin urged him on to fight Fafnir.

rth-p1.s: They tell in old stories that one of the gods, whose name was Heimdall, went on his way along a certain seashore and came to a house, where he called himself Rig. The following poem is based on these stories:

l: Men say there went | along green ways,
long ago, the god, | the aged and wise;
mighty and strong, | Rig went striding.
Onward he went | down the middle of the road,
he came to a house, | a door on its posts;
in he went, | there was a fire on the floor,
two grey-haired people | sat by the hearth,
Ai and Edda, | in old-fashioned dress.
Rig knew well | how to speak wise words;
soon he sat | in the middle of the room,
and on either side | were the others.
A loaf of bread | Edda brought,
heavy and thick | and swollen with husks;
out on the table | she set the food,
and there was broth | for the meal in a bowl.
(Boiled calf's meat | was the best of the delicacies.)
Rig knew well | how to speak wise words;
then he got up, | made ready to sleep;
soon he laid himself | down in the bed,
and on either side | were the others.
So he stayed there | for three nights,
then onward he went | down the middle of the road,
and so nine months | had soon gone by.
Edda bore a son, | they sprinkled him with water,
they covered his hair, | so black, with a cloth;
they named him Thræll, | . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
The skin was wrinkled | and rough on his hands,
his knuckles knotted, | . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
his fingers thick, | and his face ugly,
his back twisted, | and his heels big.
He began to grow | and to gain in strength,
soon he made | good use of his might;
he tied with bast, | and carried loads,
he brought brushwood home | the whole day long.
One came to their home, | her legs were crooked,
her feet were stained, | and her arms sunburnt,
her nose was flat; | her name was Thir.
Soon she sat | in the middle of the room,
and by her side | sat the son of the house;
they both whispered, | and made the bed ready,
Thræll and Thir, | till the day was over.
They had children, | they lived and were happy,
Fjosnir and Klur | they were called, I think,
Hreim and Kleggi, | Kefsir, Fulnir,
Drumb, Digraldi, | Drott and Leggjaldi,
Lut and Hosvir; | they looked after the house,
they manured the ground, | and guarded the swine,
they tended goats, | and dug turf.
They had daughters, | Drumba and Kumba,
Ökkvinkalfa, | Arinnefja,
Ysja and Ambott, | Eikintjasna,
Totrughypja | and Tronubeina;
and from them has sprung | the race of slaves.
Onward went Rig, | his road was straight,
he came to a hall, | and a door hung there;
in he went, | there was a fire on the floor:
Afi and Amma | owned the house.
There the two sat | and worked at their tasks:
the man cut wood | for the weaver's beam;
his beard was trimmed, | a curl over his brow,
his clothes fitted closely; | in the corner a chest.
The woman sat | and plied the distaff,
with arms outstretched | she worked at the weaving;
on her head was a band, | on her breast a smock;
on her shoulders was a kerchief | with clasps.
Rig knew well | how to speak wise words;
soon he sat | in the middle of the room,
and on either side | were the others.
Then Amma took | . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
she set out the vessels | full of food,
boiled calf's meat | was the best of the delicacies.
Rig knew well | how to speak wise words;
he rose from the table, | made ready to sleep;
soon he laid himself | down in the bed,
and on either side | were the others.
So he stayed there | for three nights,
then onward he went | down the middle of the road,
and so nine months | had soon gone by.
Amma bore a son, | they sprinkled him with water,
they named him Karl; | she wrapped him in a cloth,
his face was ruddy, | and his eyes flashing.
He began to grow | and to gain in strength,
he managed oxen, | and made ploughs ready,
he built houses, | and put up barns,
he made carts, | and handled the plough.
Home they brought | the bride for Karl,
dressed in goatskins, | and carrying keys;
Snör was her name, | she sat under the veil;
they made a home ready, | and exchanged rings,
they decked the bed, | and made a dwelling.
They had sons, | they lived and were happy:
Hal and Dreng, | Holth, Thegn and Smith,
Breith and Bondi, | Bundinskeggi,
Bui and Boddi, | Brattskegg and Segg.
They had daughters, | and here are their names:
Snot, Bruth, Svanni, | Svarri, Sprakki,
Fljoth, Sprund and Vif, | Feima, Ristil:
and from them has sprung | the race of yeomen.
From there went Rig, | his road was straight,
he saw a hall, | its doors faced south;
the door stood wide open, | on the posts was a ring,
then in he went; | the floor was strewn.
Inside, two gazed | into each other's eyes,
Fathir and Mothir, | and played with their fingers;
there sat the master of the house, | and wound strings for the bow,
he made arrow-shafts, | and shaped bows.
The lady sat | and looked at her arms,
she smoothed the cloth, | and fitted the sleeves;
her cap was bright, | on her breast were clasps,
her train was broad, | her gown was blue,
her brows were bright, | her breast was shining,
her neck whiter | than new-fallen snow.
Rig knew well | how to speak wise words;
soon he sat | in the middle of the room,
and on either side | were the others.
Then Mothir brought | an embroidered cloth
of bright linen, | and covered the table;
and then she took | the thin loaves,
and laid them, white | from the wheat, on the cloth.
Then she brought out | the full vessels,
covered with silver, | and set before them
well-browned meat | and well-cooked birds;
in the jug was wine, | the cups were plated,
so they drank and talked | till the day was done.
Rig knew well | how to speak wise words;
soon he got up, | made ready to sleep;
so he laid himself | down in the bed,
and on either side | were the others.
So he stayed there | for three nights,
then onward he went | down the middle of the road,
and so nine months | had soon gone by.
Mothir had a son, | they wrapped him in silk,
they sprinkled him with water, | Jarl he was;
his hair was blond, | and his cheeks bright,
grim as a snake's | were his glowing eyes.
Jarl began | to grow up in the house,
he brandished shields, | and wound bowstrings,
he shot bows, | and made arrow-shafts,
he loosed arrows, | and wielded lances,
he rode horses, | and unleashed hounds,
he handled swords, | and swam the sounds.
Straight from the grove | came Rig striding,
Rig came striding, | and taught him runes;
he called him by his own name, | claimed him as his son,
and told him to hold | his wide heritage,
his wide heritage, | the ancient homes.
Onward he rode | through the dark forest,
over the frosty crags, | till he found a hall.
He shook his spear, | he brandished his shield,
he spurred his horse, | he hewed with his sword;
he stirred up wars, | and reddened the field,
he killed warriors, | and won land.
Eighteen halls | he soon held,
he gained wealth, | and gave to all,
stones and jewels | and slim-flanked horses,
he offered rings, | and shared out arm-rings.
His messengers went | by the wet ways,
and came to the hall | where Hersir lived;
his daughter was fair | and slender-fingered,
Erna the wise | was the maiden's name.
They asked for her hand, | and brought her home,
wedded to Jarl | she wore the veil;
they lived together, | their joy was great,
they had children, | and lived happily.
Bur was the eldest, | and Barn the next,
Joth and Athal, | Arfi, Mog,
Nith and Svein | (soon they began),
Sun and Nithjung | (to play and swim);
Kund was one, | and the youngest Kon.
Soon the sons | of Jarl grew up,
they tamed beasts, | and rounded shields,
they made arrow-shafts, | and shook spears.
But Kon the Young | learned to use runes,
everlasting runes, | the runes of life;
soon he could well | shield warriors,
dull the sword-blade, | and still the seas.
He learned bird-chatter, | he could lessen flames,
he could quiet minds, | and calm sorrows;
the might and strength | of twice four men.
With Rig-Jarl soon | he shared the runes,
he was more cunning, | and greater his wisdom;
he sought the right, | and soon he won it,
to be called Rig, | and to know runes.
Young Kon rode out | through forest and grove,
let arrows fly, | and lured birds;
then a crow spoke, | sitting on a bough:
"Why do you lure, Kon, | the birds to come?
"It would be better | to ride out on your horse,
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . | and to slay the host.
"The halls of Dan | and Danp are noble,
their wealth is greater | than you have gained;
they are good | at steering the keel,
at testing weapons, | and dealing wounds.

sd-p1.s: Sigurth rode up on Hindarfjoll and turned south towards the land of the Franks. On the mountain he saw a great light, as if a fire were burning, and the glow reached up to heaven. When he came there, a tower of shields stood there, and above it was a banner. Sigurth went into the shield-tower and saw a man lying there asleep with all his weapons of war. First he took the helmet from his head, and then he saw that it was a woman. The mail-coat was as tight as if it had grown into the flesh. Then he cut the mail-coat from the neck-opening downwards, and out to both the armholes. Then he took the mail-coat off her, and she woke, sat up, saw Sigurth and said:

l: "What bit through the mail-coat? | How was my sleep broken?
Who has set me free | from the pale fetters?"
He answered:
"Sigmund's son, | with Sigurth's sword,
that lately fed | the ravens with flesh."

sd-p2.s: Sigurth sat down beside her and asked her name. She took a horn full of mead and gave him a memory-draught.

l: "Hail, day! | Hail, sons of day!
And night and her daughter now!
Look on us here | with loving eyes,
that we who wait may win victory.
"Hail to the gods! | Hail, you goddesses,
and all the generous earth!
Give us wisdom | and good speech,
and healing hands, all our lives.
"Long I slept, | long was my slumber,
and long are the griefs of life;
Othin decreed | that I could not break
the heavy spells of sleep."

sd-p3.s: Her name was Sigrdrifa, and she was a Valkyrie. She said that two kings had fought in battle; one was called Hjalmgunnar, an old man but a mighty warrior, and Othin had promised him the victory, and

l: the other was Agnar, | brother of Autha,
he found no one | willing to shield him.

sd-p4.s: Sigrdrifa killed Hjalmgunnar in the battle, and Othin pricked her with the sleep-thorn as punishment for this, and said that she would never again win victory in battle, but that she would be married. "And I told him that I had made a vow in my turn, that I would never marry a man who knew the meaning of fear." Sigurth answered and asked her to teach him wisdom, if she knew what was happening in all the worlds. Sigrdrifa said:

l: "Beer I bring you, | tree of battle,
mixed with strength | and mighty fame;
it holds charms | and healing signs,
good spells, | and gladness-runes."
Learn winning-runes, | if you long to win,
and write the runes on your sword-hilt;
some on the furrow, | and some on the flat,
and twice you shall call on Tyr.
Learn ale-runes, | so that another's wife
may not betray your trust with lies;
you shall write on the horn, | and the backs of your hands,
and mark Need on your nails.
You shall bless the drink, | and escape danger,
and throw a leek in the cup;
(for so I know | you will never see
your mead mixed with evil.)
Learn birth-runes, | if you would lend help
to bring the child from the mother;
write them on your palms, | and round your joints,
and ask the fates for aid.
Learn wave-runes, | if you would shelter well
the sail-steeds out on the sea;
you shall write on the stem, | and the steering-blade,
and burn them into the oars;
though the breakers are high, | and the waves black,
you shall reach the harbour safe.
Learn branch-runes, | if you would be a healer,
and work a cure for wounds;
you shall write on the bark, | and on trees that have
boughs bent to the east.
Learn speech-runes, | so that none may seek
to answer harm with hate;
he winds them well | and weaves them all,
and sets them side by side,
at the place of judgment, | when the people there
shall fairly win justice.
Learn thought-runes, | if all are to think
you the keenest-minded of men.
Hropt arranged them, | and he wrote them,
and he made them in thought,
out of the drink | that had dripped down
from the head of Heithdraupnir,
and the horn of Hoddrofnir.
On the mountain he stood | with Brimir's sword,
on his head he wore the helmet;
then first the head | of Mim spoke out,
and it told words of truth.
He told them to write on the shield | before the shining goddess,
on Arvak's ear, | and on Alsvith's hoof,
on the wheel of the chariot | of Hrungnir's killer,
on Sleipnir's teeth, | and the straps of the sledge.
On the paws of the bear, | and on Bragi's tongue,
on the wolf's bared claws, | and the eagle's beak,
on bloody wings, | and the bridge's end,
on freeing hands | and helping footprints.
On glass and on gold, | and on good charms,
in wine and in beer, | and on well-loved seats,
on Gungnir's point, | and on Grani's breast,
on the nails of Norns, | and the night-owl's beak.
The runes written of old | were shaved off,
and mixed with the holy mead,
and sent on wide ways;
so the gods had them, | so the elves got them,
and some for the wise Wanes,
and some for mortal men.
Beech-runes are there, | birth-runes are there,
and all the runes of ale,
and the magic runes of might;
whoever knows them rightly | and reads them truly
has them to help himself;
they always aid,
till the gods are gone.
Brynhild said:
"Now you shall choose, | for the choice is given,
you tree of the biting blade;
speech or silence, | it is yours to say,
all our evil is destined."
Sigurth said:
"I shall not flee, | though my fate is near,
I was not born to be a coward;
your loving words | I will win for mine,
as long as I live."
Then first I advise you | to be free of guilt
always towards your kinsmen;
take no vengeance, | though they do you harm,
you shall win reward after death.
Then second I advise you | to swear no oath
unless you know it to be true;
bitter is the fate | of the breaker of faith,
and wretched is the wolf of his word.
Then third I advise you | that at the Thing
you do not fight in words with fools;
for the unwise man | often utters
a worse word than he thinks.
It is bad | if you are silent,
men call you a born coward,
and perhaps they tell the truth;
fame is seldom safe,
unless wide renown is won;
on the day after | send him to his death,
let him pay the price of his lies.
Then fourth I advise you, | if you find
a wily witch on your road,
it is better to go on | than to be her guest,
though night closes fast around you.
The sons of men | need eyes that see
when they fight in fierce battle;
evil witches often | sit by the way,
who blunt blade and courage.
Then fifth I advise you, | though you see
fair maidens sitting on benches,
let the silver of kinship | not rob you of sleep,
and beware of kissing women.
Then sixth I advise you, | if men quarrel,
and ale-talk rises to anger,
have no words | with a drunken warrior,
for wine steals many men's wits.
Brawls and ale | have very often been
an ill to many a man,
death for some, | and sorrow for some;
very many are the woes of men.
Then seventh I advise you, | if you seek battle
with a foe who is full of might;
it is better to fight | than to burn alive
in the hall of the rich hero.
Then eighth I advise you | to shun evil,
and beware of lying words;
do not take a maid, | nor a man's wife,
nor lure them on to lust.
Then ninth I advise you: | give burial
if you find a fallen corpse,
dead of sickness, | or dead in the sea,
or dead of weapons' wounds.
You shall give a bath | to those who are corpses,
and wash their hands and head;
wipe them and comb them, | before they go in the coffin,
and pray that they sleep in peace.
Then tenth I advise you | never to trust
the word of the race of wolves,
(if you brought his brother to death,
or you felled his father;)
often there is a wolf | in a son,
though he gladly takes gold.
Battle and hate | and harm, I think,
very seldom fall asleep;
wits and weapons | the warrior needs
if he would be the boldest of men.
Then eleventh I advise you | to shun anger,
and false treachery with your friends;
the leader's life | shall not be long,
for great are the foes he faces.
Long ago Sigurth | sought out Gjuki,
the young Volsung, | victor in battles;
he put full trust | in the two brothers,
with mighty oaths | sworn among them.
They gave him a maid | and many jewels,
Guthrun the young, | the daughter of Gjuki;
they drank and talked | for many a day,
Sigurth the young | and Gjuki's sons.
After that they went | to woo Brynhild,
and Sigurth rode | along with them,
the young Volsung, | valiant in battle;
he would have had her himself | if he had seen it all.
The southern hero | let his naked sword,
brightly flashing, | lie between them;
(nor would he come | to kiss the maid;)
the Hunnish king | never held in his arms
the maiden he gave | to Gjuki's sons.
She had known no ill | in all her life,
and of the sorrows of men | she knew nothing;
she bore no blame, | nor dreamed she would bear it,
but cruel were the fates | that came among them.
Alone she sat | at the end of the day,
and in open words | she spoke her heart:
"I shall have Sigurth, | the young hero,
even though he die | within my arms.
"I have spoken the word; | soon I shall regret it;
his wife is Guthrun, | and I am Gunnar's;
evil Norns set for me | long desire."
Often she went | with a grieving heart
onto the glacier's ice | in the evening,
when Guthrun had gone | to her bed,
and Sigurth laid | the bedclothes about her.
"(Now Gjuki's child | goes to her lover,)
and the Hunnish king | is happy with his wife;
I am joyless | and for ever without a mate,
till cries burst out | from my heavy heart."
In her anger she roused | herself to battle:
"Gunnar, now | you must lose
my lands | and me myself;
I shall never have joy | with the hero.
"I shall go back | to where I first lived,
among the kinsmen | of my own race,
to wait there, sleeping | my life away,
if you do not dare | to bring about Sigurth's death,
(and will not be | the best of heroes.)
"The son shall go | from here with his father,
and do not let | the wolf-cub live long;
the vengeance-price | is lighter to pay
after the deed | if the son is dead."
Gunnar was sad, | and bowed with grief,
deep in thought | the whole day through;
yet it was always hidden | from his heart
what deed he should find | most fitting,
(or what would be | the best thing for him,
or whether he should seek | to kill the Volsung,
for he loved Sigurth | with a mighty longing.)
He pondered much | for many an hour;
never before | had such a wonder been known,
that a queen should leave | her kingdom so;
then he called Hogni | into counsel,
(for he held him | in the truest trust.)
"Brynhild is more | to me than all,
Buthli's child, | the best of women;
I would sooner lose | my very life
than give up the love | of that maid.
"Will you betray | the hero for wealth?
It would be good to have | the gold of the Rhine,
and to hold all the hoard | in peace,
and so to win | good fortune by waiting."
Hogni's words | were few:
"It is not fitting | for us to do this,
to cut with swords | the oaths we swore,
the oaths we swore | and all our vows.
"We know no mightier | men on earth
so long as we four | rule over the people,
and while the Hunnish | hero lives,
nor does the world hold | a higher kinship.
"If we five | soon beget sons,
our race, I think, | will grow great;
I see well | where these paths lead from;
Brynhild's hate | is far too bitter."
Gunnar said:
"We must rouse | Gotthorm to anger,
our younger brother, | blind in his rashness;
he had no part | in the oaths we swore,
the oaths we swore | and all our vows."
It was easy to rouse | the reckless one.
The sword stood | in Sigurth's heart.
In vengeance the hero | rose in the hall,
and hurled his sword | at the bold slayer;
at Gotthorm flew | the glittering steel
of Gram with full force | from the hand of the king.
The enemy fell, | cut in two;
hands and head | sank forward,
and legs and feet | fell backward.
Guthrun had slept | softly in her bed,
safe from care | at Sigurth's side;
she woke to find | her joy had fled;
she lay in the blood | of the friend of Freyr.
So hard she struck | her hands together
that the hero rose up, | iron-hearted:
"Do not weep, Guthrun, | such bitter tears,
bride so young, | for your brothers live.
"My son, I think, | is still too young;
he cannot flee | from the home of his enemies;
fearful and deadly | is the plan they found,
the new counsel | they have now heeded.
"No son will ride, | though you have seven,
to the Thing as the son | of their sister rides;
I see well | who has done this evil;
on Brynhild alone | lies the blame for all.
"The maiden loved me | above all men,
yet I was never | found false to Gunnar;
I kept the oaths | and the kinship I swore;
no one can call me | his queen's lover.
She sank in a swoon | when Sigurth died;
so hard she struck | her hands together
that all the cups | in the cupboard rang,
and the geese cried loud | in the courtyard.
Then Brynhild, daughter | of Buthli, laughed,
only once, | with all her heart,
when, as she lay, | she heard so loud
the bitter wail | of Gjuki's daughter.
Then Gunnar, monarch | of men, spoke out:
"You do not laugh, | you lover of hate,
in gladness there, | or for anything good;
why is your face | so white in hue,
mother of evil? | You are doomed to die.
"You would have been | a worthier woman
if we had killed Atli | before your eyes;
if you had seen | your brother's bleeding body
and the bloody wounds | that you would have to bind."
Brynhild said:
"No one mocks you, Gunnar! | you have fought mightily,
but Atli pays | little heed to your hatred;
he will live longer | than you, I think,
and will always remain | the greater in might.
"I tell you, | and you know it yourself,
that you shaped | all these ills early;
I knew no bonds, | and bore no sorrow,
and I had wealth | in my brother's home.
"I never sought | to have a husband
before the Gjukungs | came to our land;
three were the kings | who came on horses;
there was never | any need of their journey.
"I pledged myself | to the great hero
who sat decked in gold | on Grani's back;
the light of his eyes | was not like yours,
(nor are you like him | in form and face,)
though both of you | seemed to be kingly.
"And so Atli | said to me
that I should have | no share in our wealth,
in gold or lands, | if I did not give my hand;
(worse still, | I should give up the wealth,)
the gold that he | gave me in my childhood,
(the wealth I had | from him in my youth.)
"Often in my mind | I pondered long
whether I should still fight, | and cut down warriors,
brave in my mail-coat, | defying my brother;
that would be known | far and wide in the world,
and would bring sorrow | to many a man.
"But at last | I let the bond be made,
for I longed more | to have the hoard,
the rings that the son | of Sigmund won;
I never sought | any other man's treasure.
"One alone | of all I loved,
and I never had | a changing heart;
in the end | Atli shall know it all,
when he hears I have gone | from here on the death-road."
"Never should a wife | of fickle will
yield herself yet | to another man.
So vengeance shall come | for all my ills."
Up rose Gunnar, | the people's ruler,
and flung his arms | round her neck so fair;
and all who came, | of every kind,
tried to hold her back | with all their hearts.
But she threw back | all those who came,
and would not let them hold her | from the long road;
then he called Hogni | into counsel:
"Our need of wisdom | is now very great.
"Let the warriors here | come forward in the hall,
yours and mine, | for the need is great,
in case they can hold | the queen from death,
till her fearful thoughts | fade with time."
(Hogni's words | were few:)
"Now you shall not hold her | from the long road,
so that she may never | be born again!
Foul she came | out of her mother,
and she was born | for wicked deeds,
(to bring sorrow | to many a man.)"
Gunnar turned gloomily | from the speaker,
for the jewel-bearer | was dividing her gems;
her eyes were gazing | on all her wealth,
on the bondwomen killed | and the slaughtered slaves.
She put on her mail-coat of gold, | and grim
was her heart before the point | of her sword pierced it;
at last she laid | her head on the pillow,
and, wounded, | thought over her plan.
"I wish my women | to come here,
those who are eager | to get gold from me;
necklaces finely made | I shall give to each,
and cloth as well, | and bright garments."
All were silent | when she said this,
and all together | made answer:
"Enough have been killed; | we want to live;
your women shall not | win honour this way."
Long the woman, | dressed in linen, pondered,
young she was, | and weighed her words:
"For my sake now | none who is unwilling
or loath to die | shall lay down her life.
"But few gems | to gleam on your limbs
will you find | when you set out
to follow me, | nor any of Menja's wealth.
"Sit now, Gunnar! | for I shall speak
of your bride so fair | and so eager to die;
you have not brought | your ship home to harbour,
although I have now | lost my life.
"You will make amends to Guthrun | sooner than you think,
though the wise maiden | mourns in sadness,
she who lives with the king, | for her dead husband.
"Then the mother | shall bear a maid;
brighter by far | than the fairest day
shall Svanhild be, | or the beams of the sun.
"You give Guthrun | a noble husband,
yet she will bring woe | to many a warrior;
she does not count herself | happily wedded;
Atli shall come | here to seek her,
(Buthli's son, | and my brother.)
"I remember well | how you treated me
when you betrayed me | with treacherous tricks;
my joy was lost | for as long as I lived.
"You would gladly win | Oddrun as your wife,
but Atli withholds | this from you;
yet you two shall love | in secret meetings;
she shall hold you dear, | as I would have done
if a kindly fate | had fallen to us.
"Atli shall bring | evil upon you,
when he casts you down | into the den of snakes.
"But soon after that | Atli too
shall lose his life, | I think, as you will,
(lose his fortune | and the lives of his sons;)
Guthrun, grim of heart, | shall destroy him
in his bed | with the biting blade.
"It would better suit | your fair sister
to follow her first husband | into death,
if good counsel | were given her,
or she had a heart | like mine.
"Slowly I speak, | but for my sake
she shall not lose | her life, I think;
she shall wander over | the tossing waves,
to where Jonak rules | his father's realm.
"She shall soon | bear him sons,
heirs as well | to Jonak's wealth;
but Svanhild is sent | far away,
the child she bore | to brave Sigurth.
"Bikki's word | shall be her death,
for dreadful is the wrath | of Jormunrek;
so all of Sigurth's race | is killed,
and Guthrun's grief | grows greater.
"Yet one favour | I ask of you,
the last favour | of my life it is:
let the pyre be built | so broad in the field
that there will be ample | room for us all,
(for us who are killed | with Sigurth.)
"Beside the Hunnish | hero there
slaves shall burn, | splendidly adorned,
two at his head | and two at his feet,
a brace of hounds | and a pair of hawks,
for so shall all | be fittingly done.
"Let there lie | between us once more
the steel so sharp, | as it lay
when we were both | in one bed,
and people called us | husband and wife.
"The door of the hall | shall not strike the heel
of the fair hero | with flashing rings,
if my following | goes with him from here;
our journey out | shall be no poor one.
"Five bondwomen | shall follow him,
and eight of my slaves, | well-born they are,
children along with me, | and mine they were
as gifts that Buthli | gave his daughter.

skm-p1.s: Freyr, the son of Njorth, had sat one day in Hlithskjolf and looked out over all the worlds. He looked into Jotunheim and saw a beautiful maiden there, walking from her father's house to her bower. At once he was struck with a great love-sickness. Freyr's servant was called Skirnir; Njorth asked him to get Freyr to speak. He said:

l: "Go now, Skirnir, | and try to get
my son to speak,
and win an answer, | for whom the wise one
is so greatly moved."
Skirnir said:
"Harsh words I now | expect from your son,
if I try to get him to speak,
and win an answer, | for whom the wise one
is so greatly moved."
Skirnir said:
"Tell me, please, Freyr, | foremost of the gods,
for now I would like to know:
why do you sit here | in the wide halls,
all day long, my prince, alone?"
Freyr said:
"How shall I tell you, | young hero,
of all my great grief?
Though every day | the elfbeam dawns,
it never lights my longing."
Skirnir said:
"Your longings, I think, | are not so great
that you cannot tell them to me;
since in days gone by | we were young together,
we two might well trust each other."
Freyr said:
"From Gymir's house | I saw come out
a maiden dear to me;
her arms glittered, | and from their gleam
all the sea and sky shone.
"Dearer to me | than in days of old
any maiden ever was to a man;
but none of the gods | or elves will grant
that we two should be together."
Skirnir said:
"Then give me the horse | that goes through the dark
and the magic flickering flames,
and the sword as well | that fights by itself
against the grim giants."
Freyr said:
"I will give you the horse | that goes through the dark
and the magic flickering flames,
and the sword as well | that will fight by itself
if a worthy hero wields it."
Skirnir said to the horse:
"It is dark outside, | and I think it is time
to travel through the wild fells,
(to travel through the giants' fastness;)
we shall both come back, | or the terrible giant
will take us both together."

skm-p2.s: Skirnir rode into Jotunheim to Gymir's house. Fierce dogs were tied up in front of the gate of the fence that surrounded Gerth's hall. He rode to where a herdsman sat on a hill, and said:

l: "Tell me, herdsman, | sitting on the hill
and watching all the ways,
how can I win | a word with the maiden
past these hounds of Gymir?"
The herdsman said:
"Are you doomed to die | or already dead,
you horseman riding here?
Barred from speech | you shall always be
with Gymir's good daughter."
Skirnir said:
"Boldness is better | than any complaint
for one whose feet must travel;
my life has been doomed | to a destined day,
and the span of my life fixed to it."
Gerth said:
"What is that noise | that I now hear
so loud inside our house?
The ground shakes, | and Gymir's home
trembles around me too."
The Serving-Maid said:
"A man stands outside | who has leapt from his mount
and lets his horse loose to graze;"
Gerth said:
"Ask the man to come in | and drink good mead
here inside our hall;
though this I fear, | that out there stands
the killer of my brother.
"Are you one of the elves | or the offspring of gods,
or one of the wise Wanes?
How did you come alone | through the leaping flame
so as to look upon our home?"
Skirnir said:
"I am not one of the elves, | nor the offspring of gods,
nor one of the wise Wanes;
though I came alone | through the leaping flame
so as to look upon your home.
"Eleven apples, | all of gold,
I will give you here, Gerth,
to buy your pledge | that Freyr shall be
held dearest of all by you."
Gerth said:
"I will never take | at any man's wish
these eleven apples;
nor shall Freyr and I | share one home
as long as we two live."
Skirnir said:
"Then I bring you | the ring that was burned
long ago with Othin's son;
eight of equal weight | drop from it
on every ninth night."
Gerth said:
"I do not want the ring, | though it was burned
long ago with Othin's son;
in Gymir's home | there is no lack of gold
in the wealth my father commands."
Skirnir said:
"Do you see, maiden, | this keen, bright sword
that I hold here in my hand?
I shall cut your head | from your neck at once
if you will not do my will."
Gerth said:
"For no man's sake | will I ever allow
myself to be moved by force;
but Gymir, I think, | will gladly seek
to fight if he finds you here."
Skirnir said:
"Do you see, maiden, | this keen, bright sword
that I hold here in my hand?
Before its blade | the old giant bends;
your father is doomed to die.
"I strike you, maiden, | with my magic staff,
to tame you to work my will;
you shall go to a place | where never again
the sons of men shall see you.
"On the eagle's hill | you shall sit for ever
and gaze at the gates of Hel;
more loathsome to you | than the light-hued snake
to men shall your food become.
"A fearful sight, | if you come out,
Hrimnir will stand and stare,
(men will marvel at you;)
you shall grow more famous | than the watchman of the gods!
Peer out, then, from your prison.
"Rage and longing, | fetters and wrath,
tears and torment are yours;
where you sit down | my doom is on you
of a heavy heart
and double sorrow.
"In the giants' home | vile things shall harm you
each day with evil deeds;
you shall get grief | instead of gladness,
and sorrow to suffer with tears.
"With three-headed giants | you shall live for ever,
or never know a husband;
(let longing grip you, | let wasting waste you,)
be like the thistle | that was thrown
into the loft and crushed there.
"I go to the wood, | and to the wet forest,
to win a magic wand;
I won a magic wand.
"Othin grows angry, | the best of the gods is angered,
Freyr shall be your enemy,
most evil maiden, | who have brought on yourself
the magic wrath of the gods.
"Take heed, frost-rulers, | hear it, giants,
sons of Suttung,
and you too, gods,
how I forbid | and how I ban
the meeting of men with the maiden,
(the joy of men with the maiden.)
"Hrimgrimnir is the giant | who shall have you
in the depths by the doors of Hel;
to the frost giants' halls | you shall go each day,
crawling and craving in vain,
(crawling and having no hope.)
"Vile wretches there | by the root of the tree
will hold out horns of filth for you;
a finer drink | you shall never find,
maiden, to meet your wish,
(maiden, to meet my wish.)
"I write you a charm | and three runes with it,
longing and madness and lust;
but what I have written | I can still unwrite
if I find a need to do so."
Gerth said:
"Be welcome instead, | and with that take
the frost-cup filled with mead;
though I did not believe | that I should ever
so love one of the Wanes."
Skirnir said:
"I must know for certain | all my news
before I ride home from here:
how soon you will | arrange a meeting
with the mighty son of Njorth."
Gerth said:
"There is Barri, | which we both know well,
a fair and quiet forest;
and nine nights from now | to the son of Njorth
Gerth will there grant delight."
"Tell me, Skirnir, | before you take off the saddle
or go a step further:
what have you done | in the giants' dwelling
to gladden you or me?"
Skirnir said:
"There is Barri, | which we both know well,
a fair and quiet forest;
and nine nights from now | to the son of Njorth
Gerth will there grant delight."
Freyr said:
"One night is long, | two are longer;
how then shall I bear three?
Often a month | has seemed less to me
than half a night of desire now."
Of life and property
a fierce robber
stripped mankind;
over the roads
that he beset
no living person could pass.
He ate alone
most often,
and invited no one to his meal;
until, weary
and with failing strength,
a wandering guest
came in from the road.
In need of drink
that travel-worn man
pretended to be, and hungry:
with a trembling heart
he seemed to trust
the one who had been so evil-minded.
Food and drink
he gave to the weary one,
all with an honest heart;
he thought of God
and supplied the traveller's wants,
for he felt he was an evildoer.
The guest stood up,
he was planning evil,
he had not been kindly treated;
his sin swelled within him,
and he murdered in his sleep
his wary, cautious host.
To the God of heaven
he prayed for help
when he woke at the blow;
but the other was doomed
to take upon himself the sins
of the innocent man he had killed.
Holy angels came
from heaven above
and took his soul to themselves:
in a life of purity
it shall live for ever
with almighty God.
Riches and health
no one can command,
though all goes smoothly for him.
To many there comes
what they least expect.
No one can command his own peace of mind.
Unnar and Sævaldi
never imagined
that their happiness would fail them,
yet they were left naked,
stripped of everything,
and ran like wolves to the forest.
The power of pleasure
many have lamented.
Troubles are often caused by women;
they turn harmful,
although the mighty God
created them pure.
They were at one,
Svafud and Skarthedin,
neither could be without the other,
until they were driven to frenzy
over a woman;
she was destined to be their ruin.
Because of that fair maiden
neither of them cared
for games or joyful days;
nothing else
could they keep in mind
but that bright form.
Sorrowful to them
were the gloomy nights;
no sweet sleep could they enjoy:
but from that anguish
rose intense hatred
between the faithful friends.
Hostile deeds
are in most places
fiercely avenged.
They went to the duelling-ground
for that fair woman,
and each one met his death.
No one should harbour arrogance:
I have indeed seen
that those who follow her,
for the most part,
turn away from God.
Rich they both were,
Radey and Vebogi,
and thought only of their own well-being;
now they sit
and turn their sores
towards various hearths.
They trusted in themselves,
and thought that they alone were
above all people;
but their lot
Almighty God was pleased
to appoint otherwise.
They led a life of luxury
in many ways,
and had gold for their sport.
Now they are repaid,
so that they must walk
between frost and fire.
Your enemies
you should never trust,
although they speak fair words to you:
promise them good;
it is good to have another's injury
as a warning.
So it turned out
for Sörli the upright,
when he put himself in Vigolf's power;
he trusted him confidently,
his brother's murderer,
but he proved false.
He granted them peace
with a sincere heart;
they in return promised him gold,
and pretended to be friends
while they drank together;
but then their treachery came out.
Then afterwards,
on the second day,
when they rode in Rýgiardal,
they wounded with swords
the one who was innocent,
and let his life go out of him.
His corpse they dragged
(along a lonely path,
and cut it into pieces) into a well,
and wanted to hide it;
but the holy Lord
looked on from heaven.
His soul was summoned home
by the true God
to come into his joy;
but the evildoers
will, I think, be late
in being called from torments.
Pray to the Disir
of the Lord's words
to be kind to you in spirit:
for a week afterwards
all shall then go happily,
according to your will.
For an act of anger
that you have committed,
never atone with evil:
the one who weeps you shall
soothe with kindnesses:
that is healthy for the soul.
A man shall call
on God for good things,
on him who created mankind.
Greatly sinful is
every man
who is late in finding the Father.
One ought, we think,
to ask in all earnestness
for whatever is lacking:
he may go without everything
who asks for nothing:
few heed the needs of the silent.
Late I came,
though called early,
to the door of the supreme Judge;
that is where I long to go,
for it was promised me:
whoever craves it shall share in the feast.
Sins are the reason
that we depart in sorrow
from this world:
no one is afraid
if he does no evil:
it is good to be blameless.
Like wolves
all those seem
who have a faithless mind:
so he will prove to be
who has to walk
ways strewn with glowing embers.
Friendly counsels,
wisely framed, seven of them,
I have given you:
consider them well
and never forget them:
they are all useful to learn.
Of this I will speak:
how happy I was
in the world,
and secondly,
how the sons of men
become corpses against their will.
Pleasure and pride
deceive the sons of men
who crave after money;
shining riches
become a sorrow in the end:
riches have driven many to madness.
Steeped in joys
I seemed to men,
for I saw little of what lay before me:
our stay in this world
the Lord has created
abounding in delights.
Bowed down I sat,
long I tottered,
and greatly wished to live;
but He prevailed
who was all-powerful:
the ways of the doomed lead onward.
The cords of Hel
were tightly
bound round my sides;
I wanted to tear them,
but they were strong.
It is easy to go when free.
I alone knew
how on every side
my pains increased.
The maidens of Hel each evening
called me, to my horror,
to their home.
I saw the sun,
the true star of day,
sink in its roaring home;
but Hel's barred gates
I heard on the other side
creaking heavily.
I saw the sun
beset with blood-red beams:
(I was then fast slipping from this world)
she seemed mightier
in many ways
than she was before.
I saw the sun,
and it seemed to me
as if I saw a glorious god:
I bowed before her
for the last time
in the world of men.
I saw the sun:
she shone so brightly
that I seemed to know nothing;
but Giöll's streams
roared from the other side,
mingled much with blood.
I saw the sun
with quivering eyes,
appalled and shrinking;
for my heart
was in great part
dissolved in weakness.
I saw the sun,
seldom sadder;
I had then almost slipped from the world:
my tongue had
become like wood,
and all was cold outside me.
I saw the sun
never again
after that gloomy day;
for the mountain waters
closed over me,
and I went, called from torments.
The star of hope,
when I was born,
flew away from my breast;
high it flew,
and settled nowhere
where it might find rest.
Longer than all others
was that one night
when I lay stiff on my straw;
then is made plain
the divine word:
"Man is the same as earth."
The Creator God can
judge and know it,
(He who made heaven and earth)
how forsaken
many go from here,
although parted from kindred.
For his works
each has his reward:
happy is he who does good.
Stripped of my wealth,
I was destined for
a bed strewn with sand.
Bodily desires
often lead men astray;
