many a one has too much of them:
bath water
was of all things
the most loathsome to me.
In the Norns' seat
I sat nine days,
from there I was set on a horse:
there the giantess's sun
shone grimly
through the dripping clouds of heaven.
Outside and inside,
I seemed to pass through all
the seven lower worlds:
up and down
I looked for an easier way,
where I might have the readiest paths.
This is to be told:
what I first saw
when I came to the worlds of torment:
scorched birds,
which were souls,
flew as thick as flies.
From the west I saw
Von's dragons fly
and darken Glæval's paths:
they shook their wings;
far around me
the earth and heaven seemed to burst.
I saw the sun's hart
coming from the south,
led by two together:
his feet stood on the earth,
but his horns
reached up to heaven.
From the north I saw riding
the sons of Nidi,
seven of them in all:
from full horns
they drank the pure mead
from the heaven-god's well.
The wind was silent,
the waters stopped flowing;
then I heard a mournful sound:
for their husbands
false-faced women
were grinding earth for food.
Bloody stones
those dark women
turned sorrowfully;
bleeding hearts hung
out of their breasts,
faint with much suffering.
Many a man I saw
go wounded
on those ember-strewn paths;
their faces all seemed
to me reddened
with reeking blood.
Many men I saw
gone down to earth,
who could not have holy service;
heathen stars
stood above their heads,
painted with deadly characters.
I saw those men
who harbour much envy
at another's fortune;
bloody runes
were on their breasts,
painfully carved.
I saw men there,
many without joy;
they were all wandering astray:
this is what he earns
who is infatuated
with this world's vices.
I saw those men
who had in various ways
got hold of others' property:
in crowds they went
to Castle-covetous,
and carried burdens of lead.
I saw those men
who had robbed many
of life and property:
through the breasts
of those men passed
strong poisonous serpents.
I saw those men
who would not keep
the holy days:
their hands were
firmly nailed
on hot stones.
I saw those men
who from pride
valued themselves too highly;
their clothes
were ludicrously
wrapped in fire.
I saw those men
who had spoken many
false words about others:
Hel's ravens
miserably tore
the eyes from their heads.
All the horrors
you will not get to know
that Hel's inmates suffer.
Pleasant sins
end in painful penalties:
pain always follows pleasure.
I saw those men
who had given much
for God's laws;
pure lights were
burning brightly
above their heads.
I saw those men
who from a noble mind
gave help to the poor:
angels read
holy books
above their heads.
I saw those men
who with much fasting
had wasted their bodies:
God's angels
bowed before them:
that is the highest joy.
I saw those men
who had put food
into their mothers' mouths:
their couches were
pleasantly placed
on the rays of heaven.
Holy virgins
had washed clean
of sin the souls
of those men
who for a long time
had tormented themselves.
Lofty chariots I saw
going towards heaven;
they were on the way to God:
men drove them
who had been murdered
for no crime at all.
Almighty Father!
Greatest Son!
Holy Spirit of heaven!
I pray to you,
who created us all:
free us all from miseries.
Biugvör and Listvör
sit at Herðir's doors,
on a resounding seat;
iron gore
falls from their nostrils,
and kindles hatred among men.
Odin's wife
rows in earth's ship,
eager for pleasures;
her sails are
reefed late,
the sails that hang on the ropes of desire.
Son! I, your father,
and Solkatla's sons
alone have obtained for you
that hart's horn
which the wise Vigdvalin
carried from the grave-mound.
Here are runes
that were engraved by
Niörd's nine daughters,
Radvör the eldest,
and the youngest Kreppvör,
and their seven sisters.
How much violence
they have committed,
Svaf and Svaflogi!
They have stirred up bloodshed
and sucked wounds,
after an evil custom.
This lay,
which I have taught you,
you shall sing before the living:
the Sun-Song,
which will be seen
in many parts to be no fiction.
Here we part,
but shall meet again
on the day of men's rejoicing.
O Lord!
grant peace to the dead,
and comfort to the living.
Wild was Vingthor | when he awoke,
and found his mighty | hammer missing;
he shook his beard, | his hair was bristling,
as the son of Jorth | searched about him.
Hear now the words | that he spoke first:
"Listen, Loki, | and heed my words,
nowhere on earth | is it known to man,
nor in heaven above: | our hammer is stolen."
To Freyja's fair | dwelling they went,
hear now the words | that he spoke first:
"Will you, Freyja, | lend me your feather-dress,
so that I may | seek my hammer?"
Freyja said:
"It should be yours | though it were of bright silver,
and I would give it | though it were of gold."
Then Loki flew, | and the feather-dress whirred,
till he left behind him | the home of the gods,
and reached at last | the realm of the giants.
Thrym sat on a mound, | the giants' master,
twisting leashes of gold | for his dogs,
and he stroked and smoothed | the manes of his horses.
Thrym said:
"How is it with the gods, | how is it with the elves?
Why have you come alone | to the giants' land?"
Loki said:
"It is ill with the gods, | it is ill with the elves!
Have you hidden | Hlorrithi's hammer?"
Thrym said:
"I have hidden | Hlorrithi's hammer,
eight miles down, | deep in the earth;
and no man shall | bring it back again
unless I win Freyja | to be my wife."
Then Loki flew, | and the feather-dress whirred,
till he left behind him | the home of the giants,
and reached at last | the realm of the gods.
There in the courtyard | he met Thor:
hear now the words | that he spoke first:
"Have you found news | as well as trouble?
Tell your news now, | while still in the air;
often the sitter | forgets his story,
and he who lies down | speaks lies."
Loki said:
"Trouble I have had, | and news as well:
Thrym, king of the giants, | has your hammer,
and no man shall | bring it back again
unless he wins Freyja | to be his wife."
Then they went to find | Freyja the fair;
hear now the words | that he spoke first:
"Bind on, Freyja, | the bridal veil,
for we two must hurry | to the giants' home."
Freyja was furious, | and fiercely she snorted,
and the great dwelling | of the gods was shaken,
and the mighty | Brisings' necklace burst:
"Most lustful indeed | I should look to all
if I travelled with you | to the giants' home."
Then the gods | met together,
and the goddesses came | and held council,
and the far-famed ones | sought a plan,
how they might win | Hlorrithi's hammer.
Then Heimdall spoke, | whitest of the gods,
like the Wanes he knew | the future well:
"Let us bind on Thor | the bridal veil,
let him wear the mighty | Brisings' necklace;
"Let keys rattle | around him,
and a woman's dress | hang down to his knees;
with broad gems | on his breast,
and a pretty cap | to crown his head."
Then Thor the mighty | made his answer:
"The gods would call me | unmanly
if I let the bridal veil | be bound on me."
Then Loki spoke, | the son of Laufey:
"Be silent, Thor, | and do not speak so;
or the giants | will live in Asgarth
if your hammer is not | brought home to you."
Then they bound on Thor | the bridal veil,
and next the mighty | Brisings' necklace.
They let keys rattle | around him,
and a woman's dress | hung down to his knees;
with broad gems | on his breast,
and a pretty cap | to crown his head.
Then Loki spoke, | the son of Laufey:
"As your maidservant | I shall go there with you;
we two shall hurry | to the giants' home."
Then the goats were driven | home to the hall,
they pulled at the halters, | they were swift to run;
the mountains burst, | the earth burned with fire,
and Othin's son | made for Jotunheim.
Then Thrym spoke loudly, | the giants' leader:
"Stir yourselves, giants, | put straw on the benches;
now they are bringing Freyja | to be my bride,
the daughter of Njorth | from Noatun.
"Gold-horned cattle | go to my stables,
jet-black oxen, | the giant's joy;
many are my gems, | and many my jewels,
Freyja alone | I lacked, it seems to me."
It had early | come to evening,
and the beer was brought out | for the giants;
Thor alone ate an ox, | and eight salmon,
and all the delicacies | that were set out for the women;
and Sif's husband drank | three casks of mead.
Then Thrym spoke loudly, | the giants' leader:
"Who ever saw a bride | bite more keenly?
I never saw a bride | with a broader bite,
nor a maiden who drank | more mead than this!"
Close by sat | the wise serving-maid,
and well she answered | the giant's words:
"Freyja has fasted | from food for eight nights,
so hot was her longing | for Jotunheim."
Thrym looked under the veil, | for he longed to kiss,
but he leaped back | the length of the hall:
"Why are Freyja's eyes | so terrible?
Fire, it seems to me, | burns from her eyes."
Close by sat | the wise serving-maid,
and well she answered | the giant's words:
"Freyja has found | no sleep for eight nights,
so hot was her longing | for Jotunheim."
Soon came the giant's | luckless sister,
who was not afraid to ask | for the bridal fee:
"Take from your hands | the rings of red gold,
if you would win | my willing love,
(my willing love | and glad welcome.)"
Then Thrym spoke loudly, | the giants' leader:
"Bring in the hammer | to hallow the bride;
on the maiden's knees | let Mjollnir lie,
so that the hand of Vor | may bless us both."
The heart in the breast | of Hlorrithi laughed
when the hard-souled one | saw his hammer;
first he killed Thrym, | the king of the giants,
then he struck down | all the giants' people.
He killed the giant's | old sister,
she who had begged | for the bridal fee;
a blow she got | in place of a shilling,
and for many rings | the might of the hammer.
And so Othin's son | got his hammer.

vkv-p1.s: There was a king in Sweden called Nithuth. He had two sons and one daughter; her name was Bothvild. There were three brothers, sons of a king of the Finns: one was called Slagfith, another Egil, the third Völund. They travelled on snowshoes and hunted wild animals. They came to Ulfdalir and built themselves a house there; there was a lake there called Ulfsjar. Early one morning they found three women on the shore of the lake, spinning flax. Beside them lay their swan-garments, for they were Valkyries. Two of them were daughters of King Hlothver, Hlathguth the Swan-White and Hervor the All-Wise, and the third was Olrun, daughter of Kjar from Valland. The brothers brought them home to their hall. Egil took Olrun, Slagfith took Swan-White, and Völund All-Wise. They lived there for seven winters; but then the women flew away to seek out battles, and did not come back. Then Egil set out on his snowshoes to follow Olrun, and Slagfith followed Swan-White, but Völund stayed in Ulfdalir. He was a most skilful man, as people know from old tales. King Nithuth had him taken by force, as the poem here tells.

l: Maids from the south | flew through Myrkvidr,
fair and young, | to follow their fate;
on the shore of the sea | they sat down to rest,
the maids of the south, | and they spun flax.
Hlathguth and Hervor, | Hlothver's children,
and Olrun the Wise | was Kjar's daughter.
One then took Egil | in her arms
to her white bosom, | the fair woman.
Swan-White was second, | she wore swan-feathers,
and the third of the sisters | threw her arms
next round Völund's | neck so white.
There they stayed | for seven winters,
in the eighth at last | their longing came again,
(and in the ninth | need parted them).
The maidens yearned | for the murky wood,
the fair young maids, | to follow their fate.
Völund came home | from his hunting,
from a weary road, | the weather-wise bowman,
Slagfith and Egil | found the hall empty,
out and in they went, | searching everywhere.
East went Egil | after Olrun,
and Slagfith south | to seek Swan-White;
Völund alone | remained in Ulfdalir,
He worked red gold | with the fairest gems,
and strung rings | on ropes of bast;
so he waited long | for his wife,
in case the fair one | might come home to him.
Nithuth learned this, | the lord of the Njars,
that Völund alone | remained in Ulfdalir;
by night his men went, | their mail-coats were studded,
their shields shone | in the waning moonlight.
From their saddles they made | for the gable wall,
and in they went | at the end of the hall;
there they saw rings | on ropes of bast,
seven hundred | the hero had.
They took them off, | but left them all
except one alone, | which they carried away.
Völund came home | from his hunting,
from a weary road, | the weather-wise bowman;
he meant to roast | a brown bear's flesh on the fire;
soon the wood, so dry, | was burning well,
(the wind-dried wood | that was Völund's).
He rested on the bearskin, | and counted the rings,
the master of elves, | but one he missed;
he thought that Hlothver's | daughter had it,
and the all-wise maid | had come back again.
He sat so long | that he fell asleep,
and his waking | was empty of gladness;
he saw heavy chains | on his hands,
and fetters bound | his feet together.
Völund said:
"What men are they | who have laid on me
ropes of bast | to bind me now?"
Then Nithuth called, | the lord of the Njars:
"How did you get, Völund, | greatest of elves,
these treasures of ours | in Ulfdalir?"
Völund said:
"The gold was not | on Grani's way,
far, it seems to me, is our land | from the hills of the Rhine;
I remember that we had | more treasures
when we were happy | together at home."
Outside stood the wise | wife of Nithuth,
and in she came | from the end of the hall;
she stood on the floor, | and softly spoke:
"He does not look kind, | who comes from the wood."

vkv-p2.s: King Nithuth gave his daughter Bothvild the gold ring that he had taken from the bast rope in Völund's house, and he himself wore the sword that had been Völund's. The queen said:

l: "The glow of his eyes | is like gleaming snakes,
he gnashes his teeth | if he is now shown
the sword, or sees | Bothvild's ring;
let them at once cut | the sinews of his strength,
and then set him | in Sævarstath."

vkv-p3.s: So it was done: the sinews in his knee-joints were cut, and he was put on an island near the mainland, called Sævarstath. There he forged all kinds of precious things for the king. No one dared to go to him except the king himself. Völund said:

l: "At Nithuth's belt | gleams the sword
that I sharpened keen | with my most skilful craft,
(and hardened the steel | with my highest skill;)
the bright blade is carried | far away for ever,
(nor shall I see it | carried back to my smithy;)
now Bothvild gets | the golden ring
(that was once my bride's, | it shall never be well.)"
He sat, and did not sleep, | and struck with his hammer,
quickly he made | wonders for Nithuth;
two boys came | to look in at his door,
Nithuth's sons, | into Sævarstath.
They came to the chest, | and they asked for the keys,
the evil was open | when they looked in;
to the boys it seemed | that they saw gems,
gold in plenty | and precious stones.
Völund said:
"Come alone, | come the next day,
gold shall then | be given to you both;
do not tell the maids | or the men of the hall,
tell no one | that you have sought me."
Early brother | called to brother:
"Let us go quickly | to see the rings."
They came to the chest, | and they asked for the keys,
the evil was open | when they looked in;
he struck off their heads, | and hid their feet
under the sooty | straps of the bellows.
Their skulls, once hidden | by their hair, he took,
set them in silver | and sent them to Nithuth;
from their eyes he made | gems most fair,
to Nithuth's wife, | so wise, he gave them.
And from the teeth | of the two he made
a brooch for the breast, | and sent it to Bothvild;
Bothvild then boasted of her ring,
....... | "I have broken the ring,
I dare not tell it | except to you."
Völund said:
"I shall mend the break | in the gold so well
that your father shall find it | fairer than ever,
and your mother shall think it | much better,
and you no worse | than it ever was."
He brought beer, | he was the better in cunning,
until in her seat | she soon fell asleep.
Völund said:
"Now I have vengeance | for all my hurts,
except one alone, | on the evil woman."
Völund said: "If only | the sinews were well
that Nithuth's men | maimed in my feet."
Laughing Völund | rose into the air,
weeping Bothvild | went from the island,
for her lover's flight | and her father's anger.
Outside stood the wise | wife of Nithuth,
and in she came | from the end of the hall;
but he sat wearily | by the wall:
"Are you awake, Nithuth, | lord of the Njars?"
Nithuth said:
"I am always awake, | and ever joyless,
little I sleep | since my sons were killed;
cold is my head, | cold was your advice,
one thing I wish: | to speak with Völund.
"Answer me, Völund, | greatest of elves,
what happened to my boys, | who once were well?"
Völund said:
"First you shall swear | all the oaths,
by the rail of a ship, | and the rim of a shield,
by the shoulder of a horse, | and the edge of a sword,
that you will do no harm | to Völund's wife,
nor bring my bride | to her death,
though I should have a wife | whom you know well,
and I should have a child | within your hall.
"Go to the smithy | that you set up,
you will find the bellows | spattered with blood;
I struck off the heads | of both your sons,
and hid their feet | under the sooty straps.
"Their skulls, once hidden | by their hair, I took,
set them in silver | and sent them to Nithuth;
from their eyes I made | gems most fair,
to Nithuth's wife, | so wise, I gave them.
"And from the teeth | of the two I made
a brooch for the breast, | and gave it to Bothvild;
now Bothvild goes | big with child,
the only daughter | you two ever had."
Nithuth said:
"You never spoke a word | that could hurt me worse,
nor one that made me, Völund, | more bitter for vengeance;
there is no man so tall | as to take you from your horse,
nor so strong an archer | as to shoot you down,
while high in the clouds | you take your course."
Laughing Völund | rose into the air,
but Nithuth was left | sitting in sadness.
Then Nithuth spoke, | lord of the Njars:
"Get up, Thakkrath, | best of my slaves,
tell Bothvild to come, | the bright-browed maid,
so fairly adorned, | to speak with her father."
"Is it true, Bothvild, | what was told me:
were you once on the island | with Völund?"
Bothvild said:
"It is true, Nithuth, | what was told you,
I was once on the island | with Völund,
an hour of lust, | alas that it should be!
My strength was nothing | against such a man,
nor could I save myself | from his strength."
Othin said:
"Counsel me, Frigg, | for I long to travel,
and gladly would find Vafthruthnir;
in ancient wisdom | with the wise giant
I would seek to match myself."
Frigg said:
"Herjafödr I would keep | here at home,
where the gods live together;
among all the giants | I know of none
equal in might to Vafthruthnir."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods;
and I would gladly know | how Vafthruthnir now
lives in his lofty hall."
Frigg said:
"May you go safely, | come safely back,
and may the way you travel be safe!
Father of men, | let your mind be keen
when you seek to speak with the giant."
The wisdom then | of the wise giant
he went out to try;
he found the hall | of the father of Im,
and Ygg went in at once.
Othin said:
"Hail, Vafthruthnir! | I have come to your hall,
for I would gladly see you yourself;
and first I would ask | if you are wise,
or, giant, have won all wisdom."
Vafthruthnir said:
"Who is the man | who speaks to me,
here in my lofty hall?
Out of our dwelling | you shall never go,
unless you are wiser than I."
Othin said:
"Gagnrath they call me, | and thirsty I come
from a hard journey to your hall;
I look for a welcome, | for I have travelled long,
and a kind greeting, giant."
Vafthruthnir said:
"Why do you stand there | on the floor while you speak?
You shall have a seat in my hall;
then we shall soon know | whose knowledge is greater,
the guest's or the grey sage's."
Othin said:
"If a poor man reaches | the home of the rich,
let him speak wisely or be still;
for one who speaks | with the hard of heart
will always come to harm by chattering."
Vafthruthnir said:
"Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the horse | that each morning anew
draws the day for mankind?"
Othin said:
"Skinfaxi is he, | the horse who for men
draws the glittering day;
the best of horses | he seems to heroes,
and brightly his mane burns."
Vafthruthnir said:
"Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the horse | that from the East anew
brings night for the noble gods?"
Othin said:
"Hrimfaxi they call | the horse that anew
brings night for the noble gods;
each morning foam | falls from his bit,
and from it comes the dew in the valleys."
Vafthruthnir said:
"Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the river | that between the realms
of the gods and the giants runs?"
Othin said:
"Ifing is the river | that between the realms
of the gods and the giants runs;
for all time | it flows open,
there is no ice on the river."
Vafthruthnir said:
"Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the field | where they will meet in battle,
Surt and the gracious gods?"
Othin said:
"Vigrith is the field | where they will meet in battle,
Surt and the gracious gods;
a hundred miles | it measures each way,
and so its boundaries are set."
Vafthruthnir said:
"You are wise, guest! | Come to my bench,
let us speak together in our seats;
here in the hall, | guest, we shall wager
our heads upon our wisdom."
Othin said:
"First, answer me well, | if your wisdom serves,
and you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where in the earliest time | did the earth come from,
or the sky, you wise giant?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Out of Ymir's flesh | the earth was fashioned,
and the mountains were made of his bones;
the sky from the frost-cold | giant's skull,
and the ocean out of his blood."
Othin said:
"Next, answer me well, | if your wisdom serves,
and you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did the moon come from, | that travels over the world of men,
and the flaming sun?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Mundilferi is he | who begot the moon,
and fathered the flaming sun;
the round of heaven | they run each day,
to tell the time for men."
Othin said:
"Third, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did the day come from, | that travels over mankind,
or night with the waning moon?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"The father of day | is called Delling,
and the night was begotten by Nor;
the full moon and the old | were fashioned by the gods,
to tell the time for men."
Othin said:
"Fourth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did winter come from, | or the warm summer,
first among the gracious gods?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Vindsval he was | who was winter's father,
and Svosuth begot summer;"
Othin said:
"Fifth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
what giant was first | fashioned of old,
and the eldest of Ymir's kin?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Countless winters | before the earth was made
Bergelmir was born;
Thruthgelmir's son | was the strong giant,
and Aurgelmir's grandson of old."
Othin said:
"Sixth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did Aurgelmir come from | with the giants' kin,
long ago, you wise giant?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Down from Elivagar | poison dripped,
and grew until it was a giant;
and from it arose | our race of giants,
and that is why we are found so fierce."
Othin said:
"Seventh, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
how did he beget children, | the grim giant,
who never knew a giantess?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"They say that under the arms | of the giant of ice
a boy and a girl grew together;
and foot with foot | the wise one fashioned
a son who had six heads."
Othin said:
"Eighth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
what do you bear in mind | from farthest back?
For your wisdom is wide, giant!"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Countless winters | before the earth was made
Bergelmir was born;
the first thing I knew well | was when the wise giant
was carried long ago in a boat."
Othin said:
"Ninth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where does the wind come from | that travels over the waves
yet is never seen itself?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"In an eagle's shape | at the end of heaven
Hræsvelg sits, they say;
and from his wings | the wind comes forth
to move over the world of men."
Othin said:
"Tenth, answer me now, | if you know all
the fate that is fixed for the gods:
where did Njorth come from | to the kin of the gods,
(rich in temples | and shrines he rules,)
though he was never begotten of gods?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"In the home of the Wanes | the wise ones created him,
and gave him as a pledge to the gods;
at the fall of the world | he will go once more
home to the Wanes so wise."
Othin said:
"Eleventh, answer me well, | .......
What men...... | in......home
go out each day to fight?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"All the heroes | in Othin's hall
go out each day to fight;
they cut each other down, | and come from the fight
all quickly healed, to sit."
Othin said:
"Twelfth, answer me now | how you know all
of the fate that is fixed for the gods;
of the runes of the gods | and the giants' race
you do indeed tell the truth,
(and your wisdom is wide, giant!)"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Of the runes of the gods | and the giants' race
I can indeed tell the truth,
(for I have made my way to every world;)
to nine worlds I came, | to Niflhel beneath,
the home where dead men dwell."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what will live of mankind | when at last there comes
the mighty winter to men?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"In Hoddmimir's wood | they will hide themselves,
Lif and Lifthrasir, then;
the morning dews | they will have for food,
such food will men then find."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
where does the sun come from | back to the smooth sky,
when Fenrir has snatched it away?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"A bright daughter | Alfrothul bears
before Fenrir snatches her away;
her mother's paths | the maiden will tread
when the gods have gone to death."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what maidens are they, | so wise of mind,
who will travel out over the sea?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"Over Mogthrasir's hill | the maidens will pass,
and three are their throngs that come;
they will all protect | the dwellers on earth,
though they come of the giants' kin."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
who then will rule | the realm of the gods,
when the fires of Surt have sunk?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"In the gods' home Vithar | and Vali will live,
when the fires of Surt have sunk;
Mothi and Magni | will have Mjollnir
when Vingnir falls in battle."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what will bring the doom | of death to Othin,
when the gods go to destruction?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"The wolf will bring down | the father of men,
and this Vithar will avenge;
the terrible jaws | he will tear apart,
and so he will kill the wolf."
Othin said:
"Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what did Othin himself say | in the ears of his son,
before he burned on the funeral pyre?"
Vafthruthnir said:
"No man can tell | what in days of old
you said in the ears of your son;
with a doomed mouth | I have told of the fall of the gods
and my ancient tales;
with Othin in knowledge | I have now striven,
and you are always the wiser."
Eleven in number | the gods were known,
when Baldr was bowed | over the hill of death;
and Vali was swift | to avenge this,
when he soon killed | his brother's slayer.
The father of Baldr | was the heir of Bur,
Freyr's wife was Gerth, | the daughter of Gymir,
of the giants' brood, | and Aurbotha bore her;
to these as well | Thjazi was kin,
the dark-loving giant; | his daughter was Skathi.
Much have I told you, | and more I will tell;
there is much that I know; | will you hear still more?
Heith and Hrossthjof, | the children of Hrimnir.
The sibyls arose | from Vitholf's line,
from Vilmeith | all the seers come,
and the workers of charms | are Svarthofthi's children,
and from Ymir sprang | all the giants.
Much have I told you, | and more I will tell;
there is much that I know; | will you hear still more?
One there was born | in bygone days,
of the race of the gods, | and great was his might;
nine giant women, | at the world's edge,
once bore the man | so mighty in arms.
Gjolp bore him there, | Greip bore him there,
Eistla bore him, | and Eyrgjafa,
Ulfrun bore him, | and Angeyja,
Imth and Atla, | and Jarnsaxa.
Strong was he made | with the strength of earth,
with the ice-cold sea, | and the blood of swine.
One there was born, | the best of all,
and strong was he made | with the strength of earth;
the proudest is called | the kinsman of men
of all the rulers | throughout the world.
Much have I told you, | and more I will tell;
there is much that I know; | will you hear still more?
Loki fathered the wolf | with Angrbotha,
and he bore Sleipnir | to Svathilfari;
the worst of marvels | seemed the one
that sprang from the brother | of Byleist then.
Loki ate a heart, | it lay in the embers,
and half-cooked he found | the woman's heart;
Lopt was soon with child | from the woman,
and from this among men | came all the monsters.
The sea, storm-driven, | reaches for heaven itself,
over the earth it flows, | the air grows barren;
then follow the snows | and the furious winds,
for the gods are doomed, | and the end is death.
Then comes another, | greater than all,
though I never dare | to speak his name;
few are there now who | can see farther
than the moment when Othin | will meet the wolf.
I ask for a hearing | from the holy races,
from Heimdall's sons, | both high and low;
you wish, Valfather, | that I tell well
the old tales I remember | of men long ago.
I still remember | the giants of old,
who gave me bread | in days gone by;
nine worlds I knew, | the nine in the tree
with mighty roots | beneath the earth.
Long ago was the age | when Ymir lived;
there was no sea, no cool waves, | and no sand;
earth did not exist, | nor heaven above,
only a yawning gap, | and no grass anywhere.
Then Bur's sons lifted | the level land,
Mithgarth the mighty | they made there;
the sun from the south | warmed the stones of earth,
and the ground was green | with growing leeks.
The sun, the sister | of the moon, from the south
cast her right hand | over heaven's rim;
she had no knowledge | of where her home should be,
the moon did not know | what power was his.
The stars did not know | where their stations were.
Then the gods went | to their assembly-seats,
the holy ones, | and held council;
names they then gave | to noon and twilight,
morning they named, | and the waning moon,
night and evening, | to number the years.
The mighty gods | met at Ithavoll,
shrines and temples | they built up high;
they set up forges | and worked the ore,
they forged tongs | and fashioned tools.
At peace in their dwellings | they played at tables,
the gods then knew | no lack of gold,
until three giant-maids | came up there,
huge in might, | out of Jotunheim.
Then the gods went | to their assembly-seats,
the holy ones, | and held council;
to find who should raise | the race of dwarfs
out of Brimir's blood | and the legs of Blain.
There Motsognir | was made the mightiest
of all the dwarfs, | and Durin next;
many likenesses | of men they made,
the dwarfs in the earth, | as Durin said.
Nyi and Nithi, | Northri and Suthri,
Austri and Vestri, | Althjof, Dvalin,
Nar and Nain, | Niping, Dain,
Bifur, Bofur, | Bombur, Nori,
An and Onar, | Ai, Mjothvitnir.
Vigg and Gandalf, | Vindalf, Thrain,
Thekk and Thorin, | Thror, Vit and Lit,
Nyr and Nyrath, | now I have told,
Regin and Rathsvith, | the list correctly.
Fili, Kili, Fundin, Nali,
Heptifili, Hannar, Sviur,
Frar, Hornbori, Fræg and Loni,
Aurvang, Jari, Eikinskjaldi.
The race of the dwarfs | in Dvalin's throng
down to Lofar | I must list;
they left the rocks, | and through wet lands
they sought a home | in the fields of sand.
There were Draupnir and Dolgthrasir,
Hor, Haugspori, Hlevang, Gloin,
Dori, Ori, | Duf, Andvari,
Skirfir, Virfir, | Skafith, Ai.
Alf and Yngvi, | Eikinskjaldi,
Fjalar and Frosti, | Fith and Ginnar;
so for all time | shall the tale be known,
the list of all | the forefathers of Lofar.
Then from the throng | three came forth,
from the home of the gods, | the mighty and gracious;
two without fate | they found on the land,
Ask and Embla, | empty of might.
They had no soul, | they had no sense,
no heat or motion, | no good colour;
Othin gave soul, | Hönir gave sense,
Lothur gave heat | and good colour.
An ash I know, | Yggdrasil its name,
the great tree is wet | with white water;
from there come the dews | that fall in the dales,
green by Urdarbrunnr | it grows for ever.
From there come the maidens | mighty in wisdom,
three from the dwelling | down beneath the tree;
Urth one is named, | Verthandi the next,
on the wood they carved, | and Skuld the third.
Laws they made there, | and allotted life
to the sons of men, | and set their fates.
I remember the war, | the first in the world,
when the gods with spears | had struck Gollveig,
and in the hall | of Hor had burned her,
three times burned, | and three times born,
again and again, | yet she lives for ever.
Heith they named her | who came to their home,
the far-seeing witch, | wise in magic;
she bewitched the minds | that were moved by her magic,
to evil women | she was a joy.
Then the gods went | to their assembly-seats,
the holy ones, | and held council,
whether the gods | should give tribute,
or worship should belong | to all alike.
Othin hurled | his spear at the host,
then war first came | into the world;
the wall that ringed | the gods was broken,
and the field was trodden | by the warlike Wanes.
Then the gods went | to their assembly-seats,
the holy ones, | and held council,
to find who had filled | the air with poison,
or had given Oth's bride | to the giants' brood.
In swelling rage | Thor then rose up,
seldom he sits | when he hears such things,
and the oaths were broken, | the words and bonds,
the mighty pledges | made between them.
I know of the horn | of Heimdall, hidden
under the high-reaching | holy tree;
on it there pours | from Valfather's pledge
a mighty stream: | would you know yet more?
Alone I sat | when the Old One sought me,
the terror of gods, | and gazed into my eyes:
"What have you to ask? | Why do you come here?
Othin, I know | where your eye is hidden."
I know where Othin's | eye is hidden,
deep in the far-famed | well of Mimir;
mead from the pledge | of Othin each morning
Mimir drinks: | would you know yet more?
I had necklaces | and rings from Herfödr,
wise was my speech | and my magic wisdom;
widely I saw | over all the worlds.
On all sides I saw | Valkyries assemble,
ready to ride | to the ranks of the gods;
Skuld bore the shield, | and Skogul rode next,
Guth, Hild, Gondul, | and Geirskogul.
Of Herjan's maidens | you have heard the list,
Valkyries ready | to ride over the earth.
I saw for Baldr, | the bleeding god,
the son of Othin, | his destiny set:
famous and fair | in the lofty fields,
full grown in strength | the mistletoe stood.
From the branch which seemed | so slender and fair
came a harmful shaft | that Hoth would hurl;
but the brother of Baldr | was born before long,
and one night old | Othin's son fought.
He did not wash his hands, | he did not comb his hair,
till he carried to the blazing pyre | Baldr's foe.
But in Fensalir | Frigg wept bitterly
for Valhall's need: | would you know yet more?

vsp-s34.s: [Not in Bellows’ main text: these lines come from the Hauksbók version. In his note to stanza 35 he translates the Hauksbók lines on Váli and Loki’s binding: “I know that Vali his brother gnawed, / With his bowels then was Loki bound.”]

l: One I saw | bound in the wet woods,
a lover of evil, | and like Loki;
by his side Sigyn | sits, and is not glad
to see her husband: | would you know yet more?
From the east there | pours through poisoned valleys
with swords and daggers | the river Slith.
Northward a hall | in Nithavellir
of gold rose up | for Sindri's race;
and in Okolnir | another stood,
where the giant Brimir | had his beer-hall.
A hall I saw, | far from the sun,
on Nastrond it stands, | and the doors face north;
poison drips | down through the smoke-vent,
for around the walls | serpents wind.
I saw there wading | through wild rivers
treacherous men | and murderers too,
and those who do wrong | with the wives of men;
there Nithhogg sucked | the blood of the slain,
and the wolf tore men; | would you know yet more?
The old giantess | sat in Járnvidr,
in the east, and bore | the brood of Fenrir;
among these one | in a monster's shape
was soon to steal | the sun from the sky.
There he feeds full | on the flesh of the dead,
and the home of the gods | he reddens with gore;
dark grows the sun, | and in summer soon
come mighty storms: | would you know yet more?
On a hill there sat, | and struck his harp,
Eggther the joyful, | the giants' watchman;
above him the cock | in the bird-wood crowed,
fair and red | Fjalar stood.
Then to the gods | crowed Gollinkambi,
he wakes the heroes | in Othin's hall;
and beneath the earth | another crows,
the rust-red bird | at the bars of Hel.
Now Garm howls loud | before Gnipahellir,
the fetters will burst, | and the wolf run free;
much I know, | and more I can see
of the fate of the gods, | the mighty in battle.
Brothers shall fight | and kill each other,
and sisters' sons | shall stain their kinship;
it is hard on earth, | with mighty whoredom;
axe-time, sword-time, | shields are split,
wind-time, wolf-time, | before the world falls;
nor shall men ever | spare each other.
Fast move the sons | of Mim, and fate
is heard in the note | of the Gjallarhorn;
loud blows Heimdall, | the horn is aloft,
in fear all quake | who are on the roads to Hel.
Yggdrasil shakes, | and on high shiver
the ancient limbs, | and the giant is loose;
to the head of Mim | Othin gives heed,
but the kinsman of Surt | shall kill him soon.
How is it with the gods? | How is it with the elves?
All Jotunheim groans, | the gods are at council;
loud roar the dwarfs | by the doors of stone,
the masters of the rocks: | would you know yet more?
Now Garm howls loud | before Gnipahellir,
the fetters will burst, | and the wolf run free;
much I know, | and more I can see
of the fate of the gods, | the mighty in battle.
From the east comes Hrym | with shield held high;
in giant-rage | the serpent writhes;
over the waves he twists, | and the tawny eagle
gnaws corpses, screaming; | Naglfar is loose.
Over the sea from the north | there sails a ship
with the people of Hel, | at the helm stands Loki;
after the wolf | wild men follow,
and with them goes | the brother of Byleist.
Surt comes from the south | with the scourge of branches,
the sun of the battle-gods | shone from his sword;
the crags break apart, | the giant-women sink,
the dead throng the road to Hel, | and heaven splits apart.
Now comes to Hlin | yet another hurt,
when Othin goes | to fight with the wolf,
and Beli's fair slayer | seeks out Surt,
for there must fall | the joy of Frigg.

vsp-s54.s: [Refrain. Guðni Jónsson prints the refrain four times; Bellows prints it three times (his stanzas 44, 49 and 58), always in the same words:]

l: Now Garm howls loud | before Gnipahellir,
the fetters will burst, | and the wolf run free;
much I know, | and more I can see
of the fate of the gods, | the mighty in battle.
Then comes Sigfather's | mighty son,
Vithar, to fight | with the foaming wolf;
into the giant's son | he thrusts his sword
right to the heart: | his father is avenged.
Here there comes | the son of Hlothyn,
the bright snake gapes | to heaven above;
against the serpent | goes Othin's son.
In anger strikes | the guardian of earth,
out from their homes | must all men flee;
nine paces goes | the son of Fjorgyn,
and, slain by the serpent, | fearless he sinks.
The sun turns black, | earth sinks in the sea,
the hot stars | are whirled down from heaven;
fierce grows the steam | and the life-feeding flame,
till fire leaps high | about heaven itself.
Now Garm howls loud | before Gnipahellir,
the fetters will burst, | and the wolf run free;
much I know, | and more I can see
of the fate of the gods, | the mighty in battle.
Now I see | the earth anew
rise all green | from the waves again;
the waterfalls pour, | and the eagle flies,
and he catches fish | beneath the cliffs.
The gods in Ithavoll | meet together,
of the terrible girdler | of earth they talk,
and they call to mind | the mighty past,
and the ancient runes | of the Ruler of Gods.
In wondrous beauty | once again
shall the golden tables | stand amid the grass,
which the gods had owned | in the days of old,
Then fields unsown | bear ripened fruit,
all ills grow better, | and Baldr comes back;
Baldr and Hoth dwell | in Hropt's battle-hall,
and the mighty gods: | would you know yet more?
Then Hönir wins | the prophetic wand,
and the sons of the brothers | of Tveggi live
in Vindheim now: | would you know yet more?
Fairer than the sun, | a hall I see,
roofed with gold, | on Gimle it stands;
there shall the righteous | rulers dwell,
and happiness ever | they shall have there.
There comes on high, | to hold all power,
a mighty lord, | he rules all lands.
From below the dark | dragon comes forth,
Nithhogg flying | from Nithafjoll;
the bodies of men | he bears on his wings,
the bright serpent: | but now I must sink.
Sigrun said:
"You tell of battle, | and there King Hunding
was brought down | before Helgi;
there was carnage when you | avenged your kin,
and blood flowed fast | on the blade of the sword."

hh2-p6.s: Gothmund rode home with his news of the army; then Granmar's sons summoned their forces. Many kings came there; among them were Hogni, Sigrun's father, and his sons Bragi and Dag. There was a great battle, and all Granmar's sons were killed and all their allies; only Dag, Hogni's son, was spared, and he swore loyalty to the Volsungs. Sigrun went among the dead and found Hothbrodd at the point of death. She said:

l: Freyja said:
"Now bring my boar | the memory-beer,
so that all your words, | so well spoken,
he may hold in mind | on the third morning,
when Ottar and Angantyr | tell their lines."
Hyndla said:
"Go away from here, | for I want to sleep;
you get few favours | from me now;
my noble one, you leap | out in the night
as Heithrun goes | among the goats.
"To Oth you ran, | who always loved you,
and many have crawled | under your apron;
my noble one, you leap | out in the night
as Heithrun goes | among the goats."
Freyja said:
"Around the giantess | I shall raise flames,
so that you may not | get away unburned."
Hyndla said:
"I see flames burning, | the earth is on fire,
and each must pay | the price with his life;
then bring to Ottar | the draught of beer,
full of venom | for an evil fate."
Freyja said:
"Your evil words | shall work no harm,
though, giantess, bitter | are your baleful threats;
Ottar shall find | a fair drink,
if I win the favour | of all the gods."

hh2-s47.s: Sigrun made a bed ready in the hill.

l: "Here I have made | a bed for you, Helgi,
to rest you from care, | kinsman of the Ylfings;
I will make you sink | to sleep in my arms,
as I once lay | with the living king."

hh2-p5.s: Helgi then gathered a great fleet and went to Frekastein. At sea he met a dangerous storm; lightning flashed overhead and the bolts struck the ships. They saw nine Valkyries riding in the air, and recognised Sigrun among them. Then the storm died down, and they came safe and sound to land. Granmar's sons sat on a mountain as the ships sailed towards the land. Gothmund leapt on a horse and rode for news to a headland near the harbour; the Volsungs were just then lowering their sails. Then Gothmund said, as is written before in the Helgi lay:

l: "Who is the king | who captains the fleet,
and leads the warriors | to the land?"

hh2-p5.s: Sinfjotli, Sigmund's son, answered him, and that too is written.
